Depth: deep. Errata: none (the RFC has no errata). Status: Proposed Standard. Obsoletes: RFC 3107.

IDSectionQuoteIssueSeverityErratum
RA-10052.1"A Multiple Labels Capability whose length is not a multiple of four MUST be considered to be malformed."The document does not say what a receiver does with a malformed Multiple Labels Capability (ignore it, or send an OPEN Message Error NOTIFICATION; RFC 5492 defines no generic rule). It also does not say whether a Capability whose triples are all ignored (Count 0 or 1, "MUST be ignored") counts as having "sent" the Capability for the purposes of Section 2 ("Unless this Capability is sent on a given BGP session by both ... speakers") and for "AFI/SAFI x/y has not been specified in both Capabilities". The two "first one wins" rules (duplicate triples for one AFI/SAFI, duplicate copies of the Capability) are clear but easy to miss.ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata
RA-10062.2, 7"If a BGP implementation that is not conformant with the current document encodes multiple labels in the NLRI but has not sent and received the Multiple Labels Capability, a BGP implementation that does conform with the current document will likely reset the BGP session."Section 2.2 requires the receiver to take exactly one label and to ignore the S bit when the Capability is not in use, so a second label is parsed as the first 24 bits of the prefix. RFC 8538: Notification Message Support for BGP Graceful Restart

Depth: deep. Errata: none (the RFC has no errata). Status: Proposed Standard. Updates: RFC 4724.

IDSectionQuoteIssueSeverityErratum
RA-01334.1, 9"an implementation MUST support a (configurable) timer, called the "stale timer", that imposes this upper bound. / To mitigate the consequent risk that an attacker could use repeated session resets to prevent stale routes from ever being deleted, we make the stale timer mandatory"Security gap: With the N bit exchanged, stale routes are no longer deleted on consecutive restarts, and Section 9 relies on the stale timer to bound their lifetime. The text does not say when the stale timer starts or whether a further session termination restarts it. If each termination (or each new session) restarts it, repeated resets keep stale routes indefinitely, which is exactly the risk Section 9 claims to mitigate. The RFC 4724 Restart Time interacts in the same way.errornone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below
RA-01344"When a BGP speaker resets its session due to a HOLDTIME expiry, it should generate the relevant BGP NOTIFICATION message as mentioned in [RFC4271] but subsequently MUST follow the rules for the Receiving Speaker"The sentence is not conditioned on the N bit having been exchanged, unlike the preceding paragraph. Read literally, it extends Graceful Restart helper behaviour to hold-timer expiry on every GR session, including peers without N, for which RFC 4724 treats any NOTIFICATION as ending GR. It is also not said whether N negotiated on the previous session applies to a NOTIFICATION sent during OpenSent / OpenConfirm of the next one.ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata

Proposed erratum RA-0133 (RFC 8538, Section 4.1, 9; type: Technical):

Original Text
-------------
   To put an upper bound on the amount of time a router retains the
   stale routes, an implementation MUST support a (configurable)
   timer, called the "stale timer", that imposes this upper bound.

Corrected Text
--------------
   To put an upper bound on the amount of time a router retains the
   stale routes, an implementation MUST support a (configurable)
   timer, called the "stale timer", that imposes this upper bound.
   The stale timer is started when routes from the peer are first
   marked stale and is not restarted by subsequent session
   terminations while those routes remain stale.

Notes
-----
   Section 9 states the stale timer prevents an attacker from
   keeping stale routes alive with repeated resets, but nothing in
   Section 4.1 prevents the timer from being restarted on each
   reset.

RFC 8654: Extended Message Support for BGP

Depth: deep. Errata: none (the RFC has no errata). Status: Proposed Standard. Updates: RFC 4271.

IDSectionQuoteIssueSeverityErratum
RA-01354"the speaker SHOULD try to reduce the outgoing message size by removing attributes eligible under the "attribute discard" approach of [RFC7606]."RFC 7606 defines "attribute discard" as an error-handling action for specific malformed attributes, not a class of well-formed attributes that may be dropped for size; which attributes are "eligible" when they are well-formed is not defined (RFC 7606 names it only for a few, such as ATOMIC_AGGREGATE and AGGREGATOR). Dropping a well-formed transitive attribute also changes what downstream ASes receive, which Section 8 notes as an attack vector but does not bound.ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below
RA-01364, 5"A BGP speaker MAY send BGP Extended Messages to a peer only if the BGP Extended Message Capability was received from that peer."Sending depends only on the peer's advertisement and receiving only on one's own, so the limit can differ per direction. Section 5 bounds NOTIFICATIONs to 4096 octets toward a peer without the capability but does not say whether the data field of a NOTIFICATION reporting an oversize message (Bad Message Length, RFC 4271 6.1) is truncated, nor whether ROUTE-REFRESH and other non-UPDATE messages follow the same rule.ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata

Proposed erratum RA-0135 (RFC 8654, Section 4; type: Technical):

Original Text
-------------
   the speaker SHOULD try to reduce the outgoing message size by
   removing attributes eligible under the "attribute discard"
   approach of [RFC7606].

Corrected Text
--------------
   the speaker SHOULD try to reduce the outgoing message size by
   removing optional attributes for which [RFC7606] specifies the
   "attribute discard" approach (for example, ATOMIC_AGGREGATE and
   AGGREGATOR), as these do not affect route selection.

Notes
-----
   RFC 7606 attribute discard is a per-attribute error-handling
   rule; this section reuses it as a size-reduction rule without
   saying which well-formed attributes qualify.

RFC 8669: Segment Routing Prefix Segment Identifier Extensions for BGP

Depth: deep. Errata: 1 errata: 1 verified. Status: Proposed Standard.

IDSectionQuoteIssueSeverityErratum
RA-01374.1, 9"If multiple different prefixes are received with the same label index, all of the different prefixes MUST have their BGP Prefix-SID attribute considered to be "conflicting"."Security gap: Any speaker that can inject a prefix into the SR domain with the label index of another prefix makes both conflicting, so the victim prefix loses its SR label everywhere (falls back to a dynamic label) without any authorisation of the injected prefix. The Security Considerations address only log flooding. The rule also does not say whether locally originated prefixes take part, whether prefixes of different AFIs (IPv4 / IPv6 LU) share the index space, or how "SRGB_Start" applies when the local SRGB has several ranges (Section 3.2 allows multi-range SRGBs; the derivation L = L_I + SRGB_Start assumes one).errornone: RFC has 1 errata, none on this point
RA-01384, 5.1"A BGP speaker receiving a BGP Prefix-SID attribute from an External BGP (EBGP) neighbor residing outside the boundaries of the SR domain MUST discard the attribute unless it is configured to accept the attribute from the EBGP neighbor."The SR domain boundary is not a BGP concept, so whether a given EBGP neighbour is "outside" depends on configuration the RFC does not define; read with Section 8 ("one or more ASes"), an implementation without such configuration cannot tell, and either discards from all EBGP peers (breaking the RFC 8670 multi-AS model) or from none.ambiguitynone: RFC has 1 errata, none on this point

RFC 9012: The BGP Tunnel Encapsulation Attribute

Depth: deep. Errata: none (the RFC has no errata). Status: Proposed Standard. Obsoletes: RFC 5512, RFC 5566. Updates: RFC 5640. Updated by: RFC 9830.

IDSectionQuoteIssueSeverityErratum
RA-045713"MUST NOT occur more than once in a given Tunnel TLV: Tunnel Egress Endpoint (discussed below) ... all but the first occurrence ... MUST be disregarded. However, the Tunnel TLV containing them MUST NOT be considered to be malformed / a TLV that does not contain exactly one Tunnel Egress Endpoint sub-TLV MUST be treated as if it contained a malformed Tunnel Egress Endpoint sub-TLV."For a TLV carrying two Tunnel Egress Endpoint sub-TLVs (in the AFI/SAFIs of Section 6), the duplicate rule keeps the TLV and uses the first endpoint, while the last paragraph of the same section makes the TLV malformed, which (by the preceding paragraph) means the entire TLV is ignored and removed before propagation. Section 3.1 ("one, and only one") supports the second reading; the list's "(discussed below)" suggests the authors meant the later rule to override, but the list sentence still says the TLV "MUST NOT be considered to be malformed". Receivers that pick different rules propagate different attributes.contradictionnone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below
RA-04583.1, 13"if the Address Family subfield has any value other than IPv4, IPv6, or the special value 0, the Tunnel Egress Endpoint sub-TLV is considered "unrecognized" (3.1) / the unrecognized sub-TLV MUST remain in the attribute. (13)"Section 13 processes a TLV with an unrecognized sub-TLV "as if the unrecognized sub-TLV had not been present" and keeps it on propagation. Applied to an endpoint of unknown address family, the TLV then has no Tunnel Egress Endpoint and, in the Section 6 AFI/SAFIs, is "treated as if it contained a malformed" one, so the whole TLV MUST be removed before propagation. The "unrecognized" category therefore yields removal, not the propagation that the term implies elsewhere in Section 13; the text does not say whether that is intended (it would block later address-family extensions from transiting older speakers).ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata
RA-045913"If a Tunnel Encapsulation attribute does not have any valid TLVs, or it does not have the transitive bit set, the "Treat-as-withdraw" procedure of [RFC7606] is applied. / that BGP speaker MUST NOT consider the attribute to be malformed.""Valid TLV" is not defined. If a TLV of an unrecognized tunnel type (or one whose only defect is that it is not feasible) is not "valid", an attribute carrying only such TLVs makes the route withdrawn, although the next paragraph says the attribute MUST NOT be considered malformed and the unrecognized TLV MUST be propagated.ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata
RA-04603.1.1, 3.1"If Route_AS does not equal Egress_AS, then the Tunnel Egress Endpoint sub-TLV is considered not to be valid. ... then the Tunnel Egress Endpoint sub-TLV is considered to be "malformed"."Section 3.1 lists the AS check as a "malformed" condition, and the configured-set variant says "malformed", but the basic check says only "not to be valid", a state with no defined handling in Section 13 (malformed endpoint: TLV removed; other cases: ignored and kept). Since a reachability change can flip the result (last paragraph of 3.1.1), whether the TLV is removed from the propagated attribute or merely not used matters. In 3.1 the rule for a missing endpoint is also in lowercase ("should be treated as if it had a malformed"), while 13 states it as a MUST.ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata
RA-04619.2.2.2"the embedded label is copied into the lower 3 octets of the Virtual Network Identifier field of the encapsulation header."The VXLAN VNI and NVGRE VSID fields are themselves 3 octets (24 bits), and an MPLS label is 20 bits. "Lower 3 octets" of a 3-octet field does not say whether the 20-bit label is right-aligned (low-order 20 bits) or whether the full 3-octet NLRI label field (as RFC 8365 5.1.3 uses it to carry a 24-bit VNI) is copied.ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata

Proposed erratum RA-0457 (RFC 9012, Section 13; type: Technical):

Original Text
-------------
   The following sub-TLVs defined in this document MUST NOT occur
   more than once in a given Tunnel TLV: Tunnel Egress Endpoint
   (discussed below), Encapsulation, DS, UDP Destination Port,
   Embedded Label Handling, MPLS Label Stack, and Prefix-SID.  If a
   Tunnel TLV has more than one of any of these sub-TLVs, all but
   the first occurrence of each such sub-TLV type MUST be
   disregarded.

Corrected Text
--------------
   The following sub-TLVs defined in this document MUST NOT occur
   more than once in a given Tunnel TLV: Encapsulation, DS, UDP
   Destination Port, Embedded Label Handling, MPLS Label Stack, and
   Prefix-SID.  If a Tunnel TLV has more than one of any of these
   sub-TLVs, all but the first occurrence of each such sub-TLV type
   MUST be disregarded.  (The Tunnel Egress Endpoint sub-TLV is
   handled as described below.)

Notes
-----
   The correction assumes the exactly-one rule (Section 3.1 and the
   last paragraph of Section 13) is intended.

RA-04643.2.1 vs RFC 4271 9, RFC 7606"When parsing a message, an unknown Attribute Type Code or a length that suggests that the attribute is longer than the remaining message is treated as a malformed message, and the "treat-as-withdraw" approach is used as per [RFC7606]."Under RFC 4271 (Sections 5 and 9) an unrecognized optional attribute is not an error: an optional transitive one is propagated with the Partial bit and an optional non-transitive one is ignored. One cannot contain the other. Moreover 3.2.1.5 says the Traversal TLV means an MPLS label stack with swapping/stacking is used, whereas 7.7 signals NSH (bit 0) over MPLS transport, so it is unclear which of the two is meant to signal RFC 8596 encapsulation.contradictionnone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below
RA-04663.2.1, 3.2.1.2, 3.2.1.3"Each Hop TLV contains an SI value and a sequence of one or more SFT TLVs. (3.2.1) / The SFT Sub-TLV MAY be included in the list of Sub-TLVs of the Hop TLV. ... A hop without an SFT Sub-TLV has no SF to select (Section 5 step 3), but whether it is malformed is not stated. 3.2.1.3 also says "Hop Sub-TLV" where the SFT Sub-TLV is meant, and the document alternates between "SFT TLV" (3.2.1, 5, IANA Table 1) and "SFT Sub-TLV".ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata
RA-04678.7"[SI = 250, SFT = 44, RD = 192.0.2.4/5], / In this case, the SPI is 23, which indicates that this is a loop or branch, i.e., the next hop is on the same SFP."In the SFIR list of Section 8, RD 192.0.2.4/5 is advertised with SFT 43; SFT 44 at SFF4 is 192.0.2.4/6. Type 41 and 44"). RA-04688.9.4"RD = 192.0.2.3/11, SFT = 44 (SFIR list) / [SI = 255, SFT = 44, RD = 192.0.2.4/11], (SFP30, SFP31, SFP32)"Figure 14 places the SFT 44 instance at SFF3 (192.0.2.3) and the SFIR list advertises it as 192.0.2.3/11; no SFIR 192.0.2.4/11 exists (there is no SFF4 in Figure 14). The forward tail-end SFPs 26-28 correctly use 192.0.2.3/11, but the three reverse SFPs use 192.0.2.4/11, so their first hop has no relevant SFIR and they cannot be used.errornone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below
RA-04694.3, 5, 6.2, 8.4, 8.10, 8.10.4"SFPR-RD: The Route Descriptor of the SFPR advertisement (4.3) / between SF Type 43 located at SF2 and SF Type 44 located at SF3. RFC 9085: Border Gateway Protocol - Link State (BGP-LS) Extensions for Segment Routing

Depth: deep. Errata: 3 errata: 3 verified. Status: Proposed Standard. Updated by: RFC 9356.

IDSectionQuoteIssueSeverityErratum
RA-04702.3.5"Length: Variable. 11 or 12 octets depending on the label or index encoding of the SID."The Range TLV value is Flags (1), Reserved (1), Range Size (2) and then the Prefix-SID TLV used as a sub-TLV, which itself is 4 octets of type/length plus 7 or 8 octets of value (2.3.1). The Range TLV Length is therefore 15 or 16 when it carries one Prefix-SID sub-TLV; 11 or 12 is the total size of the Prefix-SID sub-TLV alone. A receiver that enforces 11/12 rejects every correctly encoded Range TLV.errorerratum 7734 (Verified), technical
RA-04712.4"| SRMS Preference | SRMS Preference Sub-TLV (19) | [RFC8667] |"In RFC 8667 (Section 3.4 and its IANA section) the SRMS Preference sub-TLV of the Router Capability TLV is type 24; 19 is the SR-Algorithm sub-TLV, which the row above already lists as 19. An implementer mapping IS-IS to BGP-LS from Table 5 would copy the wrong sub-TLV.errornone: RFC has 3 errata, none on this point; proposed erratum below
RA-04722.3.1"* OSPFv3 Prefix-SID flags as defined in Section 6 of [RFC8665]."OSPFv3 Prefix-SID flags are defined in Section 6 of RFC 8666 (RFC 8665 is OSPFv2; its Section 6 is the Adjacency SID). The SID/Index/Label item a few lines below correctly cites "Section 6 of [RFC8666]" for OSPFv3.errorerratum 6666 (Verified), editorial
RA-04732.3.3, 2.5"Length: Variable. 4 or 16 octets for the IPv4 or IPv6 prefix, respectively. (2.3.3) / | Source OSPF | Prefix Source Router | [RFC9084] | (Table 7)"The Source Router Identifier length depends on the family of the router identifier, not of the prefix (RFC 7794 2.2 allows an IPv4 Source Router ID on an IPv6 prefix and vice versa; an IS-IS prefix may carry both, and the text does not say whether two TLVs may then appear). Table 7 labels the Prefix Source Router Address row "Source OSPF Router Identifier" (Table 6 and Section 2.3.3 call it "Source Router Identifier"). 2.1.2 also says "One or more entries, each of which have".editorialnone: RFC has 3 errata, none on this point
RA-04742.3.5 vs RFC 7752 3.3.3.4"A Prefix NLRI, that has been advertised with a Range TLV, is considered a normal routing prefix (i.e., prefix reachability) only when there is also an IGP metric TLV (TLV 1095) associated it."Found while reading RFC 9514 5.1, which repeats this sentence. TLV 1095 is the IGP Metric Link Attribute TLV; a Prefix NLRI carries its metric in the Prefix Metric TLV, 1155 (RFC 7752 3.3.3.4). A receiver testing for 1095 never sees it on a Prefix NLRI and treats every Range-carrying prefix as a mapping-only advertisement. (Not recorded in the RFC 9085 entry above.)errorerratum 7736 (Verified), technical

RFC 9234: Route Leak Prevention and Detection Using Roles in UPDATE and OPEN Messages

Depth: deep. Errata: none (the RFC has no errata). Status: Proposed Standard.

IDSectionQuoteIssueSeverityErratum
RA-01415"On egress from the Internet-facing AS, the OTC Attribute MUST NOT contain a value other than the Internet-facing ASN. ... Once the OTC Attribute has been set, it MUST be preserved unchanged (this also applies to an AS Confederation)."If an OTC was set inside the private-ASN or confederation part of the network (to a private ASN or a Member-AS number), the egress rules require it not to leave with that value, while the preservation rule forbids changing it. The text does not say whether the egress router must rewrite the value, drop the attribute, or not advertise the route; each choice changes leak detection downstream. The confederation paragraph has the same conflict ("an UPDATE MUST NOT contain an OTC Attribute with a value corresponding to any Member-AS Number").contradictionnone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below
RA-01424.2"For backward compatibility, if the BGP Role Capability is sent but one is not received, the BGP Speaker SHOULD ignore the absence of the BGP Role Capability and proceed with session establishment."The case of a Role Capability received but none sent (no local role configured) is not covered: whether the speaker applies Section 5 with the role implied by the peer's, or ignores the capability. Section 4 makes configuring a role only a SHOULD, so the case is ordinary.ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata
RA-01435"If a route is to be advertised to a Customer, a Peer, or an RS-Client (when the sender is an RS), and the OTC Attribute is not present, then when advertising the route, an OTC Attribute MUST be added"The parenthetical "(when the sender is an RS)" is redundant by Table 2 (a remote RS-Client implies a local RS) and can be misread as applying to the whole list. The rule is applied to routes from any source, including routes originated locally, which the text does not mention.ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata

Proposed erratum RA-0141 (RFC 9234, Section 5; type: Technical):

Original Text
-------------
   Once the OTC Attribute has been set, it MUST be preserved
   unchanged (this also applies to an AS Confederation).

Corrected Text
--------------
   Once the OTC Attribute has been set, it MUST be preserved
   unchanged (this also applies to an AS Confederation), except that
   on egress from an AS Confederation or from an Internet-facing AS
   an OTC Attribute whose value is a Member-AS Number or a private
   ASN MUST be replaced by the AS Confederation Identifier or the
   Internet-facing ASN, respectively.

Notes
-----
   Either the egress rules are exceptions to preservation, or such
   routes must not be advertised; the text should say which.

RA-01444"When the procedures in [RFC8538] for sending a NOTIFICATION message with a "Cease" code and "Hard Reset" subcode are required, and the BGP connection is being terminated because BFD has gone into the Down state, the "BFD Down" subcode SHOULD be encapsulated in the Hard Reset's data portion"RFC 8538 5 decides when a Hard Reset is "required" by the Cease subcode; BFD Down (10) postdates it and is not in its list, so whether a BFD Down termination with GR negotiated is a Hard Reset (flush) or a normal GR-preserving reset is not settled by either document; RFC 5882 4.3 adds the C-bit dimension.ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata

RFC 9494: Long-Lived Graceful Restart for BGP

Depth: deep. Errata: none (the RFC has no errata). Status: Proposed Standard. Updates: RFC 6368.

IDSectionQuoteIssueSeverityErratum
RA-01454.2"However, in the case of consecutive restarts, the previously marked stale routes MUST NOT be deleted before the timer for the Long-Lived Stale Time expires."RFC 4724 4.2 requires stale routes to be deleted when the session resets again before End-of-RIB ("consecutive restarts"); this document keeps them until the LLST timer expires, and later in the same section removes "any remaining routes (for the AFI/SAFI whose LLST timer expired)" when the session resets before synchronisation. It does not say whether the RFC 4724 rule still applies to routes that are only GR-stale (still in the Restart Time period, not yet LLGR-stale) when the second reset happens, nor that it updates RFC 4724 4.2 (the header lists only RFC 6368).contradictionnone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below
RA-01464.3, 4.6, 4.7.1"The route SHOULD NOT be advertised to any neighbor from which the Long-Lived Graceful Restart Capability has not been received. The exception is described in Section 4.6."Section 4.3 restricts LLGR-stale routes only towards neighbours that did not send the LLGR Capability; an eBGP neighbour that did send it may receive them. Section 4.6 (partial deployment) only concerns internal neighbours without the capability, and Section 4.7.1 the PE-CE eBGP case. Readers sometimes take 4.6's "MUST be internal" as a general ban on eBGP.ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata
RA-01474.2"The interval for which they are retained is limited by the sum of the Restart Time in the received Graceful Restart Capability and the Long-Lived Stale Time ... the timer continues to run once the session has re-established."The first sentence bounds retention while the session is down; the later text keeps the LLST timer running after re-establishment until End-of-RIB, so retention can exceed the stated sum only by the synchronisation time, and the Selection_Deferral_Timer of RFC 4724 also ends synchronisation. Whether a local cap on LLST (allowed: "MAY be reduced by local configuration") applies to a timer already running is not said.ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata

--------------
   However, in the case of consecutive restarts, and notwithstanding
   Section 4.2 of [RFC4724], the previously marked stale routes MUST
   NOT be deleted before the timer for the Long-Lived Stale Time
   expires. This applies to routes retained during the Restart Time
   period as well as during the Long-Lived Stale Time period.

Notes
-----
   RFC 4724 4.2 says such routes MUST be deleted; implementations of
   both documents need to know which rule wins for which routes.

Proposed erratum RA-1008 (RFC 9552, Section 5.2.1, 5.3.2.1; type: Technical):

-------------
   When configured, these auxiliary TE Router-IDs (TLV 1028/1029)

   5.3.2.

Corrected Text

   When configured, these auxiliary TE Router-IDs (TLV 1028/1029)

-------------
   Node1 is the DR for the LAN; hence, its local IP address

   the pseudonode keys.

Corrected Text
--------------
   Node1 is the DR for the LAN; hence, its Router-ID 192.0.2.1 and
   its local IP address 198.51.100.1 on the LAN are used as the
   Router-ID and Interface IP for the pseudonode keys.

Notes
-----

Proposed erratum RA-1011 (RFC 9552, Section 8.2.2, 5.2; type: Technical):

Original Text
-------------
   *  The sum of all TLV lengths found in a Link-State NLRI
   corresponds to the Total NLRI Length field of all its
   descriptors.

Corrected Text
--------------
   *  The Total NLRI Length field equals the size of the fixed
   fields (Protocol-ID, Identifier and, for SAFI 72, the Route
   Distinguisher) plus the total size (including the Type and Length
   fields) of all TLVs in the NLRI.

Notes
-----
   Read literally the check fails for every valid NLRI. The relation
   between "length ... valid" (syntactic) and "length of a
   fixed-length TLV is correct" (semantic, not to be checked by a
   Propagator) should also be stated.

RA-01484.3, 4.4"Each time the local system sends a BGP message, it restarts the SendHoldTimer unless the SendHoldTime value is zero or the negotiated HoldTime value is zero""Sends" is not defined: queued by BGP, accepted by the TCP socket, or acknowledged. Depth: deep. Errata: 1 errata: 1 verified. Status: Proposed Standard.

RA-04804""The total length of sub-TLVs (including the Type and Length fields) of a TLV MUST be equal to the length of the TLV.""The BIER TLV has 4 octets of fixed fields (Sub-domain, BFR-ID, Reserved) before its sub-TLVs, and the MPLS and non-MPLS Encapsulation sub-TLVs have 4 octets (Max SI, BS Len, Label/BIFT-id) before theirs. The sub-TLVs can therefore never fill the whole Length, and a literal check fails every valid attribute and leads to "attribute discard".errornone: RFC has 1 errata, none on this point; proposed erratum below
RA-04816""Because the route from BFER1 does not include a BIER Nexthop, BFR2 uses BFR1's BFR-prefix as the next hop.""When no BIER Nexthop sub-TLV is present, Sections 4 and 5 use the BIER prefix itself, which here is BFER1's. BFR1 is upstream of BFR2 and is not on the path to BFER1.errorerratum 8463 (Verified), technical
RA-04823.1 vs 3.2""all BIER MPLS Encapsulation sub-TLVs in the BIER TLV MUST be ignored." / "If the same BitString length is repeated in multiple BIER non-MPLS Encapsulation sub-TLVs inside the same BIER TLV, the BIER TLV MUST be ignored.""The same error (a repeated BitString length) has different scopes in the two encapsulations. For MPLS, only the MPLS Encapsulation sub-TLVs are ignored. For non-MPLS, the whole BIER TLV is ignored, including a valid MPLS encapsulation and the BFR-ID for that sub-domain. It is unclear whether this difference is intended.contradictionnone: RFC has 1 errata, none on this point
RA-04833, 3.3, 4""Each BIER TLV MUST include an MPLS and/or non-MPLS Encapsulation sub-TLV" / "it MUST NOT be included more than once""No receive action is given for a BIER TLV without any Encapsulation sub-TLV, or for a repeated BIER Nexthop sub-TLV. Section 4 refers to "Semantic checking as per Section 3", but Section 3 defines no handling for these cases. Also, Section 3 requires unknown sub-TLVs to be preserved, while Section 4 requires a re-advertising BFR to "replace the MPLS or non-MPLS Encapsulation sub-TLV with its own", which drops any unknown sub-TLVs nested in it.ambiguitynone: RFC has 1 errata, none on this point
RA-04847""a boundary router of the AD that supports the BIER attribute MUST support a policy ... by default, it is NOT allowed.""Security gap: The default-deny applies only to boundary routers that "support the BIER attribute". The attribute is optional transitive, so a boundary speaker that does not implement BIER (Section 4 notes such speakers re-advertise it) passes it to EBGP peers by default. This allows the BIER domains to be joined, which Section 7 is meant to prevent. The text does not say whether a speaker that recognizes code 41 but does not implement BIER counts as "supporting" it.errornone: RFC has 1 errata, none on this point

Proposed erratum RA-0480 (RFC 9793, Section 4; type: Technical):

Original Text
-------------
   The total length of sub-TLVs (including the Type and Length
   fields) of a TLV MUST be equal to the length of the TLV.

Corrected Text
--------------
   The total length of sub-TLVs (including the Type and Length
   fields) of a TLV, plus the length of the fixed fields that
   precede them in that TLV, MUST be equal to the length of the TLV.

Notes
-----
   The BIER TLV and the Encapsulation sub-TLVs each have 4 octets of
   fixed fields before their sub-TLVs (Sections 3, 3.1, 3.2), so the
   sub-TLVs alone can never add up to the TLV length.

Proposed erratum RA-0150 (RFC 9830, Section 5 vs RFC 9012 13; type: Technical):

-------------

   TLV/sub-TLV level, the "treat-as-withdraw" strategy MUST be

--------------

   TLV/sub-TLV level (including sub-TLVs defined in [RFC9012],
   notwithstanding Section 13 of [RFC9012]), the "treat-as-withdraw"
   strategy MUST be applied to SR Policy SAFI updates.

-----
   RFC 9012 ignores malformed sub-TLVs (except the Tunnel Egress

Proposed erratum RA-1324 (RFC 9830, Section 2.1; type: Technical):

Original Text
-------------
   A BGP UPDATE message that carries the MP_REACH_NLRI or
   MP_UNREACH_NLRI attribute with the SR Policy SAFI MUST also carry
   the BGP mandatory attributes.

Corrected Text
--------------
   A BGP UPDATE message that carries the MP_REACH_NLRI attribute
   with the SR Policy SAFI MUST also carry the BGP well-known
   mandatory attributes. As specified in [RFC4760], an UPDATE
   message that carries only the MP_UNREACH_NLRI attribute is not
   required to carry any other path attributes.

Notes
-----
   RFC 4760 Section 4 and RFC 7606 Section 3 (d) do not require
   well-known mandatory attributes in an UPDATE message that
   contains only MP_UNREACH_NLRI; a receiver following this sentence
   literally could reject SR Policy withdrawals.

Proposed erratum RA-1325 (RFC 9830, Section 2.4.3; type: Technical):

Original Text
-------------
   The SRv6 Endpoint Behavior and SID Structure MUST NOT be included
   when the SRv6 SID has not been included.

Corrected Text
--------------
   (Delete the sentence in Sections 2.4.3 and 2.4.4.2.2, or state
   which value of the SRv6 SID field means "not included" and
   whether the Endpoint Behavior and SID Structure may then be
   present.)

Notes
-----
   The SRv6 Binding SID field is fixed-size and always present; the
   value 0 is explicitly allowed together with the Endpoint Behavior
   and SID Structure, so the MUST NOT can only conflict with that
   permission. In the Type B Segment sub-TLV the SID is mandatory
   and the sentence is vacuous.

RA-10167.3.15.1 a), 7.3.15.2 a), 8.2.4.1 c), 8.4.1.1 c), Security Considerations"If the PDU contains the Authentication Information field, but the Authentication Type is not equal to Password, then the PDU shall be accepted unless the IS implements the authenticatiion procedure indicated by the Authentication Type."Security gap: When receive passwords are configured, a PDU without the Authentication Information field is discarded, but a PDU whose Authentication Information carries any type other than Password (including the reserved values 2 to 254 and the private value 255) is accepted, unless the receiver implements that type. RFC 1195: Use of OSI IS-IS for Routing in TCP/IP and Dual Environments

Depth: deep. Errata: 2 errata: 2 held. Status: Proposed Standard. Updated by: RFC 1349, RFC 5302, RFC 5304.

IDSectionQuoteIssueSeverityErratum
RA-00343.3"DFI 1 octet value "xx" / AA 3 octets value "xx xx xx""The values are given as placeholders that are neither valid decimal nor hexadecimal, so the derived NSAP is not specified.ambiguityerratum 683 (Held for Document Update), technical
RA-00355.3.5"7 IP Internal Reachability Information -- IP addresses within the routing domain reachable directly via one or more interfaces"The level 2 description omits that entries may be reached indirectly through level 1 routing (section 5.3.2 says so); RFCs 3719 and 3787 clarify.editorialerratum 3741 (Held for Document Update), editorial
RA-10273.9, 5.3.1 to 5.3.10, D.1"x CODE - 133 / x LENGTH - total length of the value field / x VALUE - TBD"The normative encoding section defines the Authentication Information field with code 133 in every PDU type but leaves its value "TBD"; only the informational Annex D proposes a format (Authentication Type octet, type 1 = cleartext password). ISO 10589:2002 later defined authentication as code 10 with the same layout, which RFC 5304 and RFC 5310 build on, and the IANA IS-IS TLV Codepoints registry lists code 133 as Illegal. An implementer reading this document alone cannot tell which code to send or accept; nothing in it points to the replacement.ambiguitynone: RFC has 2 errata, none on this point
RA-10285.3.4, 5.3.5"DEFAULT METRIC is the value of the default metric for the link to the listed neighbor."The metric descriptions of the IP Internal Reachability Information field (code 128) were copied from the IS Neighbours field: they speak of "the link to the listed neighbor", but the entries list IP prefixes, not neighbours. The External Reachability description (code 130) says "for the path to the listed IP addresses" for the default and delay metrics but "for the link to the listed IP addresses" for the expense and error metrics. The default-metric octet's bit 8, here "reserved, and must be set to zero", was later assigned as the up/down bit by RFC 5302 (which updates this document), so the "must be set to zero" text is superseded.editorialnone: RFC has 2 errata, none on this point; proposed erratum below
RA-10295.2, 5.3.5, A.1, A.2"The AS tag is associated with subsequent IP External Reachability entries, until the end of the LSP, or until the next occurence of the Inter-Domain Routing Protocol Information field."The AS Number Tag (type 2) gives meaning to the order of fields within an LSP, while Section 5.2 says the variable length fields "may occur in any order", and splitting an LSP into several LSP numbers (3.6) or regenerating it can move entries across the tag boundary or into an LSP without the tag. The tag holds only a 2-octet AS number, and A.2 misspells the field as "IDPRI".ambiguitynone: RFC has 2 errata, none on this point
RA-10303.10, C.2.2, 5.3.4"Non-contiguous subnet masks can be configured to violate this assumption."The document permits non-contiguous subnet masks (C.2.2 gives an example) but its forwarding-database reduction assumes that overlapping entries are nested, and the order-of-preference rules of 3.10 rank entries by "the number of 1 bits in the mask", which is not a total order for non-contiguous masks. Nothing says whether a receiver accepts, ignores or rejects an entry with a non-contiguous mask or with address bits set outside the mask (3.10 zeroes them for comparison only).ambiguitynone: RFC has 2 errata, none on this point

RFC 3358: Optional Checksums in Intermediate System to Intermediate System (ISIS)

Depth: deep. Errata: none (the RFC has no errata). Status: Informational.

IDSectionQuoteIssueSeverityErratum
RA-04933""The checksum is a fletcher checksum computed according to [ISO98], / Annex C over the complete PDU.""ISO 8473 Annex C generates two check octets whose values depend on the octet position of the checksum field in the checked data, and verification sums the whole PDU to zero. The section does not say that the position is that of the Checksum field inside TLV 12, whether "complete PDU" ends at the PDU Length or includes octets beyond it (e.g. IIH padding up to the frame length), or whether the receiver verifies by recomputation with the field set to 0 or by the zero-sum test; the two give different results for the Annex C rule that replaces a computed 0 octet by 255. The Abstract also lists only CSNP/PSNP while Sections 1 and 2 include IIHs, and "Proviers" (Abstract) is a typo.ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata

The summary list in 2.4.2 gives a fixed 4 octets, so a receiver built from the list would reject or misparse multi-address sub-TLVs. RA-04965.2""The variables MaxPathMetric and MaxLinkMetric SHOULD retain the / values defined in Table 2 of section 8 of ISO 10589.""Step (3) of the transition algorithm in 5.1 says to "change MaxPathMetric to 0xFE000000" once wide metrics are considered, while 5.2 (which applies when both styles are considered) says MaxPathMetric and MaxLinkMetric SHOULD keep the ISO 10589 values (narrow: 1023 and 63). During the mixed phase the two sections prescribe different limits, so a path whose wide-metric cost exceeds 1023 is unreachable under 5.2 but valid under 5.1.contradictionnone: RFC has no errata
RA-04974""An implementation SHOULD use the Overload Bit to signal that it is / not ready to accept transit traffic.""The Overload Bit recommendations are in Section 4 ("Overload Bit"); Section 3 is "Unused Features" (TLVs 131 and 133). RFC 3906: Calculating Interior Gateway Protocol (IGP) Routes Over Traffic Engineering Tunnels

Depth: deep. Errata: none (the RFC has no errata). Status: Informational.

IDSectionQuoteIssueSeverityErratum
RA-01524.1, 4.2"When using an absolute metric on a TE-tunnel, the cost of the IP routes in the routing table does not depend on the topology of the network. / If an absolute metric of 5 is configured on tunnel T1, then rtrA will install routes X, Y, and Z all with metrics 5, 15, and 25 respectively."Section 4.1 says an absolute metric makes route costs independent of the topology and that the fixed metric "is not only used to compute the cost of IP routes advertised by the router that is the tail-end ... but also for all the routes that are downstream" (the POP example: all traffic to the POP uses the tunnel with metric 1). The 4.2 example instead adds the downstream distances (5, 15, 25), i.e. the absolute value replaces only the cost to the tail; the word "all" suggests an edit from "all with metric 5". Implementations differ (some install the absolute value for every prefix behind the tail).contradictionnone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below
RA-01534.1"The relative metric is bounded by minimum and maximum allowed metric values while the positive metric disables the TE-tunnel in the SPF calculation."The clause "while the positive metric disables the TE-tunnel" has no evident meaning: any positive relative metric would disable the tunnel, which contradicts the purpose of relative metrics (4.2 uses -5, and positive values are allowed "to make the route over the TE-tunnel ... more preferred" or less). Probably "a metric at the maximum value" or "a metric making the path worse than the native path" was meant; the text also does not say what happens when a negative relative metric would make a cost below the minimum (clamp or reject).ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata

Proposed erratum RA-0152 (RFC 3906, Section 4.1, 4.2; type: Technical):

Original Text
-------------
   If an absolute metric of 5 is configured on tunnel T1, then rtrA
   will install routes X, Y, and Z all with metrics 5, 15, and 25
   respectively.

Corrected Text
--------------
   (The working group should state which is intended.) Either "...
   install routes X, Y, and Z all with metric 5." or, in 4.1, "When
   using an absolute metric on a TE-tunnel, the cost to the tail-end
   router does not depend on the topology of the network;
   destinations downstream of the tail-end add their IGP distance
   from the tail-end."

Notes
-----

RA-05074 (REFERENCE clauses)""REFERENCE "{ISIS.aoi iDFieldLengthMismatches (25)}"""isisCircMaxAreaAddrMismatches cites iDFieldLengthMismatches (25), copied from isisCircIDFieldLenMismatches. isisCircNumAdj cites changesInAdjacencyState (40), copied from isisCircAdjChanges, though it is a gauge of adjacencies, not a count of changes. isisCircLevelLSPThrottle and isisCircLevelMinLSPRetransInt both give attribute number (5) for different attributes. isisSysLevelOrigLSPBuffSize cites only originatingL1LSPBufferSize for a row that also covers Level 2.editorialnone: RFC has 2 errata, none on this point; proposed erratum below
RA-05087.2.13, 4 (isisLSPTLVValue, isisPduFragment)""visible to any intruder who has access to traffic. None of the / security attributes are setable or visible through the MIB.""Security gap: isisLSPTLVTable returns every TLV of every stored LSP verbatim (isisLSPTLVValue, SIZE 0..255), including the Authentication TLV (type 10). With cleartext authentication (type 1) this gives the area or domain password to anyone with read access. With HMAC types it gives digest/plaintext pairs for offline guessing. isisPduFragment returns up to 64 octets of a received PDU, which can include the start of an IIH or LSP Authentication TLV. An intruder who can see the traffic already has this, but a remote reader with SNMP read access does not. RA-00367.1"If a router advertises MT TLV, it has to advertise all the MTs it participates in, specifically including topology ID #0 also."Read with "Lack of MT TLV ... MUST be interpreted as participation ... in MT ID #0 only", this means that every MT router is in MT 0, which excludes IPv6-only (MT 2 only) routers that the rest of the document allows. Proposed erratum RA-0036 (RFC 5120, Section 7.1; type: Technical):

Original Text
-------------
   If a router advertises MT TLV, it has to advertise all the MTs it
   participates in, specifically including topology ID #0 also.

Corrected Text
--------------
   If a router advertises the MT TLV, it MUST advertise all the MTs
   it participates in, including MT ID #0 if it participates in MT
   ID #0.

Notes
-----
   As written, every MT-capable router must be in MT #0, which
   excludes routers that participate only in other topologies (for
   example MT #2 only). "has to" is not an RFC 2119 keyword. The
   limit of 127 MTs applies to one TLV instance, since the TLV may
   appear more than once.

IDSectionQuoteIssueSeverityErratum
RA-00373, 4"all metrics greater than or equal to MAX_PATH_METRIC SHALL be considered to have a metric of MAX_PATH_METRIC."Section 3 (and 4) clamp a path metric at MAX_PATH_METRIC (0xFE000000), which leaves the destination reachable at that cost. ISO 10589 (C.2) drops a path whose cost exceeds MaxPathMetric, and section 4 itself says a prefix advertised with a metric above MAX_PATH_METRIC "MUST NOT be considered during the normal SPF computation". Whether a path whose sum overflows is usable (clamped) or unreachable (ISO behaviour) is therefore read both ways; RFC 5308 3 repeats the clamp for IPv6.contradictionnone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below
RA-00384"If a prefix is advertised with a metric larger then MAX_PATH_METRIC (0xFE000000, see paragraph 3.0), this prefix MUST NOT be considered""larger then" for "larger than"; "paragraph 3.0" is not a section (section 3 defines MAX_PATH_METRIC). The rule also leaves a prefix metric exactly equal to 0xFE000000 usable, unlike the 2^24 - 1 link rule, which excludes the maximum value itself.editorialnone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below
RA-00393"If a link is advertised with the maximum link metric (2^24 - 1), this link MUST NOT be considered during the normal SPF computation."The exclusion applies to "the normal SPF"; whether the link is still used for TE (CSPF) and for flex-algorithm computations with a TE or delay metric is left open (RFC 9350 later answers it for flex-algo only).ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata
RA-10312, 3, 4"Unknown sub-TLVs are to be ignored and skipped upon receipt. / The 6 bits of prefix length can have the values 0-32"Only unknown sub-TLVs are covered. The document does not say what a receiver does with a known sub-TLV whose Length differs from the fixed length in the Section 3 table (for example an Administrative Group of length 3), with a sub-TLV that overruns the sub-TLV area or the enclosing entry, or with a TLV 135 entry whose 6-bit prefix length is 33 to 63 (after which the rest of the TLV cannot be parsed). Choices range from skipping the sub-TLV to discarding the entry, the TLV or the LSP, and implementations differ in what they keep. Later RFCs: RFC 8918 Sections 3.3 and 4 (updates RFC 5305) make 'Unknown sub-TLVs MUST be ignored' normative and forbid rejecting the LSP for a non-conforming TLV or sub-TLV, but give no action for a known sub-TLV of the wrong length, an overrun, or a prefix length above 32; the choice remains open.ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata
RA-10323.4, 3.5, 3.6"The maximum link bandwidth is encoded in 32 bits in IEEE floating point format. The units are bytes (not bits!) per second.""IEEE floating point format" does not name IEEE 754 single precision explicitly (it follows only from "32 bits"), and nothing says how to treat negative values, infinities or NaN, or an Unreserved Bandwidth value larger than Maximum Reservable Bandwidth. A CSPF computation that compares a NaN bandwidth gives implementation-dependent results.ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata
RA-10334.3"If a router implements traffic engineering, it MUST include this TLV in its LSP. This TLV SHOULD not be included more than once in an LSP.""SHOULD not" is in mixed case (SHOULD NOT intended). The receiver action for more than one TLV 134 (in one LSP or across the fragments of one LSP set), possibly with different addresses, is not given; "in its LSP" also leaves open in which fragment it is carried.editorialnone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below
RA-10345.2.1"Taking into consideration allocations specified in this document, the registry has been initialized as follows:"The initial registry contents include code points that this document does not specify (4 Link Local/Remote Identifiers, 19 Link-attributes, 20 Link Protection Type, 21 Interface Switching Capability Descriptor, 22 Bandwidth Constraints), with no reference to the documents that define them (RFC 5307, RFC 4124 and others). A reader cannot find the definitions from this document, and the introductory sentence says the table reflects "allocations specified in this document".editorialnone: RFC has no errata

RFC 5310: IS-IS Generic Cryptographic Authentication

Depth: deep. Errata: 2 errata: 2 rejected. Status: Proposed Standard. Updated by: RFC 6232, RFC 6233.

IDSectionQuoteIssueSeverityErratum
RA-00413.3"In this application, Ko is always L octets long. ... If the Authentication Key (K) is more than L octets long, then Ko is set to H(K)."The key is hashed when it is longer than the digest length L, while RFC 2104 HMAC hashes it only when it is longer than the block size B. "Ko XOR Ipad" then combines an L-octet Ko with a B-octet Ipad without saying how (zero extension is implied). Implementations that use a plain HMAC library produce different MACs for keys with L < |K| <= B (for HMAC-SHA-256: 33 to 64 octets), so such keys do not interoperate across implementations even though both claim RFC 5310.ambiguitynone: RFC has 2 errata, none on this point; proposed erratum below
RA-00423.3"For SHA-1 and SHA-256: B == 64 / For SHA-384 and SHA-512: B == 128"SHA-224, one of the five algorithms the RFC defines, has no block size listed (it is 64).editorialnone: RFC has 2 errata, none on this point
RA-00433.5, 5"the remaining lifetime of the LSP MUST be set to zero before computing the authentication, thus this field is not authenticated."Security gap stated by the RFC itself: an on-path attacker can change Remaining Lifetime (for example to purge an LSP early or keep a dead one alive) without breaking the MAC. RFC 6232 / 6233 add purge originator identification and authenticated purges but do not close the lifetime gap for non-zero values.errornone: RFC has 2 errata, none on this point
RA-10353.3, 3.4"An implementation MUST fill the authentication type and the length before the authentication data is computed. ... The Key ID is filled."Section 3.4 requires the type and length to be in place before the HMAC is computed, then lists "The Key ID is filled." as a separate later step, and 3.3 step (2) mentions only the Authentication Data (Apad) and the Authentication Type. Whether the Key ID is part of the authenticated data (filled before the hash) or not (zero, or filled afterwards) is not stated; the two readings produce different MACs. If the Key ID were not covered, an attacker could also change it without detection.ambiguitynone: RFC has 2 errata, none on this point; proposed erratum below
RA-10362, 3.2, 3.3, 3.5"Key Identifier (Key ID): This is a two-octet unsigned integer used to uniquely identify an IS-IS SA / K is the password for the PDU type as per the International Standard ISO/IEC 10589"Section 2 makes the Key ID the identifier of a Security Association and says the receiver "determines the active SA by looking at the Key ID", while 3.2 and 3.3 keep the ISO 10589 model of one secret per PDU type (link-level for IIHs, area for L1 LSPs and SNPs, domain for L2). The scope of the Key ID space is not given (one space per router, or separate spaces per circuit, area and domain), so the same Key ID may select different keys in different implementations. The receiver action for a Key ID with no configured or no currently valid SA, and for a TLV 10 Length that does not match the algorithm of the selected SA, is not stated (only a MAC mismatch is: discard and log).ambiguitynone: RFC has 2 errata, none on this point
RA-10373.2"Implementations that support the optional checksum for the Sequence Number PDUs and IS-IS HELLO PDUs MUST NOT include the Checksum TLV."Read literally, implementations that support the optional Checksum TLV (TLV 12, RFC 3358) must never include it, which defeats the support; the intended scope is presumably "when CRYPTO_AUTH is in use". The receiver action for a PDU that carries both TLV 10 and TLV 12 is not given. In the same section, Level 2 SNPs "shall use" (lower case) the domain string while Level 1 SNPs "SHALL use" the area string.ambiguitynone: RFC has 2 errata, none on this point; proposed erratum below
RA-10383.5, 4"An implementation MAY have a transition mode where it includes CRYPTO_AUTH information in the PDUs but does not verify this information."Security gap: The transition mode only covers sending authenticated PDUs without verifying them; nothing says whether PDUs without TLV 10 (or with another authentication type) are accepted during the transition, which is the case that matters when migrating from no authentication or from RFC 5304. Section 4 also asks that keys be "changed periodically" and that implementations "MUST be able to store and use more than one key at the same time" without saying how a receiver chooses among several keys valid for accepting (only by Key ID). The rejected errata 2461 / 2462 on unauthenticated purges were later addressed by RFC 6233.errornone: RFC has 2 errata, none on this point
RA-10397.1"[RFC2119] Bradner, S., "Key words for use in RFCs to Indicate Requirement Levels", BCP 14, RFC 2119, February 2001."RFC 2119 is dated March 1997. In the same list the RFC 2104 author is spelled "Krawczk" (Krawczyk), and [ISO] cites ISO/IEC 10589:1992 while companion documents (RFC 5305, RFC 5304 context) cite the 2002 second edition.editorialnone: RFC has 2 errata, none on this point; proposed erratum below

Proposed erratum RA-0041 (RFC 5310, Section 3.3; type: Technical):

Original Text
-------------
   In this application, Ko is always L octets long.

Corrected Text
--------------
   In this application, Ko is always L octets long. Note that this
   differs from HMAC [RFC2104], which hashes the key only when it is
   longer than the block size B; for keys longer than L but not
   longer than B the two computations give different results. Before
   the XOR with Ipad and Opad, Ko is extended with zeros to B
   octets.

Notes
-----
   Implementations built on a standard HMAC library do not
   interoperate with implementations that follow this section for
   key lengths L < |K| <= B. The text also does not say how an
   L-octet Ko is combined with B-octet Ipad
   Opad. The block size of SHA-224 (B == 64) is missing from the
   list.

Proposed erratum RA-1035 (RFC 5310, Section 3.3, 3.4; type: Technical):

Original Text
-------------
   An implementation MUST fill the authentication type and the
   length before the authentication data is computed.

Corrected Text
--------------
   An implementation MUST fill the authentication type, the length,
   and the Key ID before the authentication data is computed.

Notes
-----
   Section 3.4 lists "The Key ID is filled." after the computation
   step, and Section 3.3 step (2) names only the Authentication Data
   and Authentication Type fields. Filling the Key ID before the
   computation is the common practice and makes the Key ID
   authenticated.

Depth: deep. Errata: none (the RFC has no errata). Status: Proposed Standard.

IDSectionQuoteIssueSeverityErratum
RA-01574.3"Implementations MUST NOT inject a /128 prefix for the interface address into their routing or forwarding table"Section 4.3 defines the IPv6 Neighbor Address sub-TLV, but the sentence (copied from 4.2) speaks of "the interface address"; the neighbour address is meant.editorialnone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below
RA-13283.2.3, 4.3, 4.5"The IPv6 Global Interface Address TLV is included in IIH PDUs for those interfaces using IPv6 TE extensions. / it MUST include this sub-TLV for point-to-point links"Section 4.3 makes the IPv6 Neighbor Address sub-TLV mandatory on numbered point-to-point links, and Section 3.2.3 says the only source for its value is the neighbour's IPv6 Global Interface Address TLV (233) in IIHs, because TLV 232 in IIHs holds link-local addresses. Section 4.5 states the inclusion of TLV 233 descriptively, with no requirement keyword, so a neighbour that implements IPv6 TE may omit it and leave the MUST of 4.3 impossible to meet. When TLV 233 lists several addresses, the text does not say which one (or whether all, since the sub-TLV "can occur multiple times") goes into the Neighbor Address sub-TLV, nor what a router does when the neighbour's TLV 233 is absent (omit the sub-TLV, or take an address from the neighbour's TLV 232 in its LSP, which is not tied to the link).ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below
RA-13294.4"There MUST NOT be more than one IPv6 SRLG TLV for a given link."An IS-IS TLV value holds at most 255 octets. With the fixed part of 24 octets (40 with the neighbour address), one IPv6 SRLG TLV can carry at most 57 SRLG values (53 with NA set). Because a link may have only one TLV 139, a link with more SRLGs than that cannot be described at all, while the IPv4 SRLG TLV 138 "MAY occur more than once" (RFC 5307 1.4) with no per-link limit. The text does not say whether the sender truncates, omits the TLV, or may in that case use several TLVs, nor how a receiver treats a second TLV for the same link.ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata
RA-13304.4, 7"If both an SRLG TLV and an IPv6 SRLG are received describing the SRLGs for the same link, the receiver MUST apply the SRLG TLV and ignore the IPv6 SRLG TLV."TLV 138 names a link by IPv4 addresses or link identifiers and TLV 139 by IPv6 addresses; neither carries anything the other does, so a receiver can only tell that both describe "the same link" by finding one Extended IS Reachability entry that has both the IPv4 and the IPv6 interface address sub-TLVs, which the text does not state. Neither SRLG TLV carries a topology identifier, although Section 7 registers sub-TLVs 12 and 13 for TLV 222 (multi-topology), so SRLGs of a link that appears only in a non-zero topology cannot be associated unambiguously.ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata
RA-13314.1"This TLV MUST NOT be included more than once in an LSP."The restriction applies to "an LSP", so a router could place TLV 140 in two fragments of its LSP set with different addresses; the receive behaviour for more than one IPv6 TE Router ID (from one LSP or across fragments) is not given. RFC 5305 4.3 states the same restriction for the IPv4 TE Router ID with SHOULD.ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata

Proposed erratum RA-1328 (RFC 6119, Section 3.2.3, 4.3, 4.5; type: Technical):

Original Text
-------------
   The IPv6 Global Interface Address TLV is TLV type 233.  The TLV
   structure is identical to that of the IPv6 Interface Address TLV
   defined in [IPv6], but the semantics are different.  In
   particular, the TLV is included in IIH PDUs for those interfaces
   using IPv6 TE extensions.

Corrected Text
--------------
   The IPv6 Global Interface Address TLV is TLV type 233.  The TLV
   structure is identical to that of the IPv6 Interface Address TLV
   defined in [IPv6], but the semantics are different.  A router
   that implements IPv6 traffic engineering MUST include this TLV in
   the IIH PDUs it sends on numbered point-to-point interfaces using
   IPv6 TE extensions.  A router constructing the IPv6 Neighbor
   Address sub-TLV includes one sub-TLV for each address in the
   neighbor's TLV.

Notes
-----
   Without the neighbour's global address the MUST of Section 4.3
   cannot be met; Section 3.2.3 excludes TLV 232 from IIHs as a
   source. The choice among several addresses (one sub-TLV per
   address, or one chosen address) also needs to be stated.

RA-01595, 3"all implementations in a domain implementing authentication MUST be upgraded to receive the POI TLV before any IS is allowed to generate a purge with the POI TLV."RFC 6233 Section 3 (published together, not marked as updating this document) says that an implementation that implements authentication generates a purge by removing non-purge TLVs and "The POI TLV MUST be added", while Section 3 here makes it a SHOULD. RFC 7308: Extended Administrative Groups in MPLS Traffic Engineering (MPLS-TE)

Depth: deep (read in full). Errata: none (the RFC has no errata). Status: Proposed Standard.

IDSectionQuoteIssueSeverityErratum
RA-01612.2"If an EAG's length is more than 4 bytes, numbering for these additional bytes picks up where the previous byte left off. For example, the least significant bit in the fifth byte of an 8-byte EAG is referred to as bit 32."Bits 0-31 of the EAG "have the same meaning ... as an AG", whose bit 0 is the least significant bit of a 32-bit value sent in network order, i.e. the last of the first four bytes. Numbering the EAG word by word in the same way puts bit 32 at the least significant bit of the eighth byte; the example puts it in the fifth byte, which is a byte-wise continuation that is big-endian in the first word and little-endian afterwards. The two readings give different link colours for every group above 31, and implementations (and later users of the encoding such as the flexible-algorithm Admin Group sub-TLVs of RFC 9350) are known to use the word-wise reading.contradictionnone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below

Proposed erratum RA-0161 (RFC 7308, Section 2.2; type: Technical):

Original Text
-------------
   For example, the least significant bit in the fifth byte of an
   8-byte EAG is referred to as bit 32.

Corrected Text
--------------
   The EAG is a sequence of 32-bit words in network byte order; bit
   N is bit (N mod 32) of word (N div 32), bit 0 of a word being its
   least significant bit. For example, the least significant bit in
   the eighth byte of an 8-byte EAG is referred to as bit 32.

Notes
-----
   Bits 0-31 must equal the AG, whose bit 0 is the least significant
   bit of the fourth byte. Continuing word by word gives bit 32 in
   the eighth byte; the example's fifth byte implies a different
   byte order for the second and later words. The working group
   should confirm the intended numbering.

RA-01635.2.2, 5.3"it is RECOMMENDED that the member of the set of routers {PQ} with the lowest cost S->P be the default choice for P."For a PQ node found only through extended P-space, S's shortest path to P crosses S-E by definition, so "cost S->P" is either that pre-failure cost (which the repair does not follow) or the cost of the repair path S->N->P; the text does not say which, and the tie-breaker "lowest node identifier" does not say which identifier (system ID, router ID, TE router ID). RA-13335.4"the PLR MUST NOT use a repair tunnel path whose first hop is along a link that has a cost or reverse cost equal to MaxLinkMetric (for OSPF) or the maximum cost (for IS-IS)""The maximum cost (for IS-IS)" is not defined. With wide metrics, a link advertised at 2^24 - 1 is already excluded from the SPF (RFC 5305 3), so the rule can only be meant for 2^24 - 2 (the highest usable value, the conventional "costed out" value), or for 63 with narrow metrics; the text (copied from RFC 5286 3.5) names none. Depth: deep. Errata: none (the RFC has no errata). Status: Proposed Standard.

IDSectionQuoteIssueSeverityErratum
RA-01678.3, 8.2"Among the routers in the MRT Island with the lowest numerical value advertised for GADAG Root Selection Priority, an implementation MUST pick the router with the highest Router ID to be the GADAG root.""Router ID" is not defined for IS-IS, where several candidates exist (system ID, TE Router ID TLV 134/140, the RFC 7811 mrt_node_id which is the 7-octet system ID plus pseudonode). All routers must pick the same root (RFC 7811 5.3 MUST), so the identifier must be fixed per IGP, as RFC 7811 Figure 15 does for interface ordering. RFC 7811 5.9.1 also breaks proxy-node ties "based upon the lowest Router ID" with the same undefined term. Section 8.2 has "either IPv4 and IPv6".ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata
RA-05483"block: Either a 2-connected cluster, a cut-edge, or a cut-vertex."RFC 7811 Section 4 (the algorithm this architecture mandates) says "a block is a 2-connected cluster, a cut-link or an isolated node", and both documents otherwise use "cut-link". A cut-vertex is not a block: it is shared by the blocks it joins (RFC 7811 4.4 "the first two blocks have one common node (node C)"). The definition here makes a cut-vertex a block of its own, which conflicts with the block and localroot model of RFC 7811.contradictionnone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below
RA-05497.3.1"1. The text also says the 0xFFFFFE / 0xFFFF metrics may be "set in an automated manner as with LDP IGP synchronization [RFC5443]", so rule 1 makes MRT Island membership follow LDP synchronisation state; that consequence (island and GADAG recomputation at each LDP sync change) is not discussed. Also "the overload bit is prevents".ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata
RA-05503, 4, 6.1.1.2, 8.1"the router pops the top label and uses that it to guide the next-hop selection""uses that it"; Section 3 "used to described"; Section 4 "for each pair of destination-routed MRTs" (rooted); 8.1 "in the calculations used construct the MRTs". 8.3 and 9 describe the MRT-Red, MRT-Blue and Rainbow MT-IDs as "temporary" registrations requested in a draft; they were later assigned by RFC 8320, which the text cannot reflect.editorialnone: RFC has no errata

RFC 8202: IS-IS Multi-Instance

Depth: deep. Errata: none (the RFC has no errata). Status: Proposed Standard. Obsoletes: RFC 6822.

IDSectionQuoteIssueSeverityErratum
RA-01693.6.1, 3.6.1.1, 3.6.2"MI-RTRs MUST discard IS-IS PDUs received if ... The destination multicast address is AllL1IS, AllL2IS, or AllIS and the PDU contains an IID-TLV. / all IIHs sent on a point-to-point circuit by an MI-RTR MUST include an IID-TLV. This includes IIHs associated with IID #0."In point-to-point operation over a LAN (RFC 5309), Section 3.6.1.1 sends standard-instance (IID #0) point-to-point IIHs to AllL1IS / AllL2IS / AllIS. If Section 3.6.2 ("all IIHs sent on a point-to-point circuit") applies to such circuits, those IIHs carry an IID-TLV with IID 0, and the receiving MI-RTR must discard them under the first rule of Section 3.6.1, so the IID #0 adjacency never forms. The text does not say whether a point-to-point-over-LAN circuit is a "point-to-point circuit" for Section 3.6.2, or whether the Section 3.6.1 discard rule exempts an IID-TLV with IID 0. Section 3.6.1.1 also says MI addresses "MUST" be used for non-zero-IID point-to-point IIHs and then "either address is permitted", without saying which two addresses are meant, and misspells "AllL2MI-ISs".contradictionnone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below

-----

RFC 8333: Micro-loop Prevention by Introducing a Local Convergence Delay

Depth: deep. Errata: none (the RFC has no errata). Status: Proposed Standard.

IDSectionQuoteIssueSeverityErratum
RA-01705.4"If the condition of a single local link-down event has been met, then an update of the RIB and the FIB MUST be delayed for ULOOP_DELAY_DOWN_TIMER ms. / Hence, it SHOULD only be done for a non-urgent convergence, such as administrative deactivation (maintenance) or when the traffic is protected by FRR."Step 5 makes the delay mandatory for every single local link-down, while the next paragraph says it should only be applied when the failure is non-urgent or FRR-protected. For an unprotected destination behind the failed link, the MUST keeps the old (failed) forwarding entry for ULOOP_DELAY_DOWN_TIMER (typically seconds), which black-holes traffic. The condition (protection available per destination) belongs in the MUST. In Section 6.2 "its forwarding entry to F is updated" should read "to K" (the example's destination).contradictionnone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below
RA-13389.3"| | t0+312 | E receives LSP/LSA | | / | | t0+313 | E schedules SPF (200 | |"In Table 6 the rows "E receives LSP/LSA from F and floods it" (t0+312 ms) and "E schedules SPF (200 ms)" (t0+313 ms) are placed in the "Router C Events" column; they are router E's events (E then "computes SPF" at t0+514 ms in its own column). As printed, the table shows C receiving F's LSP twice and scheduling two SPFs, which obscures the abort sequence the section illustrates (the new convergence that stops ULOOP_DELAY_DOWN_TIMER).editorialnone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below

Proposed erratum RA-0170 (RFC 8333, Section 5.4; type: Technical):

Original Text
-------------
   If the condition of a single local link-down event has been met,
   then an update of the RIB and the FIB MUST be delayed for
   ULOOP_DELAY_DOWN_TIMER ms.

Corrected Text
--------------
   If the condition of a single local link-down event has been met
   and the affected destinations are protected (for example by FRR)
   or the event is non-urgent, then an update of the RIB and the FIB
   MUST be delayed for ULOOP_DELAY_DOWN_TIMER ms.

Notes
-----
   Without the restriction, unprotected traffic is dropped for the
   whole delay.

RFC 8402: Segment Routing Architecture

Depth: deep. Errata: 2 errata: 1 verified, 1 rejected. Status: Proposed Standard. Updated by: RFC 9256.

IDSectionQuoteIssueSeverityErratum
RA-01713.1, 3.1.2"Multiple SIDs MAY be allocated to the same prefix so long as the tuple <prefix, topology, algorithm> is unique."The sentence allows "multiple SIDs" for a prefix only when each <prefix, topology, algorithm> tuple is unique, i.e. at most one SID per tuple, but it reads as permitting several SIDs for one tuple. It does not say what a receiver does when two different SIDs arrive for the same tuple (from the same or different originators), which the protocol documents (RFC 8667, RFC 8660 conflict resolution) then have to settle. Section 3.1.2's "MUST NOT allocate the same Prefix-SID to different prefixes" also conflicts on its face with Section 3.3, where an anycast prefix is advertised by several routers with one SID (same prefix, so consistent, but "different prefixes" with the same SID across algorithms is not addressed).ambiguitynone: RFC has 2 errata, none on this point
RA-05512"In SRv6, the top of the segment list is represented by the first segment in the Segment Routing Header as defined in [IPv6-SRH]."In the SRH the segment list is encoded in reverse order: Segment List[0] is the last segment of the path and the segment to be processed first is the last entry of the list (RFC 8754 2). "The first segment in the Segment Routing Header" therefore names, read by encoding order, the bottom of the list, the opposite of what PUSH means; only read as "first to be visited" does it fit. NEXT and the Introduction speak of copying "the next segment" without fixing the direction either.ambiguitynone: RFC has 2 errata, none on this point; proposed erratum below
RA-05523.1.1, 3.1.3"nodes that do not support a given algorithm will not be included in the topology associated with that algorithm-specific SPF"For algorithm 1 (Strict-SPF) Section 3.1.1 says the opposite: "Strict-SPF uses the same topology used by the Shortest Path First algorithm" and restricting it to supporting nodes "will not produce the desired forwarding paths". The SRv6 mitigation argument in 3.1.3 (traffic will normally not reach non-supporting nodes) therefore does not hold for Strict-SPF SIDs, where such nodes stay in the topology and forward by algorithm 0, overriding the strictness without the source knowing (3.1.1 makes the source responsible only for SR Policies, not for single Prefix-SIDs).ambiguitynone: RFC has 2 errata, none on this point
RA-05533.3.1, 3.5"each Provide Edge (PE) device has a path to each of the groups""Provider Edge"; 3.5 "it is assumed that the all areas are part of a single SR domain"; 3.5 "node Z allocates Node-SID 150 to his local IPv6 prefix".editorialnone: RFC has 2 errata, none on this point

   the top of the segment list is represented by the first segment
   in the Segment Routing Header

Corrected Text
--------------
   the top of the segment list is represented by the segment that is
   processed first, i.e., the last entry (Segment List[n]) of the

RFC 8405: Shortest Path First (SPF) Back-Off Delay Algorithm for Link-State IGPs

Depth: deep. Errata: none (the RFC has no errata). Status: Proposed Standard.

IDSectionQuoteIssueSeverityErratum
RA-01725.2, 5.3, 5.4"QUIET: This is the initial state, when no IGP events have occurred for at least HOLDDOWN_INTERVAL since the last routing table computation. / HOLDDOWN_TIMER: This is the FSM timer that is (re)started when an IGP event is received"The state definition measures HOLDDOWN_INTERVAL from the last routing table computation, while the timer and transitions 2, 4, 5 and 6 measure it from the last IGP event. With LONG_SPF_DELAY close to HOLDDOWN_INTERVAL the two readings return to QUIET at different times, which matters for the stated goal of identical SPF delays on all routers. The FSM also allows QUIET with SPF_TIMER still running (when SPF delay exceeds HOLDDOWN_INTERVAL, both configurable up to 6000 ms); transition 1 then keeps the long delay ("if SPF_TIMER is not already running"), which is not discussed.contradictionnone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below
