RFC 6378: MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP) Linear Protection

Depth: deep. Errata: none (the RFC has no errata). Status: Proposed Standard. Updated by: RFC 7214, RFC 7271, RFC 7324.

IDSectionQuoteIssueSeverityErratum
RA-06014.3.3.2, Appendix A"A local Signal Fail on the protection path input when in local Unavailable state ... SHALL cause the LER to remain in local Unavailable state and transmit an SF(0,0) message. / All other local inputs SHALL be ignored."The text defines a local SF-P only for local Unavailable state; in remote Unavailable state (UA:LO:R, UA:P:R) the input falls under "All other local inputs SHALL be ignored". Appendix A, Part 1 instead has UA:LO:R / SF-P = footnote [1] ("transmit SF(0,0)") and UA:P:R / SF-P = UA:P:L (a transition to local Unavailable). Appendix A says the text is authoritative on a mismatch, so an implementation following the text keeps sending NR(0,0) while one following the table sends SF(0,0), and the peer's view of the protection path differs (the local SF on protection is never reported). The (by implication) parenthesis in the text is also misleading, since a local SF-P in UA:LO:L is masked by the higher-priority Lockout. Later RFCs: RFC 7271 Section 11.1 settles this for the APS mode only; the PSC mode keeps the text of this RFC.contradictionnone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below
RA-06024.3.3.4, Appendix A"A remote Forced Switch message SHALL cause the LER go into remote Protecting administrative state, and if in local Protecting failure state, the LER SHALL transmit the SF(1,1) message / PF:W:L | [11] | [12] |PA:F:R|"In Part 2 of the table, PF:W:L with a remote FS goes to PA:F:R without a footnote, so by the Appendix A rule ("If the message to be sent ... deviates from the table below, it is noted in the footnotes") the LER sends the PA:F:R default NR(0,1), while the text requires SF(1,1). Footnote [12] also says "Transition to UA" without saying UA:P:R, the only remote Unavailable state that a remote SF-P can produce. The same row and footnote [11]/[12] are the only places where the local SF-W survives a remote-caused transition, so the missing footnote changes what the peer learns about the working path. Later RFCs: RFC 7271 Section 11 settles this for the APS mode only; the PSC mode keeps the text of this RFC.contradictionnone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below
RA-06033.5, 4.3.3.5"If the WTR timer expires prior to being stopped, it SHALL generate a WTR Expires local signal / If the WTR timer is running, then a remote NR message SHALL be ignored. If the WTR timer is stopped, then a remote NR message SHALL cause the LER to go into Normal state."The WTR timer has two states, Running and Stopped, and only a Stop command is said to put it into Stopped. Expiry generates WTR Expires but the timer's state after expiry is not given. The exit from Wait-to-Restore depends on the timer being "stopped"; if an expired timer is not "Stopped", an LER that sent NR(0,1) after expiry ignores the peer's NR for ever. Also an LER that entered WTR remotely (PF:W:R + remote WTR) never started its own timer; the rule then relies on "stopped" meaning "not running". The remote NR rule also does not distinguish NR(0,1) from NR(0,0). Later RFCs: RFC 7271 (Section 11 and its state table footnote) settles this for the APS mode only. RFC 7324 Section 4.3.3.4 adds a rule that puts both ends into Wait-to-Restore, which makes the undefined timer state after expiry decisive; Appendix A is not updated by either.ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata
RA-06044.3.2"The remote message from the far-end LER is assigned a priority just below the similar local input."Remote WTR, remote DNR and remote NR have no "similar local input" in the ten-entry local priority list (WTR Expires and No Request are not the same requests), so their priority relative to local inputs is undefined; the state tables settle individual cases but the general rule used to resolve local and remote inputs (Section 3.6.1) cannot be applied to them. The priority list has "Signal Degrade on working" but no SD on protection, although Section 3.1 defines SD for either path. Later RFCs: RFC 7271 Section 10.2 settles this for the APS mode only (single priority list including the remote requests); the PSC mode keeps the text of this RFC.ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata
RA-06054.1"If no valid PSC message is received, over a period of several continual messages intervals, the last valid received message remains applicable."No loss-of-PSC-session detection or reaction is defined: a peer that stops sending (or a protection path that silently drops the G-ACh) leaves the last remote request in force indefinitely, e.g. a remote FS keeps traffic on the protection path. "Several" intervals is not quantified. Also "it is RECOMMENDED that the default interval ... SHOULD be no longer than 3.3 ms" doubles the requirement keyword. Later RFCs: RFC 7271 Section 12 settles this for the APS mode only (alarm after 3.5 intervals without a message, no switching); the PSC mode keeps the text of this RFC.ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata
RA-06062.1, 4.2.6"MEG Managed Entity Group / 0: indicates that the protection path is not transporting user data traffic (in 1:n architecture)"MEG is "Maintenance Entity Group" (RFC 6371); the Path field text refers to the 1:n architecture, which Section 1.2 puts out of scope, where 1:1 is meant. Section 6 has "that is can be used" and "carried between in the G-ACh consenting nodes".editorialnone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below

RFC 6388: Label Distribution Protocol Extensions for Point-to-Multipoint and Multipoint-to-Multipoint Label Switched Paths

Depth: deep. Errata: none (the RFC has no errata). Status: Proposed Standard. Updated by: RFC 7358.

IDSectionQuoteIssueSeverityErratum
RA-02132.4.1.1"1. The candidate upstream LSRs are numbered from lower to higher IP address. ... 3. The selected upstream LSR U is the LSR that has the number H."The procedure exists so that all receivers on a LAN elect the same upstream LSR, but it does not say which address of a candidate is used (LSR Id, LDP transport address, or the candidate's address on the LAN), how IPv4 and IPv6 candidates are ordered against each other, or that numbering starts at 0 (H = CRC32 mod N ranges from 0 to N - 1, so numbering from 1 leaves the highest candidate unused and H = 0 unmatched). Two receivers that resolve these differently elect different forwarders, which is the duplication the procedure is meant to avoid.ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata
RA-02142.4.2.2"then Z propagates the Label Withdraw for <X, Y> to its upstream T, by sending a Label Withdraw <X, Y, L1> where L1 is the label Z had previously advertised to T"Section 2.4.1.4 uses T for the downstream LSR that sent the Label Mapping and U for the upstream LSR; here T names the upstream. The procedure is clear from "its upstream", but the letter swap makes the two sections read as if Withdraws go to the downstream peer.editorialnone: RFC has no errata
RA-02152.1, 3.1"The P2MP Capability TLV MUST be advertised in the LDP Initialization message. ... If the peer has not advertised the corresponding capability, then label messages using the P2MP FEC Element SHOULD NOT be sent to the peer."The capability is tied to Initialization only (no dynamic advertisement via RFC 5561 Capability messages, unlike RFC 6389 which says so explicitly), and sending P2MP / MP2MP FEC Elements to a peer without the capability is only a SHOULD NOT. Receive handling of such an element from a peer that did not advertise the capability is not stated (RFC 5561 leaves it to the capability document).ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata
RA-13708.3"If an LSR receives a Label Mapping message with an MBB parameter from downstream LSR-D and its upstream LSR-U has not advertised that it is MBB capable, the LSR MUST send an MBB notification immediately to LSR-U (see Section 8.4)."The MBB notification (Notification with MBB Status code 2) acknowledges a downstream LSR's MBB Label Mapping (8.1, 8.4.4), so in this case it can only be meant for LSR-D, whose switch-over would otherwise wait for the timeout. Sending it to LSR-U, as written, contradicts the sentence just before ("If an LSR has not advertised that it is MBB capable, its LDP peers MUST NOT send it messages that include MBB parameters"), since LSR-U is exactly the peer without the capability, and it gives LSR-U a notification for a label it never assigned.errornone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below
RA-13719, 3.2, 11"Type: The type of FEC Element Type. Either the P2MP FEC Element or the MP2MP FEC Element using the values defined for those FEC Elements when carried in the FEC TLV"There is no single "MP2MP FEC Element": Section 3.2 defines two, MP2MP upstream (0x07) and MP2MP downstream (0x08), whose labels go in opposite directions. Section 9 does not say whether a typed wildcard for MP2MP carries 0x07, 0x08 or either, nor whether a wildcard of one type (for example in a Label Withdraw or Release) applies to the labels of that direction only or to the whole MP2MP LSP. A sender using 0x08 to mean "all MP2MP state" and a receiver applying it to downstream labels only leave the upstream labels in place.ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below
RA-13722.2, 2.3, 3.2"Opaque Length: The length of the opaque value, in octets. / Opaque Value: One or more MP opaque value elements"The error handling of 2.2 (which 3.2 applies to MP2MP) covers only an Address Length that does not match the Address Family. It does not say what a receiver does when the opaque value elements do not exactly fill Opaque Length (an element running past it, or trailing octets), when Opaque Length is 0 although "one or more" elements are required, or when an element has the Reserved basic type 0 (Section 11). Transit LSRs need not interpret the opaque value (2.3), so the checks belong to roots and leaves, but whether a malformed opaque value is an "Unknown FEC", a malformed TLV or an opaque value that never matches is not stated. For the extended type, "Value: ... interpreted as specified by the Type field" should refer to the Extended Type field.ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata
RA-13735.2.1, 11"Since the notification does not refer to any particular message, the Message ID and Message Type fields are set to 0."The figure above the sentence shows the Notification message's own Message ID field, which RFC 5036 requires to identify the message, while "Message Type" exists only inside the Status TLV, so the sentence presumably means the Message ID and Message Type fields of the Status TLV. It is also left unstated which status code the Status TLV carries (only Section 11 names "LDP MP status", 0x00000040) and with which E and F bits.ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below
RA-13748.1, 3.3.2.2, 3"When LSR-U receives the MBB notification from LSR-U, it transitions to LSP state #3 / There is no need to send an MP2MP-U Label Withdraw <X, Y, Lu> to D because node D already removed Lu"In 8.1 the MBB notification comes from LSR-U's own upstream LSR, not from LSR-U. In 3.3.2.2 the upstream label that transit node Z assigned to D is Lu' (3.3.1.5: "sends an MP2MP-U Label Mapping <X, Y, Lu'> to node D"); Lu is the label Z received from its own upstream U, which the next paragraph releases to U. Section 3 also reads "acting equally an as Ingress or Egress LSR".editorialnone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below

RFC 6720: The Generalized TTL Security Mechanism (GTSM) for the Label Distribution Protocol (LDP)

Depth: deep (read in full). Errata: none (the RFC has no errata). Status: Proposed Standard. Updates: RFC 5036. Updated by: RFC 7552.

RA-02172.2, 2.3, 3"If an LSR that has sent and received LDP Link Hello with G flag = 1 from the directly connected neighbor, then the LSR MUST enforce GTSM procedures ... in the forthcoming TCP Transport Connection with that neighbor."The decision is described per Link Hello, but one LDP session can rest on several link adjacencies (parallel links) and on a targeted adjacency at the same time (case c of Section 3). The text does not say what to do when the Hellos on different links disagree on G, when the G flag changes on an established session, or when the only link adjacency goes away while the targeted one keeps the session up (the session is then multi-hop capable but GTSM is already enforced). RFC 6790: The Use of Entropy Labels in MPLS Forwarding

Depth: deep. Errata: 1 errata: 1 held. Status: Proposed Standard. Updates: RFC 3031, RFC 3107, RFC 3209, RFC 5036. Updated by: RFC 7274, RFC 7447, RFC 8012.

Resolved by a later RFC or re-targeted to its successor (kept for reference; not counted as open findings):

IDSectionIssue as foundOutcomeResolution
RA-00535.2The Entropy Label Capability attribute is described only as "of value 28";ResolvedRFC 7447 (updates RFC 6790) deprecates the BGP Entropy Label Capability attribute.
IDSectionQuoteIssueSeverityErratum
RA-13764.2, 4.3, 4.4"X MAY choose different values for the TTL and TC fields if it is known that the ELI will not be exposed as the top label at any point along the LSP (as may happen in cases where PHP is used and the ELI and EL are not stripped at the penultimate hop (see Section 4.4)."The example is the opposite case. When PHP is used and the penultimate hop does not strip ELI and EL (Section 4.4 makes stripping optional), the egress receives <ELI, EL, ...> with the ELI as the top label; Section 4.3 requires that egress to pop it ("an egress LSR that signals both ELC and implicit null MUST pop the ELI"). The ELI is therefore exposed exactly in the cited case, and is not exposed only with UHP or when the penultimate hop strips the pair. An implementer following the example sets non-copied TTL / TC on an ELI that becomes the top label, which an egress may use for the TTL and TC of the payload (4.1: "MAY use the tunnel TL's or ELI's TTL"). The parenthesis is also unbalanced.errornone: RFC has 1 errata, none on this point; proposed erratum below
RA-13775.1.1"If X understands the ELC TLV, and if any of the advertisements it received for FEC F does not include the ELC TLV, X MUST NOT include the ELC TLV in its own advertisements of F."An LSR using liberal label retention (the RFC 5036 default for downstream unsolicited) holds Label Mappings for F from every neighbour, including neighbours that are not next hops for F and upstream neighbours that use X as their own next hop. Read literally, a single non-ELC mapping from any of them withdraws ELC for the whole FEC, although only the mappings of the next hop(s) actually used determine whether the egress can pop ELs; conversely, a mapping from a non-next-hop neighbour cannot make the path EL-capable. Whether "the advertisements it received for FEC F" means all retained mappings or only those of the next hops used for forwarding, and what happens when the next-hop set changes without any mapping being resent (not listed among the re-evaluation triggers), is not stated.ambiguitynone: RFC has 1 errata, none on this point; proposed erratum below
RA-13786, header, 5.1, 8"This memo updates LSP traceroute by specifying that the value from the label range is to be placed in the entropy label."Section 6 states a normative change to LSP traceroute (RFC 4379, since obsoleted by RFC 8029), but the header lists "Updates: 3031, 3107, 3209, 5036" without RFC 4379, so implementers of LSP traceroute are not pointed to it. Smaller slips: 5.1 calls the Label Mapping a "Label Mapping Message TLV" and says "This bit MUST be set be set to 1"; Section 8 explains "The line with LS: shows the label stack on the wire", but the figures label those lines "Data Plane:" / "X-A:".editorialnone: RFC has 1 errata, none on this point; proposed erratum below

-----
   With liberal label retention, mappings from non-next-hop
   neighbours are retained but do not describe the path used.
   Next-hop changes (IGP reconvergence) change the egress capability
   without any LDP message, so they need to be a re-evaluation
   trigger too.

Depth: deep. Errata: none (the RFC has no errata). Status: Proposed Standard.

IDSectionQuoteIssueSeverityErratum
RA-06074.1"Ordered mode: An LSR needs to bind a label to a particular FEC if it knows how to forward packets for that FEC (i.e., it has a route corresponding to that FEC) and if it has already received at least one Label Request message from an upstream LSR."The definition does not match the one it claims to follow. RFC 5036 2.6.1.2: under Ordered control an LSR "may initiate the transmission of a label mapping only for a FEC for which it has a label mapping for the FEC next hop, or for which the LSR is the egress". Having a route and a pending Label Request describes Downstream on Demand with Independent control. The rest of 7032 (4.3.1 a., waiting for the next-next-hop label) relies on the RFC 5036 meaning, so the definition in 4.1 contradicts the procedure it introduces.errornone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below
RA-06085, 7"If the route is not available, the downstream LSR queues the request and replies as soon as the route becomes available. In the meantime, it does not send a "No Route" notification back."Security gap: A Queue Request TLV makes the downstream LSR hold state for every requested FEC without a route, with no limit, lifetime or per-peer bound, and the upstream "does not retry", so the state persists for the life of the session. An access LSR (the low-physical-security device of Section 7) can therefore make an ABR keep an unbounded number of pending requests for arbitrary FECs; Section 7.1 discusses FEC "stealing" but not this resource exhaustion. The section is also declared normative ("is to be treated as a normative reference") in an Informational document, and the receiver behaviour when a queued FEC's route later appears through a different next hop or when the queue must be dropped (e.g. memory pressure) is not specified.errornone: RFC has no errata
RA-06094.5, 4.4, 2.2"a. If it receives a Label Withdraw from the downstream access LSR/ABR. ... e. If it receives a Label Withdraw from a downstream DoD session."Items a and e of the Label Release list are the same case. Section 4.4 speaks of a Label Withdraw "with an empty label TLV", whereas RFC 5036 makes the Label TLV optional (absent), not empty. Figure 6 has a stray "2" after AGN11.editorialnone: RFC has no errata

RFC 7324: Updates to MPLS Transport Profile Linear Protection

Depth: deep. Errata: none (the RFC has no errata). Status: Proposed Standard. Updates: RFC 6378.

IDSectionQuoteIssueSeverityErratum
RA-13903, 5"If the LER is in remote Protecting Administrative state due to a remote Forced Switch, a local Signal Fail indication on the protection path SHALL cause the LER to remain in remote Protecting administrative state and transmit an SF(0,1) message."The new bullet creates a state that RFC 6378 4.3.3.3 never reached: remote Protecting administrative with an active local SF on protection. The RFC 6378 remote-message rules for that state do not cover it. A remote NR(0,0) (the far end clearing its FS) moves the LER to Normal only when "there is no active local Signal Fail indication" and handles only a local SF on working, so with a local SF-P no transition is defined (the LER should go to local Unavailable and send SF(0,0)). A remote Lockout or remote SF-P moves the LER to remote Unavailable sending NR(0,0), so the local protection failure is again reported as NR, the inaccuracy that Section 3 sets out to remove ("a node should not be sending NR if it has a local failure"). The extended states of RFC 6378 Appendix A (e.g. PA:F:R) do not distinguish a remote Protecting administrative state with an active local SF-P, so the table gives no guidance either.ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below
RA-13915"A remote No Request message SHALL be ignored if in local Protecting administrative state. / it fixes a similar issue -- if a node receives NR while in Remote administrative state, the value of FPath and Path have no bearing on the node's reaction to this NR."The change replaces only the first sentence of the RFC 6378 4.3.3.3 bullet, which concerns local Protecting administrative state, while the justification speaks of a node in remote administrative state. The following sentences of the same bullet ("If in remote Protecting administrative state and there is no active local Signal Fail indication, then the LER SHALL go to Normal state") were written for "A remote NR(0,0) message" and are not changed, so it is not clear whether a remote NR(0,1) in remote Protecting administrative state now leads to Normal (as the justification says) or is still covered by "All other remote messages SHALL be ignored". The deadlock description also says the nodes "transition into a remotely triggered WTR, and remain in remotely triggered WTR", but under RFC 6378 4.3.3.5 a remote SF-W in Wait-to-Restore leads to remote Protecting failure state, which is where the new 4.3.3.4 bullet applies.contradictionnone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below
RA-13922.1, 2.2.1, 2.2.2"Ensure the overall length of the message matches the value in the TLV Length + 12. / An implementation detecting a malformed TLV SHOULD alert the operator as described in Section 2.2.1."The PSC message (RFC 6378 Figure 2) has no length field of its own; its "overall length" is derived from the lower layer. On Ethernet, a PSC message with no TLVs is padded to the minimum frame size, so a receiver that applies the equality check literally finds extra octets and, by "MUST drop the message", discards every such message. The text does not say whether trailing octets beyond TLV Length + 12 are ignored, nor whether 12 includes the 4-octet G-ACh header (it does by Figure 2). Section 2.2.2 says only to alert the operator on a malformed TLV (Length not a multiple of 4, or a TLV that overruns TLV Length) but not whether the message is dropped or only that TLV ignored. RFC 6378 4.2.7 also still says TLV Length "MUST be 0" for basic operation, which a receiver checking "fields prior to TLV Length are consistent with RFC 6378" may apply.ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below
RA-13934.3, 4.1, 4.2"If there is a trigger that would cause the protection LSP to be used, such as SF or MS, a node MUST NOT use the protection LSP to carry traffic."The prohibition applies to an "irreconcilable" mismatch, but PSC has no negotiation and no capability signalling, so a node cannot know whether the peer supports the mode it is expected to adopt; the text gives no time or condition after which a mismatch becomes irreconcilable. Read as applying from the first mismatched message, a transient mismatch during reconfiguration blocks protection against an SF on working, and the text does not say which state the PSC state machine enters or which message is sent when a trigger is suppressed (e.g. whether SF(1,0) is still sent). "SF" is not qualified: an SF on protection never uses the protection LSP, so SF-W is presumably meant. 4.2 uses lowercase "must behave as in Section 4.3" for the same rule that 4.1 states as MUST.ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata
RA-13946"So, in the first example it is the local SF that drives the PSC Control logic / This will result in the PSC Control logic receiving both a local FS and remove FS."The first example is [L(FS), R(FS)], so the local FS (not SF) drives the logic; "remove FS" should be "remote FS". The replacement paragraph also drops the RFC 6378 4.3.3 phrase "as if the LER is in the Normal state" without saying from which state the reevaluation is applied: the transitions are defined per current state, and for the cases of this section (L(FS) removed in PA:F:L with R(FS) active) the current-state tables give a different result (Normal) from the one intended (PA:F:R).errornone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below

-------------
   o  If the LER is in remote Protecting Administrative state due to

   protection path SHALL cause the LER to remain in remote
   Protecting administrative state and transmit an SF(0,1) message.

--------------

   administrative state due to a remote Forced Switch with an active
   local Signal Fail on the protection path, a remote NR message
   SHALL cause the LER to go into local Unavailable state and
   transmit an SF(0,0) message, and a remote Lockout of protection
   or remote Signal Fail on protection message SHALL cause the LER
   to go into remote Unavailable state and transmit an SF(0,0)
   message.

Notes
-----

   state but did not adjust the remote-message reactions of RFC 6378
   4.3.3.3 for the new local condition.

"The LDP Hello message excluding the IP and the UDP headers" can mean the message alone or the whole UDP payload. If the PDU header is not covered, the LDP Identifier, which names the LSR and label space the Hello is for, is not authenticated and can be altered in transit.ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below
RA-02245.1"In this application, Ko is always L octets long. An implementation that feeds Ks to a standard HMAC routine produces different digests for 33 to 64 octet keys (HMAC-SHA-256) or 49 to 128 octet keys (HMAC-SHA-384 / -512).ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata
RA-02254, 6.2"the 2-octet LDP Cryptographic Protocol ID is appended to the authentication key prior to use (refer to Section 8)."The Protocol ID assignment is in Section 9 (IANA Considerations), not Section 8 (Security Considerations). Section 6.2 likewise says the hash is computed "as explained in Section 3", while the computation is in Section 5.editorialnone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below

RFC 7552: Updates to LDP for IPv6

Depth: deep. Errata: none (the RFC has no errata). Status: Proposed Standard. Updates: RFC 5036, RFC 6720.

IDSectionQuoteIssueSeverityErratum
RA-00546.1.1"Dual-Stack capability: TLV code point (Ox0701)"The Dual-Stack capability TLV code point is printed with a letter O ("Ox0701"); it is 0x0701.editorialnone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below
RA-02286.1.1"|TR | Reserved | MBZ |"The figure has three fields after TR (Reserved, MBZ) but the text defines only TR and Reserved, and no TLV Length is given (4 by the figure). A receiver does not know whether a Length other than 4 is an error. The section also does not say what happens when both sides agree on TR = 0110 (LDPoIPv6) but only IPv4 Hellos are received from the peer (for example, IPv6 Hellos filtered): no IPv6 transport address is known, so rule 2b cannot be applied and no session forms, while a TR mismatch (rule 1) discards all Hellos and also prevents any session.ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below
RA-02297.2"MUST NOT advertise FEC-label bindings for link-local or IPv4-mapped IPv6 addresses (defined in Section 2.5.5.2 of [RFC4291])"Section 2.5.5.2 of RFC 4291 defines IPv4-mapped addresses only; link-local unicast addresses are defined in Section 2.5.6. Section 7.1 cites 2.5.5.2 correctly for IPv4-mapped addresses alone.editorialnone: RFC has no errata
RA-13976.1.1"c) both IPv4 and IPv6 Hellos are received, then the neighbor is deemed as a noncompliant Dual-stack neighbor and is not allowed to have any LDP session. A Notification message should be sent (with status code of 'Dual-Stack Noncompliance', 0x00000033)."An LDP Notification is sent over an LDP session (TCP connection); in case 3c the neighbour "is not allowed to have any LDP session", so there is nothing to send it on unless a session already exists or one is opened only to send the notification. Rule 1 (TR mismatch) separates the two cases ("discard the Hello message and log an error"; "If an LDP session was already in place, ... send a fatal Notification"), rule 3c does not, and uses lower-case "should" for a status code that Section 10 registers as fatal (E bit 1). It also does not say whether the Hellos are discarded (rule 1) or the adjacencies kept, which decides whether the condition clears by itself when one family's Hellos stop.ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata
RA-13985.1, 9"[RFC6720] allows for the implementation to statically (via configuration) and/or dynamically override the default behavior (enable/disable GTSM) on a per-peer basis. (9) / the LDP Link Hello packets MUST have their IPv6 Hop Limit set to 255, be checked for the same upon receipt (5.1)"Section 5.1 and the last paragraph of Section 9 make the Hop Limit 255 send and check for IPv6 Link Hellos unconditional, while the paragraph in between says GTSM can be disabled per peer and that "GTSM negotiation would ultimately disable GTSM between the LSR and its peer(s)". Whether the per-peer override (and RFC 6720 negotiation) applies to IPv6 Link Hellos, or only to the LDPoIPv6 TCP connection that Section 9 merely recommends protecting, is not stated; a Link Hello from a peer that disabled GTSM would otherwise be dropped before any LDP processing.ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata
RA-139911"The extensions defined in this document only clarify the behavior of LDP; they do not define any new protocol procedures. Hence, this document does not add any new security issues to LDP."The document does define new protocol elements and procedures: the Dual-Stack capability TLV (0x0701), two fatal status codes, the transport-preference role logic, session resets on preference mismatch or non-compliance, and mandatory GTSM on IPv6 Link Hellos. A forged or mis-set TR value or Dual-Stack TLV (for example in a targeted Hello from an off-link sender when GTSM is not used for targeted Hellos) can reset an established session (6.1.1 rule 1, 3a, 3b), which the Security Considerations do not mention.editorialnone: RFC has no errata

RA-02312.2"On receipt of a valid TAC TLV, an LSR MUST generate its own TAC TLV with TAEs consisting of unique TA-Ids that it supports over the tLDP session."The procedure assumes the responder sees the initiator's TAC before sending its own Initialization, which holds only when the responder is the passive side (RFC 5036 2.5.4); a responder that has the active role sends its Initialization first. The text also allows a TAC with "zero or more TAEs" while a null intersection forces 'Targeted Application Capability Mismatch', so an empty TAC always rejects the session; the unit of "a maximum value -- that is, 0xFFFF" for the retry interval is not given; and the registry text says the range is 0x0001-0xFFFE while listing 0x0000 as Reserved and leaving 0xFFFF unassigned and unlisted.ambiguitynone: RFC has 1 errata, none on this point

Depth: deep. Errata: none (the RFC has no errata). Status: Proposed Standard. Updates: RFC 7271.

IDSectionQuoteIssueSeverityErratum
RA-14844.1"the node starts at the WTR state sending NR(0,1) or at the DNR state sending DNR(0,1) / Stop the WTR timer if it is running."A node that remembers the protection path as active restarts in the WTR state after the first action has stopped the WTR timer, and the section does not say whether the timer is started on entry. RFC 7271 Section 11 starts the timer only when a node that has recovered from a local failure or degradation enters WTR, which an initializing node with no local request is not. If the timer is not started, the node leaves WTR only through a remote message, so when and whether it reverts depends on the reading; two implementations of this section can therefore revert at different times or not at all.ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata
RA-14854.3"Therefore, the last received message MUST be treated as if it were NR and only the local request shall be evaluated."RFC 7271 gives NR messages different meanings by their Path value: NR with Path=1 leads to WTR (footnote 11) and NR(0,0) does not. The rule does not say which Path value the substituted NR carries, so after the protection path recovers, one implementation re-evaluates as for NR(0,0) and another as for NR(0,1). "Only the local request shall be evaluated" also uses a lower-case "shall" next to the MUST.ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata
RA-14864.3"If it is set, the state machine will transit to the supposed state, which can be Normal or DNR as indicated in the footnotes to the state transition table in Section 11.1 of [RFC7271]."The new text for the "i" flag depends on whether "re-evaluation is triggered", a condition this document does not define (RFC 7271 Section 11 uses re-evaluation for several events). The "supposed state" is taken from the footnotes of the local-request table (11.1), while "i" cells also occur in the remote-message table (11.2), whose footnotes are different. The text does not say which footnote applies to an "i" in 11.2, or what happens where no footnote names a state.ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata
RA-14874.1, 5"Clear any operator command in the Local Request Logic. / tightening the description of the initializing behavior may help to protect networks from restart attacks."Every operator command, including Lockout of protection and Forced Switch, is lost when the PSC Control Logic re-initializes, and the node may then start on the protection path (WTR or DNR state) or move traffic once a local failure is seen. The document does not say whether configured commands are restored, or whether the operator is notified that a Lockout set for maintenance is no longer in force. The Security Considerations do not mention that a forced restart removes such commands.ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata

The RLD advertised for the link""A Link MSD is advertised by a node for one of its own links. The text does not say which link applies when a NAS-pushing node evaluates a downstream node: the downstream node's link on which the packet arrives, or its link toward the next hop. RFC 9994: MPLS Network Action (MNA) Sub-Stack Specification Including In-Stack Network Actions and Data

Depth: deep. Errata: none (the RFC has no errata). Status: Proposed Standard. Updates: RFC 9789.

IDSectionQuoteIssueSeverityErratum
RA-140213.2.1, 4.2, 4.3, 6.2"There are, at most, 14 Format D LSEs per opcode (due to the NASL limit of 15 and the constraint of Format D requiring a Format C LSE), so there are at most 20 + 14 * 30 = 440 bit positions."The number of Format D LSEs following an opcode is given by that LSE's NAL field, which is 3 bits (4.2, 4.3), so at most 7 Format D LSEs can belong to one opcode; the bound of 14 derived from NASL is not reachable, and bit positions 230 to 439 of the registry cannot be encoded. The text also says Format D requires a Format C LSE, but 4.2, 5 and 6.2 ("LSE Formats: B, C, D") allow Format D after a Format B LSE; with Format B the Data field has 13 bits, so the numbering "Bit Position 20 is the most significant bit in the first LSE Format D Data field" leaves positions 13-19 undefined and does not say whether flags in the first Format D after a Format B start at 13 or at 20.errornone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below
RA-14035.2, 4.3"Thus, the available bits for data that can change by a transit node or differ among packets of the same flow in Format A and Format B LSEs is 0, in a Format C LSE 7 (bits 20-22 and 25-28)"In Format C (Figure 4) bits 20-22 are the low bits of the 16-bit Data field, bit 23 is S, bits 24-27 are the 4-bit Data field, bit 28 is U and bits 29-31 are NAL. The mutable data bits outside the label field are therefore 20-22 and 24-27; "25-28" omits data bit 24 and includes the U bit, so an implementation following the text would place flow-varying data in the U bit. The count (7) and the Format D range (20-22 and 24-31) are correct.errornone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below
RA-14044.2, 4.3, 4.4, 5"The NAL value MUST be less than or equal to the NASL value in the Format B LSE. If not, the packet MUST be dropped. (4.3) / The most significant bit MUST be set. (4.4)"The only length check given for a Format C LSE is NAL <= NASL; nothing requires that the Format B NAL plus, for each Format C LSE, 1 + its NAL add up to NASL, or says what a receiver does when a Format C NAL runs past the end of the NAS as given by NASL (or when the LSE expected to be Format C has its most significant bit set, i.e. looks like Format D). The receiver action for a Format D LSE whose most significant bit is 0 is also not stated. Different parsers will therefore treat a malformed NAS differently (drop, skip the NAS, or misparse the following labels as NAS LSEs), which matters because a misparsed NAS changes which LSEs are later treated as forwarding labels.ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata
RA-14057, 5.3, 9.3"The behavior of a node where a NAS with I2E and HbH scopes is also removed along with popping the forwarding label on a PHP node is outside the scope of this document. (7) / the penultimate node and penultimate SR-MPLS segment node MUST NOT remove the last copy of an HbH or I2E NAS (9.3)"Section 9.3 (and 5.3 for HbH: "the penultimate node MUST NOT remove a NAS with HbH scope") forbids exactly the removal that Section 7 declares out of scope, without saying whether Section 7 means MNA-incapable PHP nodes only. Section 5.3 also states that for HbH "All nodes along the path MUST process the NAS", while Section 7 requires that the NAS never be on top at an MNA-incapable node, which can then neither process nor remove it; the rule should be limited to MNA-capable nodes. Which node processes an I2E NAS when an MNA-incapable penultimate node pops it together with the transport label is left open.contradictionnone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below
RA-140612.3, 5.2"If a transit LSR chooses to use as much of the whole label stack as feasible as a key for the load-balancing function, the MNA-reserved label MUST NOT be used as a key for the load-balancing function, as specified in Section 4.3 of [RFC6790]."Only the Format A LSE (bSPL 4) is excluded. The Format B, C and D LSEs that follow are not labels, but an MNA-incapable LSR hashing the whole stack uses their 20-bit label fields as keys; Section 5.2 forbids flow-varying data there in general but then permits mutable data in the label field "where it is known that a load-balancing of data flows is not used", without saying that every LSR on the path, including MNA-incapable ones, must then avoid label-stack hashing. The text also does not say whether an MNA-capable LSR should exclude the whole NAS from the key.ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata
RA-140713.2.2, 11"Opcode is an integer with value 1-126. (13.2.2) / The RLD on the filtering node MUST be higher than the RLD on all other nodes in the provider MPLS domain. (11)"The registry field is limited to 1-126, but Table 5 assigns a registration procedure to 127 and Table 6 registers opcodes 0 and 127. In Section 11, "higher than the RLD on all other nodes" cannot be met when a domain has two or more filtering border nodes with the same RLD, since each is among the "other nodes" of the other; "at least as high as" (or "not lower than that of any non-filtering node") is presumably meant.editorialnone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below

Proposed erratum RA-1402 (RFC 9994, Section 13.2.1, 4.2, 4.3, 6.2; type: Technical):

Original Text
-------------
   There are, at most, 14 Format D LSEs per opcode (due to the NASL
   limit of 15 and the constraint of Format D requiring a Format C
   LSE), so there are at most 20 + 14 * 30 = 440 bit positions.  The
   value listed in the Bit Position column is an integer with value
   between 0-439.

Corrected Text
--------------
   There are, at most, 7 Format D LSEs per opcode (due to the 3-bit
   NAL field), so there are at most 20 + 7 * 30 = 230 bit positions.
    The value listed in the Bit Position column is an integer with
   value between 0-229.  When opcode 1 is carried in a Format B LSE,
   Bit Positions 13-19 are not present and Bit Position 20 is the
   most significant bit of the first Format D LSE that follows it.

Notes
-----
   Sections 4.2 and 4.3 define NAL as a 3-bit count of the Format D
   LSEs following an opcode LSE; Sections 4.2, 5 and 6.2 allow
   Format D after Format B. Table 4 (ranges up to 439) would need
   the same correction.

Proposed erratum RA-1403 (RFC 9994, Section 5.2, 4.3; type: Technical):

Original Text
-------------
   in a Format C LSE 7 (bits 20-22 and 25-28), and in a Format D LSE
   11 (bits 20-22 and 24-31).

Corrected Text
--------------
   in a Format C LSE 7 (bits 20-22 and 24-27), and in a Format D LSE
   11 (bits 20-22 and 24-31).

Notes
-----
   Per Figure 4, bit 28 of a Format C LSE is the U bit and bits
   24-27 are the 4-bit Data field.

Proposed erratum RA-1405 (RFC 9994, Section 7, 5.3, 9.3; type: Technical):

Original Text
-------------
   The behavior of a node where a NAS with I2E and HbH scopes is
   also removed along with popping the forwarding label on a PHP
   node is outside the scope of this document.

Corrected Text
--------------
   The behavior of an MNA-incapable node that removes a NAS with I2E
   or HbH scope along with the forwarding label when performing PHP
   is outside the scope of this document; an MNA-capable PHP node
   follows Section 9.3.

Notes
-----

Proposed erratum RA-1407 (RFC 9994, Section 13.2.2, 11; type: Editorial):

Original Text
-------------
   Opcode is an integer with value 1-126.

Corrected Text
--------------
   Opcode is an integer with value 0-127.

Notes
-----
   Tables 5 and 6 cover 0 and 127.

RFC 10041: Advertising Unreachable Links in OSPF

Depth: deep. Errata: 1 errata: 1 reported. Status: Proposed Standard. Updates: RFC 5443, RFC 6987, RFC 8379, RFC 8770.

IDSectionQuoteIssueSeverityErratum
RA-12273.1, 3.2"if the OSPF metric of a link is advertised as LSLinkInfinity (0xffff), it MUST NOT be considered during the associated SPF computation."Section 3.1 states the exclusion unconditionally, while Section 3.2 says "OSPF routers MUST NOT treat links with an advertised metric of LSLinkInfinity as unreachable unless all routers in the OSPF area ... have advertised this capability". Section 3.1 itself has no reference to the condition (only the Introduction says "subject to backward-compatibility, refer to Section 3.2"). An implementer reading Section 3.1 as the normative rule excludes such links in a mixed area, which is exactly the looping case of Figure 5.contradictionnone: RFC has 1 errata, none on this point; proposed erratum below
RA-12284.2.5"when "derived-from(/rt:routing/rt:control-plane-protocols/" + "rt:control-plane-protocol/rt:type, 'ospf:ospfv2') or ""The interface augment uses derived-from(), which (RFC 7950 Section 10.4.1) is true only for identities derived from 'ospf:ospfv2' / 'ospf:ospfv3', not for those identities themselves; a control-plane-protocol of type ospf:ospfv2 or ospf:ospfv3 therefore never satisfies the condition and the advertise-unreachable-link leaf is never available. The area augment in the same module uses derived-from-or-self(). The when expression also uses an absolute path to rt:type of every control-plane protocol, so it does not test the protocol instance that contains the interface (the same class of problem that erratum 9289 reports for the must expression). The "when" statements of ietf-ospf-functional-capability (Section 4.2.4) use the same absolute path.errornone: RFC has 1 errata, none on this point; proposed erratum below
RA-12294.2.3, 6.3"This document defines the initial version of the IANA-maintained "iana-ospf-functional-cap-bits" module, which mirrors the IANA "OSPF Router Functional Capability Bits" registry"Sections 4.2, 4.2.3 and 6.3 say the document defines three modules including the initial "iana-ospf-functional-cap-bits", but only two modules appear between CODE BEGINS / CODE ENDS (4.2.4 and 4.2.5). The base identity "functional-capability" that ietf-ospf-functional-capability imports and uses ("base iana-ospf-fc-bits:functional-capability"), and the identity for bit 0, are therefore not specified anywhere in the RFC; Section 6.3 gives naming rules for future identities but not the initial module's text, revision or identity names.errornone: RFC has 1 errata, none on this point; proposed erratum below
RA-12303.2"unless all routers in the OSPF area, i.e., all routers with router-LSAs in the area Link State Database (LSDB), have advertised this capability in an OSPFv2 Router Information Opaque LSA or an OSPFv3 Router Information LSA."The condition does not say whether only area-scoped Router Information LSAs count (Section 3.2 earlier says "area-scoped", but this sentence names any RI LSA, and the YANG module models the capability in link-, area- and AS-scoped RI LSAs), whether router-LSAs that are MaxAge or of routers unreachable in the SPF tree are counted, or how a router with several RI LSA instances (RFC 7770 multi-instance) is evaluated when the instances disagree. Different readings lead to different routers deciding differently, which is the inconsistency that Figure 5 shows leads to loops.ambiguitynone: RFC has 1 errata, none on this point
RA-12313.3, 3.4, 3.5, 4.1"When an OSPF router supports the Unreachable Link capability defined in this document, the OSPF stub router MaxLinkMetric (0xffff) MUST be updated to MaxReachableLinkMetric (0xfffe).""Supports" is not tied to the configuration of Section 4.1 ("Support of the Unreachable Link capability MUST be configurable. The default MUST be to not advertise the capability"). It is open whether a router that implements the capability but has it disabled (or is in an area where not all routers advertise it) advertises 0xfffe or 0xffff for stub-router, LDP-IGP-sync and graceful-shutdown links. Section 3.1's list of applicable LSAs also does not say whether router-LSA stub network (type 3) and virtual link (type 4) entries with 0xffff are covered.ambiguitynone: RFC has 1 errata, none on this point
RA-12325, 3.2"A compromised OSPF router could advertise changes to its Unreachable Link capability rapidly resulting in repeated route recalculations"Security gap: Besides recalculation load, a single router that omits or withdraws the capability (compromised, misconfigured, or a newly attached legacy router) makes every router in the area treat LSLinkInfinity links as reachable again (Section 3.2), so links meant only for TE or for a Flexible Algorithm start carrying default-topology traffic. The Security Considerations do not mention this traffic-steering effect or any means (such as monitoring the count of non-supporting routers) to detect it.errornone: RFC has 1 errata, none on this point
RA-12331, 3.2, 3.3, 3.4, 4.2.5"will revert to treating links with MaxLinkMetric as being reachable."The value 0xffff is called LSLinkInfinity where it means "unreachable" and MaxLinkMetric elsewhere, but the two names are mixed in the normative text (Section 3.2 last paragraph, 3.3 "Since MaxLinkMetric will not be used to indicate that a link is unreachable", and the YANG descriptions "interpretation of MaxLinkMetric as unreachable", "a metric of MaxLinkMetric (0xffff)"). LSLinkInfinity is never formally defined and is easily confused with LSInfinity (0xffffff) of RFC 2328 Appendix B, which Section 3.2 cites. Section 3.4 "in case of LDP packets between OSPF router loopbacks addresses" is garbled.editorialnone: RFC has 1 errata, none on this point

Proposed erratum RA-1227 (RFC 10041, Section 3.1, 3.2; type: Technical):

Original Text
-------------
   This document specifies that if the OSPF metric of a link is
   advertised as LSLinkInfinity (0xffff), it MUST NOT be considered
   during the associated SPF computation.

Corrected Text
--------------
   This document specifies that if the OSPF metric of a link is
   advertised as LSLinkInfinity (0xffff) and the condition of
   Section 3.2 is met, it MUST NOT be considered during the
   associated SPF computation.

Notes
-----
   Section 3.2 makes the exclusion conditional on every router in
   the area advertising the Unreachable Link capability; Section 3.1
   states it without that condition.

Proposed erratum RA-1228 (RFC 10041, Section 4.2.5; type: Technical):

Original Text
-------------
   when "derived-from(/rt:routing/rt:control-plane-protocols/" +
   "rt:control-plane-protocol/rt:type, 'ospf:ospfv2') or " +
   "derived-from(/rt:routing/rt:control-plane-protocols/" +
   "rt:control-plane-protocol/rt:type, 'ospf:ospfv3')" {

Corrected Text
--------------
   when "derived-from-or-self(../../../../../rt:type, 'ospf:ospfv2')
   or " + "derived-from-or-self(../../../../../rt:type,
   'ospf:ospfv3')" {

Notes
-----
   derived-from() excludes the named identity itself (RFC 7950
   Section 10.4.1), so for OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 instances the augment
   never applies; the area augment of the same module correctly uses
   derived-from-or-self(). The absolute path also tests every
   control-plane protocol rather than the containing one; erratum
   9289 reports the corresponding problem in the must expression.
   The corrected relative path assumes the context node is the
   augmented interface (interface, interfaces, area, areas, ospf,
   control-plane-protocol) and should be checked by the working
   group; the when statements of Section 4.2.4 have the same
   absolute-path issue.

Proposed erratum RA-1229 (RFC 10041, Section 4.2.3, 6.3; type: Technical):

Original Text
-------------
   This document defines the initial version of the IANA-maintained
   "iana-ospf-functional-cap-bits" module, which mirrors the IANA
   "OSPF Router Functional Capability Bits" registry
   [IANA-OSPF-FC-Bits].

Corrected Text
--------------
   (Add the initial "iana-ospf-functional-cap-bits" module, with the
   base identity "functional-capability" and the identity for bit 0
   "unreachable-link", in a CODE BEGINS
   CODE ENDS block in Section 4.2.3.)

Notes
-----
   The ietf-ospf-functional-capability module imports
   iana-ospf-functional-cap-bits and uses its base identity, but the

Pseudowires, VPLS and ICCP

RFC 4385: Pseudowire Emulation Edge-to-Edge (PWE3) Control Word for Use over an MPLS PSN

Depth: deep. Errata: 1 errata: 1 verified. Status: Proposed Standard. Updated by: RFC 5586.

IDSectionQuoteIssueSeverityErratum
RA-00554, 4.1, 4.2"The sequence number that follows 65535 (maximum unsigned 16-bit number) is one."The rules that exclude zero (wrap from 65535 to 1, zero meaning "not used") are written for every PW type, but TDM pseudowires (SAToP, CESoPSN, TDMoIP) use zero as an ordinary sequence number. The erratum limits the zero-excluding rules to non-TDM PWs and says a zero sequence number on a non-TDM PW is treated as in order.errorerratum 1743 (Verified), technical
RA-02374.2, Appendix"If the packet sequence number was not zero, then the expected sequence number is set to the packet sequence number plus one."In Section 4.2 this sentence follows all the cases and so applies to every packet with a non-zero sequence number, including one found "out of order" (outside the window); the non-normative Appendix calls updateExpected() only for in-order and in-window packets and not in processOutOfWindow(). Under the normative text a single stale or forged packet resets the expected number backwards, making all subsequent genuine packets appear out of window. Errata: Verified erratum 1743 changes the zero rules for TDM pseudowires; it does not address the out-of-window update.contradictionnone: RFC has 1 errata, none on this point (related: erratum 1743 (Verified), technical); proposed erratum below

Proposed erratum RA-0237 (RFC 4385, Section 4.2, Appendix; type: Technical):

Original Text
-------------
   If the packet sequence number was not zero, then the expected
   sequence number is set to the packet sequence number plus one.

Corrected Text
--------------
   If the packet was found to be in order or within the allowed
   receive sequence number window, and its sequence number was not
   zero, then the expected sequence number is set to the packet
   sequence number plus one.

Notes
-----
   The Appendix leaves the expected number unchanged for packets
   outside the window; the normative text should say the same.

RA-06203.5, 3.6"For the definition of the "PW Associated Channel Type" please refer to [RFC4385]."The sentence appears twice, once at the end of 3.5 (Pseudowire Status) where it does not belong, and again as the whole of 3.6. -------------

RA-06275, 5.1, 5.4.3, 6.2, 7.1"The PEs will establish an LDP session using the Extended Discovery mechanism described in [LDP, sections 2.4.2 and 2.5]."Several small errors: the tag [LDP] is not in the reference list (it is [RFC3036]); the 5.1 table gives "FEC" as the "Defined for Message" of two TLVs, which is not an LDP message (Label Mapping is meant); 5.4.3 says the PW Status TLV is sent "following the PW FEC and the interface parameter sub-TLVs" while its figure places it after the Generic Label TLV; 6.2 "the one that prefers not to use it is has no extra protocol"; 7.1 names 0x096C "Group ID TLV" while 5.3.2.2 calls it "PW Grouping ID TLV"; 7.2 truncates the 0x2B name ("Label Withdraw PW Status Method"). Later RFCs: RFC 8077 (obsoletes RFC 4447) fixes the reference tag, the TLV name, the message table and the grammar slip, but keeps 'following the PW FEC and the Interface Parameter Sub-TLVs' (Section 6.3.3).editorialnone: RFC has 10 errata, none on this point

RFC 4448: Encapsulation Methods for Transport of Ethernet over MPLS Networks

Depth: deep. Errata: 1 errata: 1 held. Status: Proposed Standard. Updated by: RFC 5462, RFC 8469.

IDSectionQuoteIssueSeverityErratum
RA-02384.6"Thus, if the source MAC address of an Ethernet frame carried over the PW without a control word present begins with 0x4 or 0x6, it could be mistaken for an IPv4 or IPv6 packet."An Ethernet frame (preamble and FCS stripped, 4.4) begins with the destination MAC address, so the nibble after the bottom label is the first nibble of the destination address, not the source address.errornone: RFC has 1 errata, none on this point; proposed erratum below
RA-02394.4.1, 4.1, 4.2"If an Ethernet PW is operating in tagged mode, every frame sent on the PW MUST have a service-delimiting VLAN tag. ... This is the default operating mode. This is the only REQUIRED mode."Tagged mode (PW type 0x0004) is the only REQUIRED and the default mode, while raw mode (0x0005) is the one that carries a whole port (4.2) and is the more common deployment; an implementation supporting only raw mode does not conform. The "dummy VLAN tag" to be prepended is not specified (VLAN ID, PRI, TPID), although 4.7 says a default PRI of zero MUST be supported "if an 802.1Q VLAN field is added".ambiguitynone: RFC has 1 errata, none on this point

Proposed erratum RA-0238 (RFC 4448, Section 4.6; type: Technical):

Original Text
-------------
   Thus, if the source MAC address of an Ethernet frame carried over
   the PW without a control word present begins with 0x4 or 0x6, it
   could be mistaken for an IPv4 or IPv6 packet.

Corrected Text
--------------
   Thus, if the destination MAC address of an Ethernet frame carried
   over the PW without a control word present begins with 0x4 or
   0x6, it could be mistaken for an IPv4 or IPv6 packet.

Notes
-----
   The destination MAC address is the first field of the transported
   frame and so immediately follows the label stack when no control
   word is used.

RFC 4761: Virtual Private LAN Service (VPLS) Using BGP for Auto-Discovery and Signaling

Depth: deep. Errata: none (the RFC has no errata). Status: Proposed Standard. Updated by: RFC 5462, RFC 8395, RFC 8614.

RA-06313.2.1, 3.2.2, 3.2.3"A label block defined by <LB, VBO, VBS> is the set {LB+VBO, LB+VBO+1, ..., LB+VBO+VBS-1}."Section 3.2.1 places the labels of a block at LB+VBO through LB+VBO+VBS-1 (and says the receiver adds "its (unique) VE ID to the label base"), while Section 3.2.2 says the label block for V is "labels from LB to (LB + VBS - 1)" with "VE ID (VBO + n) corresponds to label (LB + n)", and Section 3.2.3 computes the label as (LB + W - VBO). RA-06323.2.2"| Label Base (3 octets) | / The Length field is in octets."The encoding of the 3-octet Label Base is not given (a 20-bit label in the high-order bits as in RFC 3107, with the low 4 bits set to what, or a 24-bit number), and it is not said whether the 2-octet Length counts itself (implementations use 17, the octets that follow). RA-06333.3, 3.5"Two VPLS NLRIs are considered equivalent from a path selection point of view if the Route Distinguisher, the VE ID, and the VE Block Offset are the same."Multi-homing relies on BGP selecting one of two "equivalent" NLRIs, but the NLRIs also differ in Label Base (and possibly VE Block Size), so a standard BGP speaker or route reflector treats them as different prefixes and does not run path selection between them; the special comparison is not defined as a change to BGP route selection. Proposed erratum RA-0631 (RFC 4761, Section 3.2.1, 3.2.2, 3.2.3; type: Technical):

Original Text
-------------
   A label block defined by <LB, VBO, VBS> is the set {LB+VBO,
   LB+VBO+1, ..., LB+VBO+VBS-1}.

Corrected Text
--------------
   A label block defined by <LB, VBO, VBS> is the set {LB, LB+1,
   ..., LB+VBS-1}, where label LB+n is used by the PE with VE ID
   VBO+n.

Notes
-----
   Section 3.2.3 step 2 computes the label as LB + W - VBO; the
   3.2.1 sentence about adding the VE ID to the label base holds
   only for VBO = 0.

RFC 4762: Virtual Private LAN Service (VPLS) Using Label Distribution Protocol (LDP) Signaling

Depth: deep. Errata: 2 errata: 1 verified, 1 held. Status: Proposed Standard.

IDSectionQuoteIssueSeverityErratum
RA-0056Appendix A"In a VPLS, we use a VCID (which, when using the PWid FEC, has been substituted with a more general identifier (AGI)"The PWid FEC (FEC 128) has a PW ID, not a VCID field, and the AGI belongs to the Generalized PWid FEC (FEC 129), not the PWid FEC. Read literally, the sentence mixes the two encodings.editorialerratum 4144 (Verified), editorial
RA-10636.2.1"The MAC Address Withdraw Message contains a FEC TLV (to identify the VPLS affected), a MAC Address TLV, and optional parameters."The message is an LDP Address Withdraw message, whose format in RFC 5036 Section 3.5.6 has a mandatory Address List TLV and no FEC TLV. The text does not say whether an (empty) Address List TLV is included, so a sender that omits it can be answered by an RFC 5036 receiver with a "Missing Message Parameters" notification, and a receiver that requires it rejects senders that omit it. The statement that a PE that "does not understand" the message "MUST ignore the message" cannot apply as written, since every LDP speaker understands Address Withdraw; only the unknown MAC List TLV (U = 1) is ignored, after which an RFC 5036 receiver processes the message as an address withdrawal. The text also names the TLV "MAC Address TLV" here and "MAC List TLV" elsewhere.contradictionnone: RFC has 2 errata, none on this point; proposed erratum below
RA-10646.2.2"- Remove the association between the MAC address and the AC or PW over which this message is received."The message is received over an LDP session, not over an AC or PW. Read as "the PW to the sender", a listed MAC is unlearned only where it is associated with the sender's PW, which is the opposite of the empty-list rule two lines later ("Remove all the MAC addresses ... except the MAC addresses learned over the PW associated with this signaling session") and of the use in Section 10.2.2, where the sender withdraws MACs that have moved towards it. The intended scope (the listed MACs wherever learned in the VPLS, or only those not learned over the sender's PW) is not stated.ambiguitynone: RFC has 2 errata, none on this point; proposed erratum below
RA-10656.2.1, 6.2.2"The scope of a MAC List TLV is the VPLS specified in the FEC TLV in the MAC Address Withdraw Message."Which FEC element identifies the VPLS is not stated: the PWid FEC element of one PW (Appendix A, with a PW ID that may be the VPLS-wide VCID), or a Generalized PWid FEC element (with AGI and which SAII / TAII). Where an H-VPLS spoke and mesh PWs to the same peer carry different identifiers, the receiver cannot tell from the text which VSI is meant.ambiguitynone: RFC has 2 errata, none on this point
RA-10666.1.1, 8.1, 15, Appendix A"PW type: The allowed PW types are Ethernet (0x0005) and Ethernet tagged mode (0x004), as specified in [RFC4446]."Ethernet tagged mode is written "0x004" next to "0x0005" (the RFC 4446 value is 0x0004); Section 15 gives the MAC List TLV type as "0x404" while Section 6.2.1 says 0x0404. The Appendix A figure labels the first octet "PW TLV" although it is the PWid FEC element type (0x80) of RFC 4447. Sections 8.1 and 14 cite RFC 3036, since obsoleted by RFC 5036 (the "Unknown FEC" status code and the authentication method are unchanged there).editorialnone: RFC has 2 errata, none on this point

Proposed erratum RA-1063 (RFC 4762, Section 6.2.1; type: Technical):

Original Text
-------------
   The MAC Address Withdraw Message contains a FEC TLV (to identify
   the VPLS affected), a MAC Address TLV, and optional parameters.

Corrected Text
--------------
   The MAC Address Withdraw Message is an LDP Address Withdraw
   Message [RFC5036] that contains an Address List TLV with no
   addresses, a FEC TLV (to identify the VPLS affected), a MAC List
   TLV, and optional parameters. A receiver MUST NOT treat the empty
   Address List TLV as withdrawing any address.

Notes
-----
   RFC 5036 Section 3.5.6 makes the Address List TLV mandatory in
   Address Withdraw. Implementations differ on whether an empty
   Address List TLV is sent, which affects interoperability with
   receivers that check mandatory parameters.

Proposed erratum RA-1064 (RFC 4762, Section 6.2.2; type: Technical):

Original Text
-------------
   -  Remove the association between the MAC address and the AC or
   PW over which this message is received.

Corrected Text
--------------
   -  Remove the association between the MAC address and the AC or
   PW with which it is currently associated in the VPLS instance
   specified by the FEC TLV.

Notes
-----
   An LDP Address Withdraw message is not received over an AC or PW.
   Read as the sender's PW, the per-MAC rule would only unlearn MACs
   already pointing at the sender, which defeats its purpose in
   Section 10.2.2.

RA-02414, 5.3, 7"The decision of the type of VCCV control channel is left completely to the receiving control entity ... RA-024310"For this reason implementations MUST provide a method to secure the data plane."Security gap: The MUST is met by "providing the ability to architect the MPLS network in such a way that no external MPLS packets can be injected", which is a deployment property, not an implementation method; the requirement is therefore not testable. IDSectionIssue as foundOutcomeResolution
RA-024414.5, 7.4.1Length of sub-TLV 0x06 is 14 octets per Section 7.4.1, not 12.ResolvedRFC 7267 Section 6 (updates RFC 6073) sets the length of sub-TLV 0x06 to 14.
IDSectionQuoteIssueSeverityErratum
RA-02457.4.1, 7.6"The SP-PE TLV MUST contain the appropriate mandatory sub-TLVs specified below."None of the sub-TLVs that follow is marked mandatory: 0x01 and 0x05 apply only to FEC 128 or FEC 129 segments, the description, local and remote IP address sub-TLVs are "OPTIONAL", and 0x06 is "recommended". Loop detection (7.6) compares the S-PE's "own IP address" with the received TLVs, which only works when each S-PE includes the optional Local IP address sub-TLV (0x03); VCCV to an S-PE (9.5) needs the same. The text therefore requires a set of mandatory sub-TLVs that it never defines.contradictionnone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below
RA-024610"Only one SP-PE TLV can be present in this message. The message is therefore never relayed unchanged: at least its FEC (and, per 10.1.5 / 10.2, possibly its SP-PE TLV) is rewritten at each S-PE.contradictionnone: RFC has no errata
RA-02477.2.1"The SAII and TAII are compared as unsigned integers; if the SAII is larger, then the T-PE assumes the active role."For AII Type 2 the identifiers are 12-octet structures (Global ID, Prefix, AC ID) and AII Type 1 is 4 octets; "compared as unsigned integers" does not say whether the AII Type and Length octets take part, how identifiers of different types or lengths compare, or what happens when they are equal.ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata
RA-14089.6.1.3"The operation to be taken by the node receiving the echo reply in response to an echo request depends on the VCCV mode of operation described above. The detailed procedures for handling echo replies in each mode (connectivity verification, path verification, path trace) are in Section 9.6.2.errornone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below
RA-14099.5.1, 9.6.2.1"When using CC Type 1 for MS-PWs, the PE transmitting the VCCV packet MUST set the TTL to the appropriate value to reach the destination S-PE. (9.5.1) / However, VCCV Type 1 (which can be use for end-to-end verification only) is only supported if the CW is enabled. (9.6.2.1)"Section 9.5.1 describes CC Type 1 aimed at an S-PE by setting the PW label TTL, while 9.6.2.1 says CC Type 1 can be used for end-to-end verification only; 9.6.2.2 then tells an S-PE that a TTL-expired packet is recognised as VCCV "by checking the CW", which again supposes CC Type 1 to an intermediate node. Whether a T-PE may target an S-PE with CC Type 1 is therefore stated both ways. 9.6.2.3 also says "support the Control Word CC Type 3", mixing CC Type 1 (control word) and CC Type 3 (TTL expiry); and "can be use" should be "can be used".contradictionnone: RFC has no errata
RA-14109.6.1.1, 7.4.1"The necessary SP-PE sub-TLVs are: 0x01 PWid of last PW segment traversed / 0x03 Local IP address of PW Switching Point / 0x04 Remote IP address of last PW Switching Point traversed or of the T-PE"The list covers only FEC 128 segments. For a segment signalled with FEC 129, the target FEC of the echo request has to be built from sub-TLV 0x05 (FEC Element of last PW segment traversed), which is not listed; 0x04 is itself optional ("SHOULD only be included if ...") so the previous-hop address may have to be taken from the 0x03 of the preceding SP-PE TLV. 9.6.2.5 (iii) likewise speaks only of "the FEC 128 information for the next segment".ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata
RA-141110.1"however, only the failure from the remote closest S-PE will be stored (last PW status message received). The PW status word received is just ORed to any existing remote PW status already stored on the T-PE."The two sentences give different rules for the T-PE's remote status: keeping only the last received status message replaces the stored word, ORing accumulates bits from every S-PE and from the remote T-PE. (4)"In Figure 3, PE1 is a T-PE; the switching point is S-PE1 (SPE1), as the next sentence says ("selection of S-PE1"). -------------

   specified below.

Corrected Text
--------------

   Point" sub-TLV and, for the segment just traversed, either the
   "PWid of last PW segment traversed" (FEC 128) or the "FEC Element
   of last PW segment traversed" (FEC 129) sub-TLV.

-----
   Every sub-TLV in 7.4.1 is optional or conditional; Section 7.6

Whether "the 8 bytes of the VPLS-id" are the Extended Community octets including type and sub-type, or an RD-style encoding of the 6-octet value (2-octet RD type, then AS / IPv4 address and number), is not stated; implementations are known to use the RD-style form, which is not what a literal reading gives. RA-02493.2.2.1"If a PE receives a BGP update from which any of the elements specified above is absent, the update should be ignored.""Ignored" (lower-case "should") is not defined against BGP route handling: if a previous advertisement of the same NLRI was valid, ignoring the update leaves the old route and its PWs in place although the advertiser replaced it; RFC 7606 would instead treat such a route as withdrawn, or keep it but not use it. The text also does not say whether a route reflector, which does not import the route, should still reflect it.ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata

No code "Attachment Circuit already bound to remote Attachment Circuit" exists, so the duplicate-pool case of 3.3.3 cannot be encoded; an implementer must either reuse 0x2D / 28 (whose name describes a different condition, a binding to a different remote AC) or invent a value.errornone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below
RA-14144.1"For VPWS, the BGP advertisement and PW signaling are exactly as described in Section 3.3. ... RA-14153.4, 3.3.2.1"During BGP-based auto-discovery, the pool color is still encoded in the RD, but if the pool is configured with a set of "export RTs", these are encoded in the RTs of the BGP Update messages INSTEAD of the color (3.4)"Section 3.3.2.1, to which 3.4 refers as the full-mesh base case, does not encode the color in the RD: the RD is an identifier of the VPWS instance prepended to the pool number, the VPWS identifier is carried in an Extended Community, and the color is encoded in the RT ("with the RT that encodes the pool's color"). RA-14163.5.1, 3.5.2"A "Remote" list: {<IP address, k>} ... In the above example, E would be given the remote list: {<2, F>}. More importantly, 3.5.2 says an N-PE advertises "the number of U-PEs for each VPLS" and points to 3.2.2, which defines no field for such a count: 3.2.2.1 only says an N-PE advertises one NLRI per VSI (RD plus a U-PE address). Declaring 128 invalid (and "MUST be rejected as having a bad packet format") forbids the normal advertisement; only 129 to 159 cut into the AC ID.    cannot be aggregated.

--------------
   Lengths of 129 bits to 159 bits are invalid, as the AC ID field
   cannot be aggregated.

Notes
-----
   RD 64 + Global ID 32 + Prefix 32 = 128 bits ends exactly at the
   AC ID; only lengths inside the AC ID (129-159) are partial AC
   IDs.

RFC 7275: Inter-Chassis Communication Protocol for Layer 2 Virtual Private Network (L2VPN) Provider Edge (PE) Redundancy

Depth: deep. Errata: none (the RFC has no errata). Status: Proposed Standard.

IDSectionQuoteIssueSeverityErratum
RA-02524.2.1, 4.4.2, 4.2"CAPREC ... Receive any other ICCP message CAPREC Action: Transmit NAK TLV in RG Notification message"In CAPREC and CONNECTING, every ICCP message other than an acceptable RG Connect is answered with a NAK, and an RG Notification carrying a NAK is itself "any other ICCP message". Two PEs that are both in CAPREC (for example after one rejected the other's Connect, which per 4.2 makes the sender "stop attempting") therefore answer each other's NAKs with NAKs indefinitely. The application state machine has the same pattern ("Receive any other Application TLV ... Transmit NAK TLV" in RESET, CONNSENT, CONNREC, CONNECTING). The text in 4.2 that a rejected PE stops is not reflected in the tables, which have no "Receive NAK" event at the ICCP level.contradictionnone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below
RA-02534.4.2"CONNSENT ... Receive Application Connect TLV with A-bit=1 OPERATIONAL ... Receive any other Application TLV RESET Action: Transmit NAK TLV"When both PEs send their Application Connect (A-bit = 0) at the same time, each is in CONNSENT and receives a Connect with A-bit = 0, which the table treats as "any other Application TLV": both reset and NAK, and after 4.4 ("MUST stop attempting ... until it receives a new Application Connection request") neither retries. The ICCP connection table likewise has no OPERATIONAL entry for a received RG Connect, so a repeated Connect after a restart of the peer's application is undefined.contradictionnone: RFC has no errata
RA-02544.2.1, 8"S-bit ... 0 - The TLV is withdrawing the capability specified by the TLV Code Point."Section 8 lets a peer withdraw the ICCP capability with a Capability message (S = 0, RFC 5561 dynamic capabilities), but the ICCP Connection state machine has no event for a withdrawn capability: CAPREC, CONNECTING and OPERATIONAL leave only on "LDP session torn down" or an RG Disconnect. Whether a withdrawal takes the RG connections (and their applications) down, and to which state they return, is not specified.ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata
RA-02556.4.1"iii. ICCP Application Connection Count Exceeded (0x00010003) This is used to reject a new incoming Application Connection that would cause the local PE's ICCP connection count to exceed its capabilities."The code is for the Application Connection count; the text says "ICCP connection count", which is the condition of code ii.editorialnone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below
RA-02564.6"A PE that requires a separate LDP session will advertise a separate LDP adjacency with a non-zero label space identifier."The ICCP connection state machine is per LDP session (NONEXISTENT means "no LDP session"); with a dedicated session the text does not say which of the two sessions carries the RG, whether the ICCP capability is advertised on both, or what happens to the RG when only one of them fails. A non-zero label space identifier also denotes a per-interface label space in RFC 5036.ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata
RA-14187.2.7"Partner Port Number ... 2 octets encoding the LACP Partner Port Number ... The Port Number MUST be encoded with the Node ID, as discussed above."The Node ID encoding of 7.2.3 (most significant bit 1, next three bits the RG member's Node ID) exists to make the Port Numbers of the PEs in an RG unique. The Partner Port Number is the port number chosen by the partner system (the multi-homed CE, 9.2.2.3 "on the Partner (i.e., multi-homed device) side"), which knows nothing about the RG Node IDs, so the sender cannot encode it with a Node ID and a receiver that checks the encoding rejects valid State TLVs. The requirement can only apply to the Actor Port Number (which carries the same sentence).errornone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below
RA-14199.2.2.1, 9.2.2.2, 7.2.3"every PE MUST use the values for the two parameters that are supplied by the PE with the numerically lowest value (among RG members) of System Aggregation Priority.""System Aggregation Priority" is not defined; the mLACP System Config TLV (7.2.3) carries only "System Priority" (and System ID, Node ID). 9.2.2.2 uses the same undefined term to choose the Aggregator MAC address. Neither rule says how equal priorities are resolved (two PEs with the default LACP priority are the common case), so PEs can select different System IDs and MAC addresses and present two LACP systems to the CE.ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below
RA-14209.1.3.1, 9.1.3.2, 7.1.3, 7.1.4"If this condition is not satisfied after the PEs have exchanged "PW-RED State TLVs", a PE MUST disable the associated pseudowire(s)"Both mode sections evaluate PW Priority "after the PEs have exchanged 'PW-RED State TLVs'" and choose the active PE "after all of the PEs in an RG have exchanged their 'PW-RED State TLVs'", but the PW Priority is carried only in the PW-RED Config TLV (7.1.3); the State TLV (7.1.4) carries ROID and local / remote PW status. An implementer cannot tell whether the priority check and the election wait for State TLVs, for Config TLVs, or for both (for example after a Config change that only alters the priority).errornone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below
RA-14216.4, 6.4.1, 4.2"The Notification message MUST only be sent to a PE that is already part of an RG."4.2 requires a PE to reject an RG Connect for an RG it is not a member of, and 6.4.1 i defines "Unknown ICCP RG" for exactly that case ("an RG that is not configured on the local PE"). The rejecting PE has no RG in common with the sender, so the 6.4 restriction, read literally, forbids the Notification that 4.2 and 6.4.1 i require. Whether "already part of an RG" means an RG configured locally, the RG named in the message, or any LDP peer with the ICCP capability is not stated.ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below
RA-14224.4.2, 6.3, 6.4.1, 9.1.3, 9.2.2.3, 7.2.2.1"RESET: This state indicates that an ICCP connection is operational between the PEs but that the Application Connection has not been initialized yet or has been resent."Editorial inconsistencies: (a) 4.4.2 "has been resent" for "has been reset"; (b) 9.1.3 and 9.2.2.3 order the response by the "'Synchronization Response TLV' with the 'Synchronization Data Start' flag", a TLV name that does not exist (7.1.6 / 7.2.10 define the "Synchronization Data TLV"); (c) status codes are named differently in the text and in 12.4 ("RG Removed" / "ICCP RG Removed" in 6.3, "Rejected Message" / "ICCP Rejected Message" and "Incompatible Protocol Version" / "Incompatible ICCP Protocol Version" in 6.4.1 and 4.4.1); (d) the mLACP Disconnect Cause String (7.2.2.1) has no encoding, while the PW-RED one (7.1.2.1) is UTF-8 without terminating null.editorialnone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below

Proposed erratum RA-0252 (RFC 7275, Section 4.2.1, 4.4.2, 4.2; type: Technical):

Original Text
-------------
   Receive any other ICCP message CAPREC
   Action: Transmit NAK TLV in RG Notification message

Corrected Text
--------------
   Receive RG Notification message CAPREC
   (no action)
   Receive any other ICCP message CAPREC
   Action: Transmit NAK TLV in RG Notification message

Notes
-----
   An RG Notification is an ICCP message, so "any other ICCP
   message" includes the NAK sent in reply; two PEs in CAPREC or
   CONNECTING exchange NAKs without end. The same applies to the
   Application Connection state machine. Section 4.2 says a rejected
   PE stops attempting, but the tables have no event for receiving a
   NAK.
