RFC 9776: Internet Group Management Protocol, Version 3

Depth: deep. Errata: none (the RFC has no errata). Status: Internet Standard (STD 100). Obsoletes: RFC 3376. Updates: RFC 2236.

IDSectionQuoteIssueSeverityErratum
RA-03768.12 vs 9777 9.12"This value SHOULD be [Robustness Variable] times [Query Interval] plus (10 times the Max Response Time in the last received Query Message)."Section 4.1.1 defines Max Response Time "in units of 1/10 second", so converting it to seconds divides by 10; "10 times the Max Response Time" gives a value 100 times too large if read in seconds, or one second-unit per 1/100 s if read in units. The MLDv2 republication (RFC 9777 9.12) keeps "plus ([Query Response Interval])" for the same timer, so the two documents, updated together, disagree on the formula. The text also turns the RFC 3376 MUST into a SHOULD and says hosts should use default values for a figure that depends on the last received Query.errornone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below
RA-03778.4, 8.13"This value MUST be ([Robustness Variable] times [Query Interval]) plus (2 * [Query Response Interval]). (8.4) / This value MUST be ([Robustness Variable] times [Query Interval]) plus [Query Response Interval]. (8.13)"In RFC 3376 the Older Host Present Interval equalled the Group Membership Interval, so a group kept its older-version compatibility mode for as long as the older host's membership lasted. With 8.4 changed (Erratum 6725) and 8.13 unchanged, compatibility mode now ends one Query Response Interval before the membership created by the older report expires; during that window IGMPv3 BLOCK and TO_IN records are processed for a group whose only member may be an IGMPv1/v2 host. Whether 8.13 was meant to follow 8.4 is not said. RFC 9777 9.4 / 9.13 has the same split.ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata
RA-14509"IGMP provides any form of confidentiality. This means any device on a link can passively receive any IGMP message on the link."A word is missing and the sentence states the opposite of what is meant: IGMP provides no confidentiality, as the next sentence and the rest of the section explain.editorialnone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below
RA-14516.6.2, 7.3.1"If a router receives an older version General Query, it MUST use the oldest version of IGMP on the network. (6.6.2) / This must be administratively assured; routers that desire to be compatible with IGMPv1 and IGMPv2 MUST have a configuration option (7.3.1)"Section 6.6.2 reads as an automatic downgrade triggered by receipt of an older-version General Query, while Section 7.3.1 says the lowest version is "administratively assured" through configuration and that a router "not explicitly configured to use IGMPv1 or IGMPv2" that receives such a Query only logs a rate-limited warning. An implementer cannot tell whether a received IGMPv1/IGMPv2 General Query must change the router's operating version or only be reported. The same pair of statements was in RFC 3376.contradictionnone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below
RA-14527.2.1"When the IGMPv2 Querier Present timer expires, a host switches to Host Compatibility Mode of IGMPv3."Table 11 keeps IGMPv1 mode while the IGMPv1 Querier Present timer runs, whatever the IGMPv2 timer does; the sentence switches the host to IGMPv3 when the IGMPv2 timer expires even if the IGMPv1 timer is still running. The router-side text in Section 7.3.2 was given the missing condition ("When the IGMPv2-Host-Present Timer expires and the IGMPv1-Host-Present Timer is not running"), the host-side text was not.contradictionnone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below
RA-14536.2.3, 6.4.2"Source timers are always updated (for a particular group) whenever the source is present in a received record for that group."Table 9 does not update source timers for every source present in a record: for INCLUDE (A) + BLOCK (B) no timer is set (only Q(G,A*B) is sent), and for EXCLUDE (X,Y) + BLOCK (A) or TO_EX (A) only A-X-Y is set (to the Group Timer), so sources of A already in X or Y keep their timers. The general statement in 6.2.3 contradicts the tables, which are the operative rules.contradictionnone: RFC has no errata
RA-14544.1.12, 5.2, 9.1"a system MUST accept and process any Query whose IP Destination Address field contains any of the addresses (unicast or multicast) assigned to the interface (4.1.12) / Hosts SHOULD ignore v1, v2, or v3 General Queries sent to a multicast address other than 224.0.0.1 (9.1)"A General Query sent to a group the interface has joined (an address "assigned to the interface") must be accepted by 4.1.12 and should be ignored by 9.1. Section 9.1 also says hosts "SHOULD ignore v2 or v3 Queries without the Router Alert option", 4.1.12 has no such exception, and 5.2 describes only the processing of "a Query with the Router Alert option", leaving open how an IGMPv1 Query (which carries no Router Alert) or an accepted Query without it is processed.contradictionnone: RFC has no errata
RA-14555.1, 6.4, 8.14.3, 9.3"the non-existent pending report to merge with can be treated as a Source-Change Report with empty ALLOW and BLOCK records (5.1) / ignore IGMPv1/IGMPv2 Report and IGMPv2 DONE messages (6.4)"Terminology slips: "Source-Change Report" is not defined (State-Change Report / Source-List-Change Record are); "DONE" is the MLD message name, the IGMPv2 message is Leave Group; 8.14.3 and 9.3 say "Source-and-Group Specific Query" where the rest of the document says "Group-and-Source Specific Query". Section 8.3 says the number of seconds of the Query Response Interval "must be less than the [Query Interval]" while 8.14.2 says the Query Interval "MUST be equal to or longer than" the Max Response Time, so the equal case is allowed by one and excluded by the other.editorialnone: RFC has no errata

Proposed erratum RA-0376 (RFC 9776, Section 8.12 vs 9777 9.12; type: Technical):

Original Text
-------------
   This value SHOULD be [Robustness Variable] times [Query Interval]
   plus (10 times the Max Response Time in the last received Query
   Message).

Corrected Text
--------------
   This value SHOULD be [Robustness Variable] times [Query Interval]
   plus (the Max Response Time in the last received Query Message,
   converted to seconds, i.e., one tenth of its value in units of
   1/10 second).

Notes
-----
   RFC 3376 Erratum 4375 (Held for Document Update) proposed "plus
   (one Query Response Interval in the last Query received)", i.e.
   the received Max Response Time converted to seconds; the
   published text multiplies by 10 instead of dividing. Whichever
   formula is intended, IGMPv3 and MLDv2 should agree.

Proposed erratum RA-1450 (RFC 9776, Section 9; type: Editorial):

Original Text
-------------
   IGMP provides any form of confidentiality.

Corrected Text
--------------
   IGMP does not provide any form of confidentiality.

Notes
-----
   The following sentence ("any device on a link can passively
   receive any IGMP message") shows that the intended statement is
   that IGMP provides no confidentiality.

Proposed erratum RA-1451 (RFC 9776, Section 6.6.2, 7.3.1; type: Technical):

Original Text
-------------
   If a router receives an older version General Query, it MUST use
   the oldest version of IGMP on the network.

Corrected Text
--------------
   If a router receives an older version General Query, the oldest
   version of IGMP on the network has to be used; as described in
   Section 7.3.1, this is assured administratively, and a router
   that is not configured for that version logs a warning.

Notes
-----
   Section 7.3.1 requires a configuration option and only a
   rate-limited warning when an unconfigured router receives an
   IGMPv1 or IGMPv2 General Query, so the MUST in Section 6.6.2
   cannot be met automatically as written. The text is unchanged
   from RFC 3376.

Proposed erratum RA-1452 (RFC 9776, Section 7.2.1; type: Technical):

Original Text
-------------
   When the IGMPv2 Querier Present timer expires, a host switches to
   Host Compatibility Mode of IGMPv3.

Corrected Text
--------------
   When the IGMPv2 Querier Present timer expires and the IGMPv1
   Querier Present timer is not running, a host switches to Host
   Compatibility Mode of IGMPv3.

Notes
-----
   Section 7.3.2 contains the corresponding condition for routers;
   Table 11 keeps IGMPv1 mode while the IGMPv1 Querier Present timer
   runs.

IDSectionQuoteIssueSeverityErratum
RA-077611.3"the 100th percentile is 18; and the 0th percentile is -infinity, as is the 15th percentile."With the definition just given ("the smallest value of x for which F(x) >= a given percentage") and the example data (-2, 7, 7, 4, 18, -5), F(-5) = 1/6 (about 16.7%) >= 15%, so the 15th percentile is -5, not -infinity; only the 0th percentile is -infinity.errornone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below
RA-077718 (Appendix)"If we wish to test whether a set of values, X, is consistent with a given distribution G(x), we first compute Y = G_inverse(X)"The probability integral transform that maps X to Unif(0, 1) is Y = G(X), the distribution function itself; the code that follows does exactly that (x[i] = 1.0 - exp(-x[i] / mean) for the exponential case). Applying the inverse would not give uniform values. Also Section 11.4 "uniformly distributed across [T, dT]" should be [T, T+dT] (as in 11.1.1).errornone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below
RA-07784, 6.1, 6.2, 10.1"if the methodology is used multiple times under identical conditions, the same measurements should result in the same measurements."The sentence is garbled (6.2 restates it correctly: "it should result in consistent measurements"). RFC 4656: A One-way Active Measurement Protocol (OWAMP)

Depth: deep. Errata: none (the RFC has no errata). Status: Proposed Standard. Updated by: RFC 7717, RFC 7718, RFC 8545.

IDSectionQuoteIssueSeverityErratum
RA-07793.3"The message receiver MUST interpret all values of Accept other than these reserved values as 1."The sentence says the opposite of what is intended: "all values other than the reserved values" are 0 to 5, so taken literally a receiver would read OK (0) and the specific codes 2 to 5 as 1 (failure, unspecified). The intent, given "All other values are reserved ... This way, other values are available for future extensions", is that the reserved values (6 to 255) are read as 1.errornone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below
RA-07803.9"Each packet record is 25 octets and includes 4 octets of sequence number, 8 octets of send timestamp, 2 octets of send timestamp error estimate, 8 octets of receive timestamp, 2 octets of receive timestamp error estimate, and 1 octet of Time To Live"The prose lists the fields in the order sequence number, send timestamp, send error estimate, receive timestamp, receive error estimate, TTL, while the figure with octet offsets places both error estimates at offsets 4 and 6, before the timestamps (send timestamp at 8, receive timestamp at 16, TTL at 24). A Fetch-Client built from the prose cannot parse records written according to the figure.contradictionnone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below
RA-07813.9, 4.1.2"A send error estimate filled with Multiplier=1, Scale=64, and S=0"Scale is a six-bit field (4.1.2: "The next six bits, Scale, form an unsigned integer"), so its maximum is 63; the value 64 prescribed for lost-packet records cannot be encoded. Implementations must choose between 63 and a wrapped value of 0, which makes lost-packet records ambiguous (Scale 0, Multiplier 1 is a valid, very small error estimate).errornone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below
RA-07823.8"the Control-Client MUST account for each accepted Request-Session where Conf-Receiver was set; the Control-Server MUST account for each accepted Request-Session where Conf-Sender was set"Number of Sessions counts "the send sessions started by the local side". The Control-Client sends when Conf-Sender was not set; "Conf-Receiver was set" also covers a request with both Conf-Sender and Conf-Receiver set (3.5 allows it), in which the server configures both endpoints and the client sends nothing. The client rule then requires a session description for a session it did not send, and a server applying "exactly the send sessions controlled by that side" would declare the message invalid. "Control-Server" is not one of the roles of 1.2 (Server). Section 3.8 also refers to "the Session Packets Sent values", a field that no message has (Next Seqno and Skip Ranges are meant).errornone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below
RA-07833.8"If the OWAMP-Control connection breaks when the Stop-Sessions command is sent, the receiver MAY not completely invalidate the session results. It MUST discard all record of packets that follow""MAY not" is not an RFC 2119 form and can mean "is not required to" or "must not". The following rule ("packets that follow ... the last packet that was actually received before any lost packet records") does not define a unique cut-off when received and lost records are interleaved (lost records may be placed "at any later point", 4.2).ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata
RA-07845.3, 6.6, Appendix A"Output the i_th quartet of octets from s starting from high-order octets, converted to native byte order and represented as OWPNum64 value (as in 3.b)."There is no "3.b" in the document, and "OWPNum64" is not defined (5.2 uses u_int64_t). Other editorial points: Appendix A says the seed is initialized "as the shared secret in OWAMP, for example", while 5.3 uses the SID as the seed; its comment says the Q values were "rounded to the nearest integer", but Q[11] rounds to 2^32 and is given as 0xFFFFFFFF; "typedef u_int64_t u_int64_t;" is self-referential; the 5.3 prototypes are void but described as returning values; in 6.6 the bullet on authenticated-mode timestamps sits under "Regarding DTLS".editorialnone: RFC has no errata

RA-00914.1.2, 4.2.1"unauthenticated mode is 41 octets, and 104 octets in both"The minimum authenticated / encrypted TWAMP-Test packet is 112 octets, not 104, and sender padding is at least 64 octets, not 56 ("least 56 octets"). RA-00928.1, 8.2"document. Thus, this registry may contain sixteen possible values."The Command Number field is one octet, so the registry has 256 values.errorerratum 1593 (Verified), technical
RA-03794.2"In authenticated or encrypted mode, decrypt the appropriate sections of the packet body (first block (16 octets) for authenticated, 96 octets for encrypted), and then check integrity of sections covered by the HMAC."The packet the Session-Reflector receives is a Session-Sender packet, whose format is that of OWAMP-Test (Section 4.1.2, referring to RFC 4656 4.1.2): in encrypted mode only "the first two blocks (32 octets) are encrypted" and covered by the HMAC (RFC 4656 4.1.2). 96 octets is the coverage of the Session-Reflector's own packet (Section 4.2.1). RA-03804.2 vs 4.2.1"Copy the packet sequence number into the corresponding reflected packet to the Session-Sender. (4.2.1)"The 4.2 step reads as copying the received sequence number into the reflected Sequence Number field, while 4.2.1 makes that field the reflector's own counter and puts the received value in Sender Sequence Number. Appendix I (TWAMP Light) then lets a stateless reflector copy it, which RFC 8762 later formalised as "stateless" mode. Errata: Verified erratum 1590 scopes the reflector Sequence Number per session; it does not reconcile the 4.2 copy step with 4.2.1.ambiguitynone: RFC has 14 errata, none on this point (related: erratum 1590 (Verified), technical)
RA-03813.8"If the Accept-Session message was not transmitted at all (for whatever reason, including failure of the TCP connection used for TWAMP-Control), the results of all TWAMP-Test sessions spawned by this TWAMP-Control session MAY be considered invalid."The paragraph discusses the Accept field of the Stop-Sessions command; the message that may not have been transmitted is the Stop-Sessions message, not Accept-Session (which is the Server's reply to Request-TW-Session).editorialnone: RFC has 14 errata, none on this point; proposed erratum below
RA-03824.2.1, 6"Thus, in authenticated mode, HMAC covers the first block (16 octets); in encrypted mode, HMAC covers the first six blocks (96 octets)."Security gap: In authenticated mode the reflected packet's first block holds only the reflector Sequence Number and MBZ; the Timestamp, Receive Timestamp, Sender Sequence Number, Sender Timestamp and Sender TTL are neither encrypted nor integrity-protected, so an on-path attacker can alter every value used to compute delay and loss without detection. Section 6 (Security Considerations) does not state this limitation of authenticated mode.errornone: RFC has 14 errata, none on this point
RA-14603.8"Upon receipt of a TWAMP-Control Stop-Sessions command, the Session-Reflector MUST discard any TWAMP-Test packets that arrive at the current time plus the Timeout (in the Request-TW-Session command)."Read literally the requirement applies only to packets arriving at one instant (now + Timeout). Sections 3.5 ("MUST reflect them if they arrive within the Timeout interval ... MUST NOT reflect packets that are received beyond the timeout") and 4.2 make clear that packets arriving later than that instant are meant. The same paragraph set also says the Control-Client "MUST account for each accepted Request-Session", the OWAMP command that TWAMP replaces with Request-TW-Session (3.4).errornone: RFC has 14 errata, none on this point; proposed erratum below

The erratum was held for a future revision without text.ambiguityerratum 7240 (Held for Document Update), technical
RA-11616.7.3, 6.7.4"if the sequence number lies outside of the range of bfd.RcvAuthSeq to bfd.RcvAuthSeq+(3*Detect Mult) inclusive"The replay window is "3*Detect Mult", written as a packet field name (Section 6 says "the Xxx field" refers to packet fields) without saying whether the received packet's Detect Mult, the remote value recorded earlier, or the local bfd.DetectMult is meant. The window must cover the packets the remote system may send while the local system is still waiting (the remote's multiplier governs the local Detection Time, Section 6.8.4), so with asymmetric multipliers (or a multiplier changed without a Poll, Section 6.8.12) implementations that pick different values accept or discard different packets, and a legitimate packet after a loss burst can be rejected. Errata: Errata 7082 and 7083 (verified) change when bfd.RcvAuthSeq is updated in these paragraphs; which Detect Mult value sets the window is not addressed.ambiguitynone: RFC has 8 errata, none on this point (related: erratum 7082 (Verified), technical; erratum 7083 (Verified), technical); proposed erratum below
RA-11626.8.6"If the Length field is less than the minimum correct value (24 if the A bit is clear, or 26 if the A bit is set), the packet MUST be discarded."With the A bit set the smallest valid packet is 28 octets (24 + an Authentication Section of at least 4 octets: Simple Password of 1 octet, Section 4.2); 26 only guarantees that Auth Type and Auth Len can be read. No rule ties Auth Len to Length: a packet whose Length exceeds 24 + Auth Len (trailing octets), or with the A bit clear and Length above 24, is neither required to be accepted nor to be discarded. The digest of Sections 6.7.3 / 6.7.4 is computed over "the entire BFD Control packet", so the result depends on whether the receiver uses Length or 24 + Auth Len. Section 6 warns against enforcing anything beyond this section, which leaves receivers in doubt whether a consistency check is permitted.ambiguitynone: RFC has 8 errata, none on this point; proposed erratum below
RA-11636.2"A session remains in Down state until the remote system indicates that it agrees that the session is down by sending a BFD Control packet with the State field set to anything other than Up."The text implies that any non-Up state (including AdminDown) ends the Down state, but then lists only Down (to Init) and Init (to Up); the diagram and Section 6.8.6 keep the session in Down on a received AdminDown. Likewise the Init paragraph ("A session will remain in Init state until either a BFD Control Packet is received that is signaling Init or Up state ... or the Detection Time expires") omits the transition to Down on a received AdminDown that Section 6.8.6 requires. Section 6.8.6 is authoritative; the overview text should not suggest otherwise.ambiguitynone: RFC has 8 errata, none on this point; proposed erratum below
RA-11644.3, 4.4, 6.7.4, 6.8.6"The shared key MUST be encoded and configured to section 6.7.3.""configured to section 6.7.3" (and "to section 6.7.4" in 4.4) lacks "according"; in 6.7.4 the parenthesis "(when treated as an unsigned 32-bit circular number space, the received packet" is not closed; in 6.8.6 "Update the transmit interval as described in section 6.8.2" points to a section that only refers on to 6.8.7, where the transmit interval is defined.editorialnone: RFC has 8 errata, none on this point; proposed erratum below

Proposed erratum RA-1161 (RFC 5880, Section 6.7.3, 6.7.4; type: Technical):

Original Text
-------------
   For Keyed MD5, if the sequence number lies outside of the range
   of bfd.RcvAuthSeq to bfd.RcvAuthSeq+(3*Detect Mult) inclusive

Corrected Text
--------------
   For Keyed MD5, if the sequence number lies outside of the range
   of bfd.RcvAuthSeq to bfd.RcvAuthSeq+(3*Detect Mult) inclusive,
   where Detect Mult is the value of the Detect Mult field of the
   received packet

Notes
-----
   Applies to all four occurrences in Sections 6.7.3 and 6.7.4.
   "Detect Mult" is the name of the packet field, but whether the
   received value, the remote value previously stored, or
   bfd.DetectMult is meant is not stated; the values differ when the
   multipliers are asymmetric or change.

Proposed erratum RA-1162 (RFC 5880, Section 6.8.6; type: Technical):

Original Text
-------------
   If the Length field is less than the minimum correct value (24 if
   the A bit is clear, or 26 if the A bit is set), the packet MUST
   be discarded.

Corrected Text
--------------
   If the Length field is less than the minimum correct value (24 if
   the A bit is clear, or 28 if the A bit is set), the packet MUST
   be discarded. If the A bit is set and the Length field is not
   equal to 24 plus the Auth Len field, the packet MUST be
   discarded.

Notes
-----
   The smallest Authentication Section is 4 octets (Simple Password
   with a 1-octet password). Without a rule relating Length to Auth
   Len, the octets covered by the digest are ambiguous when they
   differ.

-------------
   by sending a BFD Control packet with the State field set to
   anything other than Up.

Corrected Text
--------------
   by sending a BFD Control packet with the State field set to Down
   or Init. (A received AdminDown state keeps the session in Down
   state; see Section 6.8.6.)

Notes
-----
   Section 6.8.6 keeps Down on a received AdminDown and moves Init
   and Up to Down; the overview text in Section 6.2 says otherwise
   for Down and omits the Init case.

RA-14633.6"Thus, the Server SHALL suspend monitoring control connection activity after receiving any Start-N-Sessions command, and after receiving a Stop-N-Sessions command for all corresponding SIDs (and no test sessions are in progress), OR when REFWAIT expires on ALL test sessions initiated by a TWAMP-Control connection, then the SERVWAIT monitoring SHALL resume"The sentence joins the suspend rule and the resume rule into one clause ("SHALL suspend ... after receiving any Start-N-Sessions command, and after receiving a Stop-N-Sessions command ..."), so read literally the Server also suspends SERVWAIT after the final Stop-N-Sessions, which contradicts the preceding paragraph (suspension covers only the time when any session is in progress) and the resume clause that follows. It also leaves open whether a Start-N-Sessions whose sessions are all refused (non-zero Accept in every Start-N-Ack) suspends SERVWAIT, and how "all corresponding SIDs" is counted when some sessions were stopped by REFWAIT and others by Stop-N-Sessions.ambiguitynone: RFC has 1 errata, none on this point; proposed erratum below
RA-14643.2, 3.4, 5"The number of SID fields that follow MUST be equal to the value in the Number of Sessions field (otherwise, the command MUST NOT be affirmed with a zero Accept field in the Start-N-Ack response)."The receiver cannot detect a count mismatch: TWAMP-Control has no message length, so the Server reads Number of Sessions SIDs and then the HMAC; a wrong count desynchronises the stream rather than producing a refusable command. The text does not say how a Start-N-Ack or Stop-N-Ack reports SIDs that the Server does not know (which Accept value, and whether they are listed), nor what a Stop-N-Sessions for a session never started does.ambiguitynone: RFC has 1 errata, none on this point

Section 6 also says "four command numbers" were assigned "and this memo describes the use of the new commands", while 6.3 says "One experimental value has been assigned" without saying it is value 6 from RFC 5357 rather than an assignment by this memo.editorialnone: RFC has 1 errata, none on this point

-------------
   Thus, the Server SHALL suspend monitoring control connection
   activity after receiving any Start-N-Sessions command, and after
   receiving a Stop-N-Sessions command for all corresponding SIDs

Corrected Text
--------------

   activity after accepting any session in a Start-N-Sessions
   command. After a Stop-N-Sessions command has been received for
   all started SIDs, or REFWAIT has expired on them (so that no test
   session is in progress), SERVWAIT monitoring SHALL resume (as
   though a Stop-N-Sessions command had been received).

Notes
-----
   Read literally, the sentence says the Server suspends SERVWAIT
   both after Start-N-Sessions and after the last Stop-N-Sessions,
   while the preceding paragraph says suspension covers only the
   time when any test session is in progress.

RFC 7750: Differentiated Service Code Point and Explicit Congestion Notification Monitoring in the Two-Way Active Measurement Protocol (TWAMP)

Depth: deep. Errata: none (the RFC has no errata). Status: Proposed Standard. Updates: RFC 5357.

IDSectionQuoteIssueSeverityErratum
RA-04042.2.1"the six (least-significant) bits of the Differentiated Service field MUST be copied from the received Session-Sender test packet into the Sender DSCP (S-DSCP) field;"In the IPv4 TOS / IPv6 Traffic Class octet the DSCP is the six most significant bits and ECN the two least significant ones (RFC 2474, RFC 3168). "Least-significant" is only correct if "Differentiated Service field" means the 6-bit DS field of RFC 3260; read against the 8-bit octet, an implementer copies ECN plus four DSCP bits. Figure 1 places S-DSCP in bits 0-5 and S-ECN in bits 6-7 of the new octet, which matches the most-significant reading.ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below
RA-14712.2.2, 2.2.1"because Sender DSCP and Sender ECN increase the size of the unauthenticated Session-Reflector packet by 4 octets, the Padding Length value SHOULD be greater than or equal to 28 octets"The unauthenticated Session-Reflector packet of RFC 5357 4.2.1 ends with the 1-octet Sender TTL (41 octets before padding); Figure 2 replaces that with a 4-octet word (Sender TTL, S-DSCP-ECN, 2 octets MBZ), giving 44 octets, an increase of 3, not 4. To keep the reflected packet the same size as the Session-Sender packet (14 octets before padding), the reflector must truncate 30 octets of padding (instead of the 27 of RFC 5357 4.2.1), so the sender's padding must be at least 30 octets; the text asks for 28 and Figure 4 draws the symmetrical Session-Sender packet with "MBZ (28 octets)" (14 + 28 = 42 octets, versus RFC 6038's 27 octets for the base format). None of 3, 4, 28 and 30 agree, so implementations of Symmetrical Size / Reflect Octets with this mode will disagree on truncation length and minimum padding.errornone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below
RA-14722.1, 2.2"If the Control-Client agrees to monitor DSCP and ECN on some or all test sessions invoked with this control connection, it MUST set the DSCP and ECN Monitoring flag in the Modes field in the Setup Response message."The mode is negotiated once per control connection, but the text allows monitoring on only "some" of its test sessions and defines no per-session indication (e.g. in Request-TW-Session). In unauthenticated mode the Session-Reflector packet format changes (Figure 2 adds 3 octets before the padding), so the Session-Sender must know which format each reflected packet uses; with no per-session signal, the only interoperable reading is that every test session of the connection uses the new format, contradicting "some".ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below

Proposed erratum RA-0404 (RFC 7750, Section 2.2.1; type: Technical):

Original Text
-------------
   the six (least-significant) bits of the Differentiated Service
   field MUST be copied

Corrected Text
--------------
   the six bits of the DSCP (the most significant six bits of the
   IPv4 TOS octet or IPv6 Traffic Class octet [RFC2474]) MUST be
   copied

Notes
-----
   Correct only under the RFC 3260 6-bit DS field definition; Figure
   1 and RFC 3168 suggest the most-significant reading.

Proposed erratum RA-1471 (RFC 7750, Section 2.2.2, 2.2.1; type: Technical):

Original Text
-------------
   because Sender DSCP and Sender ECN increase the size of the
   unauthenticated Session-Reflector packet by 4 octets, the Padding
   Length value SHOULD be greater than or equal to 28 octets

Corrected Text
--------------
   because the Sender DSCP and ECN field and the following MBZ field
   increase the size of the unauthenticated Session-Reflector packet
   by 3 octets (to 44 octets), the Padding Length value SHOULD be
   greater than or equal to 30 octets (and Figure 4: "MBZ (30
   octets)")

Notes
-----
   Counted from Figure 2: 4 + 8 + 4 + 8 + 4 + 8 + 4 + 4 = 44 octets;
   RFC 5357 base reflector 41 octets; Session-Sender 14 octets. In
   authenticated and encrypted modes (Figure 3) S-DSCP-ECN takes one
   octet of the existing MBZ, so the size is unchanged there.

Proposed erratum RA-1472 (RFC 7750, Section 2.1, 2.2; type: Technical):

Original Text
-------------
   If the Control-Client agrees to monitor DSCP and ECN on some or
   all test sessions invoked with this control connection, it MUST

Corrected Text
--------------
   If the Control-Client agrees to monitor DSCP and ECN on the test
   sessions invoked with this control connection, it MUST set the
   DSCP and ECN Monitoring flag in the Modes field in the Setup
   Response message; the Session-Reflector then uses the formats of

RFC 7820: UDP Checksum Complement in the One-Way Active Measurement Protocol (OWAMP) and Two-Way Active Measurement Protocol (TWAMP)

Depth: deep. Errata: none (the RFC has no errata). Status: Experimental.

IDSectionQuoteIssueSeverityErratum
RA-08023.2, App. A"the Checksum Complement is always the last 2 octets of the UDP payload, and thus the field is located at (UDP Length - 2 octets) after the beginning of the UDP header."The Packet Padding length is any number of octets, so the UDP length may be odd and the Checksum Complement then starts at an odd offset. The Internet checksum sums 16-bit words aligned to the start of the UDP header, so a complement at an odd offset contributes its two octets byte-swapped and split across two words; Equation (2) of Appendix A ("checksum(C) = checksum(T) - checksum(T')") holds only for an even offset. The document neither requires an even UDP length (or padding parity) when the complement is used nor tells the timestamping engine to swap the octets at an odd offset; an engine written from the example produces a wrong checksum for odd-length packets.ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata
RA-08033.2"In TWAMP, the padding length is at least 29 octets in unauthenticated mode and at least 58 octets in authenticated mode."The 27 / 56-octet differences come from the RFC 5357 sender format. With the RFC 6038 Symmetrical Size feature the sender packet already carries 27 MBZ octets after the Error Estimate (RFC 6038 5.1.4), so sender and reflector packets have the same header length and 2 octets of padding suffice; the third bullet speaks of the RFC 6038 features only in terms of the reflect-octets length fields. Whether the 29/58 minimum still applies under Symmetrical Size is left open.ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata

RFC 8029: Detecting Multiprotocol Label Switched (MPLS) Data-Plane Failures

Depth: deep. Errata: 6 errata: 2 verified, 3 held, 1 rejected. Status: Proposed Standard. Obsoletes: RFC 4379, RFC 6424, RFC 6829, RFC 7537. Updates: RFC 1122. Updated by: RFC 8611, RFC 9041, RFC 9570.

IDSectionQuoteIssueSeverityErratum
RA-01003.4, 3.7, 3.8, A.2"If an LSR does not know the IP address of its neighbor, then it MUST set the Address Type to either IPv4 Unnumbered or IPv6 Unnumbered.""IPv6 Unnumbered" (Router ID plus interface index) has no defined IPv6 Router ID semantics; erratum 8788, held for document update, proposes deprecating the IPv6 Unnumbered address types and also reports a K-octets mismatch in Appendix A.2. Until the RFC is revised, what to send and accept for IPv6 unnumbered links is unclear.ambiguityerratum 8788 (Held for Document Update), technical
RA-11684.4 (steps 4, 5), 3.4"If an LSR receives an echo request packet with the all-routers multicast address, then this indicates that it MUST bypass both interface and label stack validation (3.4) / Verify that the IP address, interface address, and label stack in the Downstream Detailed Mapping TLV match Interface-I and Stack-R. If there is a mismatch, set Best-return-code to 5 (4.4)"In the step 4 pseudocode only 127.0.0.1 / 0::1 are tested before the "Else" branch; a DDMAP carrying 224.0.0.2 / FF02::2 falls into the Else branch, fails the comparison and is answered with Return Code 5 ("Downstream Mapping Mismatch") before the later test "or the Downstream IP Address is set to the ALLROUTERS multicast address, go to step 7" can be reached. Step 5 (egress) likewise bypasses only 127.0.0.1 / 0::1. The procedure of Section 4.8, which sends ALLROUTERS on every probe past a silent hop, therefore gets Return Code 5 from compliant transit and egress LSRs if they follow the pseudocode literally.contradictionnone: RFC has 6 errata, none on this point; proposed erratum below
RA-11693.4.1.1.1"The maximum prefix length is 27. Following the prefix is a mask of length 2^(32 - prefix length) bits for IPv4 and 2^(128 - prefix length) bits for IPv6."For IPv6 a prefix length of 27 would require a mask of 2^101 bits; the IPv6 example that follows encodes ::ffff:127.2.1.0 with a 32-bit mask, i.e. a prefix length of 123. The maximum (and the implied minimum mask of 32 bits) only fits IPv4. The prefix length itself is not carried in the encoding: the receiver must derive it from the Multipath Length, which the text does not say.contradictionnone: RFC has 6 errata, none on this point; proposed erratum below
RA-11703.4.1.1.1"to U, with Multipath Type 4 (127.1.1.1->127.1.1.127); to V, with Multipath Type 4 (127.1.1.127->127.1.1.255)"The paragraph first assigns 127.1.1.128 -> 127.1.1.255 to V; the DDMAP for V then starts at 127.1.1.127, which overlaps U's range, although the section requires that Type 4 ranges "MUST NOT overlap".errornone: RFC has 6 errata, none on this point; proposed erratum below
RA-11714.4"If the Return Code is 1, set Best-return-code to FEC-return-code and Best-rtn-subcode to FEC-stack-depth."The variable tested should be FEC-status (the value returned by the FEC Checking algorithm, 1 meaning failure), not the Return Code (1 is "Malformed echo request received"). The variable list also initialises Label-stack-depth to "the number of labels in the received label stack S", where S is not defined (Stack-R is meant).editorialnone: RFC has 6 errata, none on this point; proposed erratum below
RA-11723.2.17, 4.5.1, 4.4.1"The value of the label in the Nil FEC MUST be set to zero. (4.5.1) / Label is the actual label value inserted in the label stack (3.2.17)"For FEC hiding, Section 4.5.1 requires the Nil FEC label to be zero while the label actually pushed is a real tunnel label, contrary to the definition in Section 3.2.17. Zero is also the IPv4 Explicit NULL value, which Section 4.4.1 step 2 accepts for a Nil FEC. Validation of such a Nil FEC is skipped only when it is the outermost FEC (4.4.1); once the ingress has popped back below it, a node validating a Nil FEC with label 0 against a real Label-L returns Return Code 10.ambiguitynone: RFC has 6 errata, none on this point
RA-11736.2.2"Assignments in the ranges 0-16383 and 32768-49161 are made via Standards Action as defined in [RFC5226]; assignments in the ranges 16384-31743 and 49162-64511 are made via "Specification Required""The optional-TLV half mirrors the mandatory half (0-16383, 16384-31743, 31744-32767 against 64512-65535) except at the Standards Action boundary, which is 49161/49162 instead of 49151/49152 (32768 + 16383). The text does not say whether the 10-value shift is intended. Later RFCs: RFC 9041 (updates RFC 8029), Tables 1 and 9, restates the same ranges (32768-49161 Standards Action, 49162-64507 RFC Required), so the asymmetric boundary is confirmed but still unexplained.editorialnone: RFC has 6 errata, none on this point

Proposed erratum RA-1168 (RFC 8029, Section 4.4 (steps 4, 5), 3.4; type: Technical):

Original Text
-------------
   If the IP address in the TLV is 127.0.0.1 or 0::1 {

Corrected Text
--------------
   If the IP address in the TLV is 224.0.0.2 or FF02::2
   (ALLROUTERS), skip the verification below. If the IP address in
   the TLV is 127.0.0.1 or 0::1 {

Notes
-----
   Section 3.4 requires both interface and label stack validation to

Proposed erratum RA-1169 (RFC 8029, Section 3.4.1.1.1; type: Technical):

Original Text
-------------
   The maximum prefix length is 27.

Corrected Text
--------------
   The prefix length is not encoded; it is derived from the
   Multipath Length (the mask occupies the remainder of the
   Multipath Information). The maximum prefix length is 27 for IPv4
   and 123 for IPv6, so that the mask is at least 32 bits.

Notes
-----
   The IPv6 example contradicts the stated maximum of 27, and the
   way a receiver determines the prefix length is not specified.

RFC 8545: Well-Known Port Assignments for the One-Way Active Measurement Protocol (OWAMP) and the Two-Way Active Measurement Protocol (TWAMP)

Depth: deep. Errata: none (the RFC has no errata). Status: Proposed Standard. Updates: RFC 4656, RFC 5357.

IDSectionQuoteIssueSeverityErratum
RA-08045.1, 5.2 vs RFC 5357 3.5"If the Server does not support the allocated TWAMP-Test Receiver Port, then it sends an alternate port number in the Accept-Session message with Accept field = 0. (5.1)"RFC 5357 3.5 says that "When the Accept field = 0, the Port field confirms (repeats) the port" requested, and the quoted erratum text lets the Control-Client "either accept the alternate port or compose a new Session-Request". With Accept = 0 the session has already been accepted by the Server, so it is unclear whether an Accept-Session with Accept = 0 and a different Port is an acceptance on that port (contradicting "confirms (repeats)") or a counter-proposal, and how a Control-Client that does not want the alternate port releases the accepted session (neither protocol has a per-session cancel before Start-Sessions). Section 5.2 applies the same alternate-port rule to OWAMP, where RFC 4656 3.5 defines no alternate-port behaviour at all and the meaning of Port depends on Conf-Sender / Conf-Receiver.ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below

Proposed erratum RA-0804 (RFC 8545, Section 5.1, 5.2 vs RFC 5357 3.5; type: Technical):

Original Text
-------------
   If the Server does not support the allocated TWAMP-Test Receiver
   Port, then it sends an alternate port number in the
   Accept-Session message with Accept field = 0.

Corrected Text
--------------
   If the Server does not support the allocated TWAMP-Test Receiver
   Port, then it sends an alternate port number in the
   Accept-Session message with Accept field = 0; this accepts the
   session on the alternate port (an exception to the "confirms
   (repeats)" rule of Section 3.5 of [RFC5357]). A Control-Client
   that does not accept the alternate port does not start the
   session and closes or reuses the control connection.

Notes
-----
   The same clarification is needed for OWAMP (5.2), taking the
   Conf-Sender
   Conf-Receiver dependent meaning of Port from RFC 4656 Section 3.5
   into account.

It also does not say which combinations are "allowed": Table 1 lists Protocol 1, 2 and "Any" (0) only, so the length of an IGP-Adjacency sub-TLV with any other Protocol value, or with an Adj. Type other than 0, 1, 4 and 6, is undefined.ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below

RFC 8762: Simple Two-Way Active Measurement Protocol

Depth: deep. Errata: 1 errata: 1 rejected. Status: Proposed Standard. Updated by: RFC 8972.

IDSectionQuoteIssueSeverityErratum
RA-04074.6, 4.3, 7"A STAMP Session-Reflector ... will transmit the base packet (Figure 5) if it receives a packet smaller than the STAMP base packet. (4.6)"Security gap: For TWAMP Light interworking the reflector answers a packet shorter than the 44-octet base packet with a 44-octet reply, so its reply can be larger than the request; with UDP and no source validation (unauthenticated mode, Section 4.4 being optional) this makes a reflector an amplifier for spoofed senders. RFC 8972 later adds the SSID, which this document lacks.ambiguitynone: RFC has 1 errata, none on this point
RA-04094.3, 4"The Session-Reflector receives the STAMP-Test packet and verifies it. If the base STAMP-Test packet is validated, the Session-Reflector ... prepares and transmits the reflected test packet"The checks that make a base packet "validated" are not listed (length, MBZ, HMAC in authenticated mode, Error Estimate), and nothing in the packet indicates whether it is authenticated or not, so the receiver can only know the mode from configuration.ambiguitynone: RFC has 1 errata, none on this point

Proposed erratum RA-0407 (RFC 8762, Section 4.6, 4.3, 7; type: Technical):

Original Text
-------------
   (Section 7, new paragraph)

Corrected Text
--------------
   A Session-Reflector that answers packets shorter than the base
   packet (Section 4.6) returns more octets than it receives. Such a
   reflector SHOULD restrict the senders it answers (for example by
   access list or rate limit), since otherwise it can be used to
   amplify traffic towards a spoofed source.

Notes
-----
   Symmetrical size (Section 4) avoids amplification only for
   packets at least as large as the base packet.

Proposed erratum RA-0805 (RFC 8972, Section 4.8; type: Technical):

Original Text
-------------
   HMAC:  A 16-octet field that carries the HMAC digest of the text
   of all preceding TLVs.

Corrected Text
--------------

   over the Sequence Number field of the base STAMP packet and all
   preceding TLVs. A Session-Reflector that returns TLVs computes a
   new HMAC over the Sequence Number field of the reflected packet
   and the TLVs as transmitted, using the same key as the base STAMP
   authenticated mode or, in unauthenticated mode, a key provisioned
   for the test session.

-----
   The flags set by the Session-Reflector are inside the HMAC input,
   so a copied HMAC can never verify at the Session-Sender.

RFC 9570: Deprecating the Use of Router Alert in LSP Ping

Depth: deep. Errata: none (the RFC has no errata). Status: Proposed Standard. Updates: RFC 8029.

IDSectionQuoteIssueSeverityErratum
RA-12694, 7"The IPv6 loopback address ::1/128 SHOULD be used."An MPLS echo request is sent over the LSP under test to another node (the egress LSR or a transit LSR whose TTL expires). RFC 4291 2.5.3, which this document cites as the reason for the choice, says "An IPv6 packet with a destination address of loopback must never be sent outside of a single node and must never be forwarded by an IPv6 router. A packet received on an interface with a destination address of loopback must be dropped." A conformant receiver therefore drops an echo request addressed to ::1 when it arrives without labels (after penultimate-hop popping, or for an unlabeled request, which RFC 8029 4.3 allows when all FECs map to Implicit Null) unless its MPLS OAM path is specifically exempted, which the document does not ask for. Section 7 says the change "strengthens security ... because it is standardized and has well-defined behavior", but the well-defined behavior is the drop. RFC 8029 4.3 (the procedure for sending an echo request) still says the destination is "an IPv6 address from the range 0:0:0:0:0:FFFF:7F00:0/104" and is not updated, so the two sections of the updated RFC 8029 disagree on the address.contradictionnone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below
RA-12704, 5, 2.2"The Router Alert IP Option of value 0x0 [RFC2113] for IPv4 or value 69 [RFC7506] for IPv6 MUST NOT be set in the IP header. / "Deprecated" means that the deprecated values SHOULD NOT be used in new implementations, and that deployed implementations that already use these values continue to work seamlessly."Section 4 turns the RFC 8029 4.3 MUST into MUST NOT, while Section 5 describes the change as a deprecation (SHOULD NOT in new implementations, deployed ones "continue to work seamlessly") and says the receiver SHOULD ignore a received RAO. Section 5 claims no harm to backward compatibility because "other mechanisms will also be in use by all legacy implementations", but it does not address receivers that, following RFC 8029 4.3 and 4.4, use the router alert to recognise an unlabeled echo request at the egress after penultimate-hop popping: such a receiver drops requests from a conformant RFC 9570 sender. Reply Mode 3 is "removed", but the document does not say what a responder does with a request that still carries Reply Mode 3 (reply in mode 2, return an error, or drop), nor does it update the RFC 8029 Section 3 text that recommends mode 3 ("If the normal IP return path is deemed unreliable, one may use 3").ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below
RA-12714"The sender of an MPLS echo request MAY select the IPv6 destination address from the 0:0:0:0:0:FFFF:7F00/104 range.""0:0:0:0:0:FFFF:7F00" has seven groups and is not a valid IPv6 address text form (RFC 4291 2.2); Section 2.1 of this document and RFC 8029 write the prefix as 0:0:0:0:0:FFFF:7F00:0/104.editorialnone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below

Corrected Text

   exception to Section 2.5.3 of [RFC4291], an LSR MUST NOT drop an
   MPLS echo request (UDP destination port 3503) addressed to
   ::1/128 that it receives on an LSP, or unlabeled from its
   upstream neighbor on the LSP under test, and MUST process it as
   specified in Section 4.4 of [RFC8029]; the packet MUST NOT be IP
   forwarded.  [Section 4.3 of RFC 8029 is updated accordingly.]

Notes
-----
   RFC 4291 Section 2.5.3 forbids sending a packet to the loopback
   address outside a node and requires a receiver to drop one
   received on an interface. RFC 8029 Section 4.3, which specifies
   the echo request header, still requires the IPv4-mapped 127/8
   range and is not changed by this document.

RFC 768: User Datagram Protocol

RA-0807Fields"Length is the length in octets of this user datagram including this header and the data."The document does not say what a receiver does when the Length field disagrees with the length of the IP payload (Length below 8, Length greater than the IP payload, or Length smaller than the IP payload with trailing octets). Whether trailing octets are ignored, whether the checksum covers them, and whether the datagram is discarded is left to the implementation (later clarified in part by RFC 1122 4.1.3.4 and RFC 8085). Later RFCs: RFC 9868 Section 10 (updates RFC 768) settles the main cases: the UDP Length must be at least 8 and at most the IP payload, other values are silently dropped, and octets beyond the UDP Length form the options area (Sections 7, 17 and 21). RA-08093.2 (Example Reassembly Procedure)"(14) THEN TL <- TDL+(IHL*4)"Step (14) computes the reassembled Total Length from IHL, which at that point is the IHL of the fragment just processed (often the last one), while the header placed in the header buffer at step (11) is the first fragment's header. The first fragment can carry options that are not copied into later fragments (Record Route, Timestamp), so its IHL is larger and the computed Total Length is too small by the length of those options. The IHL of the stored (first-fragment) header is meant.errorerratum 6356 (Verified), technical
RA-08103.2 (Example Reassembly Procedure)"In the case that two or more fragments contain the same data either identically or through a partial overlap, this procedure will use the more recently arrived copy"Security gap: The example procedure accepts overlapping fragments with "last arrival wins" and places data at FO*8 without checking that FO*8 plus the fragment data stays within 65,535 octets (step 8), although Fragment Offset can address up to 65,528 and the reassembled datagram can then exceed the Total Length field. Both behaviours are the basis of the overlapping-fragment filter evasion described in RFC 1858 and of oversized-reassembly attacks; the document gives no bound check and no warning. (The statement "2**13 = 8192 fragments of 8 octets each for a total of 65,536 octets ... consistent with the the datagram total length field" also glosses over the header octets.)errornone: RFC has 22 errata, none on this point

RFC 1071: Computing the Internet Checksum

Depth: deep. Errata: 4 errata: 3 verified, 1 held. Status: Informational. Updated by: RFC 1141.

IDSectionQuoteIssueSeverityErratum
RA-04114.1"sum += * (unsigned short) addr++;"The cast converts the address itself to unsigned short and then dereferences it, which is not valid C; a pointer cast "* (unsigned short *) addr" is meant (with addr advanced by 2 octets, not by sizeof(*addr) of whatever type addr has). The odd-byte line "sum += * (unsigned char *) addr;" adds the last octet as the low-order byte, which is correct only on little-endian hosts; Section 2 (A) defines the pad as a zero octet after the last octet, i.e. the high-order byte of the final 16-bit word in network order. The fragment also begins with the stray text "in 6" and has no function header.errorerratum 4918 (Verified), editorial; erratum 560 (Verified), editorial; erratum 3133 (Held for Document Update), technical
RA-08232 (4) Incremental Update"given the original value m, the new value m', and the old checksum C, the new checksum C' is: C' = C + (-m) + m' = C + (m' - m)"C is called the "checksum", i.e. the value carried in the checksum field, which is the one's complement of the sum. Adding the difference to the field value has the wrong sign: the update must be applied to the sum (~C), giving C' = ~(~C + ~m + m'). RFC 1141 used the formula as given and RFC 1624 (Section 3) shows that it is incorrect and also fails in the 0x0000 / 0xFFFF corner case. RFC 1624 does not carry an "Updates: 1071" header, so a reader of RFC 1071 is not directed to the correction. Later RFCs: RFC 1141 gives the checksum-field form, but RFC 1624 Section 3 shows that form fails in the 0x0000 / 0xFFFF case; the correct form for RFC 1071 is RFC 1624 Eqn. 3.errornone: RFC has 4 errata, none on this point; proposed erratum below
RA-08243 (Numerical Examples, odd boundary)"Byte 4/5: 03 f4 03f4 / Byte 6/7: f5 f6 f5f6 / Byte 8/: f7 (00) f700"The second group starts at byte 3 (value 03) of the 8-byte example data 00 01 f2 03 f4 f5 f6 f7, so the rows are bytes 3/4, 5/6 and 7/ (the values and sums are correct; only the labels are off by one). Same section: "byte by bye", "Carrys"; Section 2: "underlaying"; Section 4.4 uses an undefined register "R3" ("AR RADDR,R3") where the other registers are named.editorialnone: RFC has 4 errata, none on this point; proposed erratum below
RA-0825Appendix (IEN 45, 3 Product Codes)"Ms' = Ms*R + T(R-1)(Rj) + P2((R-1)2) / = Ms*R + T*(R(j+1)) + T*(Rj) + P2*(R**2) - 2*P2*R - P2"With Mo = H1*(Rj) + H2 and Mo' = H1*(R(j+1)) + T*(Rj) + H2, Ms' - Ms*R = T(R-1)(Rj) - H2((R-1)2). The reprinted formula uses an undefined "P2" (H2 is meant), has the wrong sign on the last term, and its expansion gives "+ T*(Rj)" for "- T*(Rj)" and "- P2" for the constant term of (R-1)2. Informational appendix only.errornone: RFC has 4 errata, none on this point

IDSectionQuoteIssueSeverityErratum
RA-08263.2.2.8"o If a Source-route option is received in an ICMP Echo Request, the return route MUST be reversed and used as a Source Route option for the Timestamp Reply message."The rule is in the Timestamp section and governs the Timestamp Reply, but its trigger names an ICMP Echo Request (copied from 3.2.2.6). Read literally, a source route received in a Timestamp Request need not be reversed, and an Echo Request would cause a Timestamp Reply. The summary table ("Reverse and reflect Source Route option | 3.2.2.8 | MUST") confirms the intended reading. The same summary block lists "Reflect Record Route, Time Stamp options" for Timestamp under section 3.2.2.6 instead of 3.2.2.8.errornone: RFC has 13 errata, none on this point; proposed erratum below
RA-08273.5, 3.2.2.6"Echo server and Echo client |3.2.2.6 |x| / A host SHOULD also implement an application-layer interface for sending an Echo Request and receiving an Echo Reply"The Internet layer summary marks "Echo server and Echo client" as MUST, while 3.2.2.6 makes only the Echo server a MUST and the client interface a SHOULD (the next summary line "Echo client" is SHOULD). The two summary lines contradict each other and the first contradicts the text, which governs (1.3.1: "summaries should never be used or referenced separately").contradictionnone: RFC has 13 errata, none on this point; proposed erratum below
RA-08294.2.3.9"o Destination Unreachable -- codes 2-4 These are hard error conditions, so TCP SHOULD abort the connection."Code 4 (fragmentation needed and DF set) is classed as a hard error that should abort the connection, but RFC 1191 (published a year later, in this set) uses exactly that message as the Path MTU Discovery signal and requires the sender to reduce the PMTU and continue; aborting on code 4 breaks PMTUD. RFC 1191 does not carry an "Updates: 1122" header, so the conflict is not flagged in either document (RFC 5927 / RFC 8201 later discuss it). Later RFCs: RFC 9293 Section 3.9.2.2 (which obsoletes the TCP material of RFC 1122) repeats 'Destination Unreachable -- codes 2-4 ... SHOULD abort', so the conflict with Path MTU Discovery remains in the current TCP specification.contradictionnone: RFC has 13 errata, none on this point
RA-08301.1.1, 4.2.3.4, 4.2.3.5, 4.2.3.7, 5"A host is generally said to be multihomed if it has more than one interface to the same or to different networks. See Section 1.1.3 on "Terminology"."Terminology is Section 1.3.3 (1.1.3 is "Internet Protocol Suite"). Further editorial points: 4.2.3.4 rule (3) "min(D.U)" for "min(D,U)"; 4.2.3.5 has two items labelled "(d)"; 4.2.3.7 "TCP MUST use the same local address is used that was used in those previous segments" is garbled; in the references the note "This RFC first described directed broadcast addresses" follows [IP:14] (RFC 1016, SQUID) but belongs to [IP:12] (RFC 922); 3.5 summary "Pass interface ident up to transport layer" has no matching requirement in 3.4 (which requires SpecDest). Later RFCs: RFC 9293 Section 3.8.6.2.1 writes min(D,U); the other items are outside TCP and stay open. Errata: Erratum 4446 covers the Section 1.1.3 reference; the other editorial points are not in any erratum.editorialerratum 4446 (Verified), editorial

RFC 1321: The MD5 Message-Digest Algorithm

Depth: deep. Errata: 7 errata: 5 verified, 1 held, 1 rejected. Status: Informational. Updated by: RFC 6151.

IDSectionQuoteIssueSeverityErratum
RA-08343.4"/* Let [abcd k s t] denote the operation a = b + ((a + H(b,c,d) + X[k] + T[i]) <<< s). */"Rounds 3 and 4 name the fourth parameter "t" while the formula uses "T[i]" (rounds 1 and 2 use "[abcd k s i]"). Also in 3.2 "In the unlikely event that b is greater than 2^64" should read "greater than or equal to 2^64" (a 64-bit field holds at most 2^64 - 1); further typos: "1,2]" (Section 1, missing bracket), unbalanced parentheses in 3.3 ("low-order bytes first):") and 3.4 ("... in the same bit position.)"), "Acknowlegements", "plaforms".editorialerratum 585 (Verified), technical; erratum 551 (Verified), technical
RA-0835Appendix A.1, A.3"/* UINT4 defines a four byte word */ typedef unsigned long int UINT4; / #define ROTATE_LEFT(x, n) (((x) << (n)) | ((x) >> (32-(n))))"The reference code assumes unsigned long is exactly 32 bits. On platforms where it is 64 bits, sums in FF..II keep carries above bit 31 and ROTATE_LEFT shifts them back into the low word, so the code produces wrong digests. The text calls the implementation "portable". (Minor: MDTimeTrial passes TEST_BLOCK_LEN and TEST_BLOCK_COUNT in the wrong order for "Digesting %d %d-byte blocks"; harmless only because both are 1000.) Errata: Rejected erratum 7814 reported the same 64-bit "unsigned long" problem; it was rejected because the code was correct for the platforms of its time and the document will not be updated. The finding is kept as a warning to implementers; no new erratum is proposed.errorerratum 7814 (Rejected), technical
RA-0836Security Considerations"The level of security discussed in this memo is considered to be sufficient for implementing very high security hybrid digital-signature schemes based on MD5"Security gap: The security claim (and Section 4: collisions "on the order of 2^64 operations") no longer holds: practical collisions exist. RFC 6151 updates RFC 1321 with revised security considerations (MD5 not for signatures; HMAC-MD5 still usable for some purposes). A reader of RFC 1321 alone is not warned beyond the "Updated by" header.errornone: RFC has 7 errata, none on this point

IDSectionQuoteIssueSeverityErratum
RA-01024.3.3.4"is reduced to 0, the requirements of section [5.2.3.8] apply."Section 5.2.3.8 does not cover TTL expiry; the TTL rules are in 5.3.1.errorerratum 5553 (Held for Document Update), editorial

RA-11745.2.4.4"For BGP routes, the originating AS is the first AS listed in the route's AS_PATH attribute."In BGP the AS_PATH is prepended by each AS on the way, so the first (leftmost) AS is the neighbouring AS that sent the route and the originating AS is the last (rightmost) AS of the path (RFC 4271 5.1.2). A preference rule implemented as written matches on the neighbour AS, which the same section lists separately ("Source router") and which 7.3.2.2 (1) distinguishes from "the autonomous system that originated the route".errornone: RFC has 5 errata, none on this point; proposed erratum below
RA-11756.2"A router that implements TCP MUST be compliant, and SHOULD be unconditionally compliant, with the requirements of [INTRO:2], except that: / o For similar reasons, a router need not comply with any of the requirements of [INTRO:2]."The second bullet, read as written, exempts a router from every RFC 1122 requirement, which cancels the opening MUST and the following bullets that amend specific RFC 1122 TCP requirements. The bullet evidently lost its object (presumably the RFC 1122 requirements on the application interface, like those listed in the first bullet). The next bullet also files the ICMP soft-error rule under "The requirements concerning the Maximum Segment Size Option", a copy of the preceding heading; the soft-error rules are in RFC 1122 4.2.3.9 (TCP ICMP processing).contradictionnone: RFC has 5 errata, none on this point; proposed erratum below

Section 1 also attributes the title of RFC 1009 to RFC 1716 ("replaces for RFC 1716, 'Requirements for Internet Gateways' ([INTRO:1])"). Implementers cannot tell whether RFC 1009 Chapter 3 is still a requirement.contradictionnone: RFC has 5 errata, none on this point; proposed erratum below
RA-11774.3.2.4, 5.2.1, 5.3.13"the router's router-id (see Section [5.2.5]) is used instead. / As noted in Section [5.2.4], the address inserted MUST be the address of the logical interface / Section [5.2.5] discusses how a router must choose which of its addresses to insert into an option."Section 5.2.5 is "Unused IP Header Bits" and 5.2.4 is next-hop determination; neither defines the router-id nor the choice of address for options. Both are in Section 4.2.2.2 ("Addresses in Options"), with the router-id introduced in 2.2.7. RA-11784.3.3.6, 10.3.2, 10.3.2.1, 4.3.2.7, 5.2.1.1, 5.3.7"As stated in Section [10.3.3], a router MUST also implement a user/application-layer interface for sending an Echo Request / 10.3.2 Out Of Band Access / 10.3.2 Router O&M Functions"There is no Section 10.3.3: two consecutive sections are both numbered 10.3.2 (also in the table of contents), and 4.3.3.6 and 10.3.2.1 refer to 10.3.3, meaning the second 10.3.2 (the echo requirement is in 10.3.2.7 (2)). Other wrong references: 4.3.2.7 and 5.2.1.1 refer to Section [3.1] for the link-layer information passed to IP, which is in 3.2; 5.3.7 defines invalid source addresses "as defined in 4.2.2.11 or 5.3.7", referring to itself.editorialnone: RFC has 5 errata, none on this point; proposed erratum below
RA-11792.2.5.1, 4.2.2.11"Routers outside the network treat <Network-prefix> and <Host-number> together as an uninterpreted rest part of the 32-bit IP address."The paragraph describes subnetting: routers outside the subnetted network do not see the subnet structure, so it is the <Subnet-number> and <Host-number> that they treat together as the rest field; the network prefix is exactly what they route on. The same subsection calls Class D a "28 bit prefix", while 4.2.2.11 correctly calls a multicast address a "28-bit logical address" (the class D prefix is 4 bits, 1110).editorialnone: RFC has 5 errata, none on this point; proposed erratum below
RA-11804.3.2.3, 4.3.3.5"Note that the requirements of Section [4.3.3.5] supersede this requirement in some cases / Section [4.3.2] defines an exception to this requirement."Each section says the other one overrides it: 4.3.2.3 lets a router return the header with forwarding modifications (decremented TTL, updated options) except that 4.3.3.5 supersedes it for Parameter Problem, while 4.3.3.5 requires the field at the pointer to be returned unchanged but says 4.3.2 defines an exception. For a Parameter Problem whose pointer is at a field the router already modified (e.g. an option it updated), the text does not settle whether the original value must be restored.ambiguitynone: RFC has 5 errata, none on this point
RA-11815.2.4.3"EDITORS+COMMENTS ... If the packet contains an SSRR, the router MUST discard the packet and reply with an ICMP Bad Source Route error."Section 1.1.1 defines DISCUSSION and IMPLEMENTATION blocks as not part of the standard but never defines "EDITORS+COMMENTS"; the only statement of what to do with a strict source route whose next address is not adjacent is inside such a block, so its normative force is unclear. The same section numbers its route types (1), (2), (5), with (3) and (4) missing.ambiguitynone: RFC has 5 errata, none on this point
RA-11825.3.5.2, 4.2.2.11"Given a route and no overriding policy, then, a router MUST forward network-prefix-directed broadcasts. / These options MUST default to permit receiving and forwarding network-prefix-directed broadcasts."RFC 2644 (BCP 34), which updates this document, reverses the default: a router MAY have an option to enable forwarding of network-prefix-directed broadcasts, and such options MUST default to blocking them (smurf amplification). The text here still requires forwarding by default and is not marked as updated in the document itself, so an implementer reading only RFC 1812 builds the vulnerable default. The section also does not say how the last-hop router recognises the directed broadcast of a connected prefix (all-ones host part) and with which link-layer address it sends it. Later RFCs: RFC 2644 replaces RFC 1812 4.2.2.11 (d) and the second paragraph of 5.3.5.2: routers MAY have an option to enable forwarding of directed broadcasts, and the default MUST be not to forward. The first paragraph of 5.3.5.2 ('MUST forward network-prefix-directed broadcasts') is not replaced.ambiguitynone: RFC has 5 errata, none on this point
RA-11838.2, 10.3.2.7"The initial state of the community table SHOULD contain one entry, with the community name string public and read-only access."Security gap: A well-known default read community gives anyone who can reach the router its full read-only MIB (routing table, interfaces, ARP cache) from first boot, and 10.3.2.7 (1) exempts exactly this ("except as required by Section [8.2]") from the rule that in-band access SHOULD be disabled by default. 10.4.2 asks that remote reconfiguration default to off and not send secrets in the clear, but the SNMPv1 community is such a secret.errornone: RFC has 5 errata, none on this point
RA-1184Appendix C, F.2.1, F.2.2"A router implementing RIP SHOULD implement RIP Version 2 [ROUTE:?], as it supports CIDR routes.""[ROUTE:?]" is an unresolved reference placeholder (twice in F.2.1: RIP Version 2 and Demand RIP; neither is in Section 11). In F.2.2 the poisoned-reverse formula "MAX(0, Ul - INT(seconds that the route has been stale/Ut)" uses an undefined "Ut" (the update timer is defined as Tu) and has unbalanced parentheses. Appendix C numbers its items 1, 2, 7, 8, 9, 10, 12, 13, 15, 15, 16 ... (two items 15, several missing).editorialnone: RFC has 5 errata, none on this point; proposed erratum below

RA-12743"Section 5.3.5.2, second paragraph replaced with: A router MAY have an option to enable receiving network-prefix-directed broadcasts on an interface and MAY have an option to enable forwarding"Only the second paragraph of RFC 1812 5.3.5.2 is replaced. The first paragraph, left in force, still says "Given a route and no overriding policy, then, a router MUST forward network-prefix-directed broadcasts." With the replacement, forwarding must be blocked by default and the option to enable it is only a MAY, so a router without the option can never forward them; the two paragraphs then contradict each other unless the default block is read as the "overriding policy", which neither document says. RFC 3128: Protection Against a Variant of the Tiny Fragment Attack

Depth: deep. Errata: none (the RFC has no errata). Status: Informational. Updates: RFC 1858.

IDSectionQuoteIssueSeverityErratum
RA-12752, 3"if FO=0 and PROTOCOL=TCP and TRANSPORTLEN < tmin then DROP PACKET"tmin is not defined in this document (it comes from RFC 1858 Section 3.2.1, where it is the length needed to cover the "interesting" TCP header fields). Section 2 describes Fragment 1 as "length >= 16" and "Includes whole header", although a TCP header is at least 20 octets; a reader cannot tell whether tmin is 16 (up to and including the flags) or the full header length (20 or the Data Offset value), and with 16 the window, checksum and options of the first fragment can still be replaced by an overlapping FO=0 or FO=1 fragment. The countermeasure is also limited to TCP over IPv4; nothing is said about overlapping zero-offset fragments of other protocols or about IPv6 (later addressed by RFC 5722 and RFC 7112).ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata
RA-12763"In addition to blocking FO=1 packets, it is also necessary to block FO=0 that hold less than a complete header."Security gap: The countermeasure stops the 8-octet variant but still lets two complete FO=0 fragments of the same datagram through when each one individually matches a permit rule (for example two full TCP headers to two permitted ports with different flags), leaving the outcome to the receiver's reassembly policy for overlapping data. The document does not recommend dropping datagrams with more than one zero-offset fragment or with overlapping fragments in general, which is the robust fix the attack class calls for.errornone: RFC has no errata
RA-12771, 1.1, 2, 2.1"Depending on the precise implementation of the fragment reassembly in the target machine's IP stack, fragment B may overwrite fragment A to produce:-"The fragments are numbered 1, 2 and 3 in Section 2 and the example; "fragment B" and "fragment A" mean Fragment 2 and Fragment 1. IDSectionQuoteIssueSeverityErratum
RA-12783, 2.4, 5"replace <ESC><hexpair> with the octet indicated by the <hexpair>."Security gap: the hexpair escape can produce any octet, including NUL (2.4 requires NUL to be escaped, so "\00" is the only way to carry it) and octet sequences that are not valid UTF-8 (for example a lone "\C4"), although Section 3 says the string representation "is restricted to UTF-8 [RFC3629] encoded Unicode [Unicode] characters". The document does not say whether a parser must reject a value whose unescaped octets are not valid UTF-8 or contain NUL, nor whether the BER in a <hexstring> must be validated. Values with embedded NUL are the basis of the known certificate-name truncation attacks (a name that compares or displays differently once handled as a NUL-terminated string); Section 5 discusses disclosure and DER reconstruction only.errornone: RFC has 2 errata, none on this point; proposed erratum below
RA-1279Appendix A"It is recommended that human interfaces use the optional hex pair escaping mechanism (Section 2.3) to produce a string representation suitable for display to the user."The hex pair escaping mechanism is defined in Section 2.4; Section 2.3 is "Converting AttributeTypeAndValue". The same appendix recommends line-wrapping long DN strings "by inserting whitespace after the RDN separator character" and two paragraphs later says "Inserting whitespace is not advised". The examples "OU=Sales+CN=J. Smith" (Section 4) and "CN=Kurt D. Zeilenga" (Appendix A) contain two spaces after the period, which become part of the value if copied literally.editorialnone: RFC has 2 errata, none on this point; proposed erratum below

Proposed erratum RA-1278 (RFC 4514, Section 3, 2.4, 5; type: Technical):

Original Text
-------------
   replace <ESC><hexpair> with the octet indicated by the <hexpair>.

Corrected Text
--------------
   replace <ESC><hexpair> with the octet indicated by the <hexpair>.
    The resulting sequence of octets MUST be valid UTF-8 [RFC3629];
   a string that does not satisfy this is not a valid string
   representation and MUST be rejected.  Applications that process
   the resulting value as a NUL-terminated string MUST reject values
   containing the NUL (U+0000) character.

Notes
-----
   Section 3 restricts the string representation to UTF-8 but the
   hexpair escape bypasses that restriction. Embedded NUL characters
   in names have been used to make a name compare or display
   differently from what was certified.

Proposed erratum RA-1279 (RFC 4514, Section Appendix A; type: Editorial):

Original Text
-------------
   It is recommended that human interfaces use the optional hex pair
   escaping mechanism (Section 2.3) to produce a string
   representation suitable for display to the user.

Corrected Text
--------------
   It is recommended that human interfaces use the optional hex pair
   escaping mechanism (Section 2.4) to produce a string
   representation suitable for display to the user.

Notes
-----
   Section 2.4 defines "Each octet of the character to be escaped is
   replaced by a backslash and two hex digits". Appendix A also both
   recommends ("Line wrapping should be done by inserting
   whitespace") and advises against ("Inserting whitespace is not
   advised") inserting whitespace.

IDSectionQuoteIssueSeverityErratum
RA-08663.3, 6, 8, 12"The Base 32 encoding is designed to represent arbitrary sequences of octets in a form that needs to be case insensitive / Base 16 encoding is the standard case-insensitive hex encoding"Sections 6 and 8 describe base32 and base16 as case-insensitive, but Tables 3 to 5 list only upper-case letters, and Section 3.3 says decoders "MUST reject the encoded data if it contains characters outside the base alphabet". Whether lower-case input is part of the alphabet (accepted) or a non-alphabet character (rejected) is therefore not determined; Section 12 ("when the base 16 and base 32 alphabets are handled case insensitively") treats case folding as an option. RA-08675"This encoding is technically identical to the previous one, except for the 62:nd and 63:rd alphabet character, as indicated in Table 2."The changed characters are those with values 62 and 63, which are the 63rd and 64th characters of the alphabet; "62:nd and 63:rd" mixes value and ordinal. Proposed erratum RA-0866 (RFC 4648, Section 3.3, 6, 8, 12; type: Technical):

Original Text
-------------
   Base 16 encoding is the standard case-insensitive hex encoding
   and may be referred to as "base16" or "hex".

Corrected Text
--------------
   Base 16 encoding is the standard hex encoding and may be referred
   to as "base16" or "hex". Encoders MUST use the upper-case

   document (see Section 3.3).

-----
   The same applies to Section 6 (base32). Section 12 already notes

RA-01056.2.1"MUST be no less than 3 seconds and no greater than .75 * MaxRtrAdvInterval. RA-0106Appendix C"This appendix contains a summary of the rules specified in Sections 7.2 and 7.3."The summary table disagrees with 7.2.5: it has no row for a solicited NA without a target link-layer address in PROBE (so a reachable neighbour can be discarded), and labels a Solicited = 1 row INCOMPLETE where PROBE is meant. An implementation built from the table rather than 7.2.5 gets NUD wrong.errorerratum 2709 (Verified), technical; erratum 2797 (Held for Document Update), technical
RA-11857.2.6"a node MAY send up to MAX_NEIGHBOR_ADVERTISEMENT unsolicited Neighbor Advertisement messages to the all-nodes multicast address. RA-11867.2.6, 7.2.5"The Override flag MAY be set to either zero or one. So with Override clear, receivers in DELAY or PROBE keep probing the old address and do not move to STALE, contrary to "in either case".contradictionnone: RFC has 15 errata, none on this point; proposed erratum below
RA-1187Appendix C, 7.2.5"!INCOMPLETE NA, Solicited=0, - unchanged / Override=0"The row covers every link-layer address, but Section 7.2.5 rule I.a requires an entry in REACHABLE to move to STALE when an advertisement with Override=0 carries a different link-layer address, whatever the Solicited flag. An implementation built from the table leaves REACHABLE entries untouched when a neighbour announces a new address without Override (e.g., anycast or proxy), so NUD does not start until ReachableTime expires.contradictionnone: RFC has 15 errata, none on this point; proposed erratum below
RA-11884.4, 7.2.4, 7.2.8"It SHOULD NOT be set in solicited advertisements for anycast addresses and in solicited proxy advertisements. / All solicited proxy Neighbor Advertisement messages MUST have the Override flag set to zero."The Override rule for solicited proxy advertisements is SHOULD NOT in 4.4 and 7.2.4 but MUST in 7.2.8. Implementers get two requirement levels for the same behaviour; a proxy that sets Override=1 under the SHOULD reading overrides the real owner's entry, which is the case 7.2.8 says must not happen.contradictionnone: RFC has 15 errata, none on this point
RA-11894.2, 6.2.7, 6.3.2"The default value that should be placed in the Hop Count field of the IP header for outgoing IP packets."The IPv6 header field is "Hop Limit" (RFC 8200); there is no Hop Count field. Proposed erratum RA-1185 (RFC 4861, Section 7.2.6; type: Technical):

Original Text
-------------
   These advertisements MUST be separated by at least RetransTimer
   seconds.

Corrected Text
--------------
   These advertisements MUST be separated by at least RetransTimer
   milliseconds.

Notes
-----
   RetransTimer is expressed in milliseconds everywhere else in the
   document.

Proposed erratum RA-1186 (RFC 4861, Section 7.2.6, 7.2.5; type: Technical):

Original Text
-------------
   The Override flag MAY be set to either zero or one.  In either
   case, neighboring nodes will immediately change the state of
   their Neighbor Cache entries for the Target Address to STALE,
   prompting them to verify the path for reachability.

Corrected Text
--------------
   The Override flag MAY be set to either zero or one.  If it is set
   to one, neighboring nodes will install the new link-layer address
   and change the state of their Neighbor Cache entries for the
   Target Address to STALE.  If it is set to zero, neighboring nodes
   with a REACHABLE entry change it to STALE (Section 7.2.5),
   prompting them to verify the path for reachability; entries in
   other states are not changed.

Notes
-----
   Rule I.b says an Override=0 advertisement with a different
   link-layer address is ignored unless the entry is REACHABLE.

Proposed erratum RA-1187 (RFC 4861, Section Appendix C, 7.2.5; type: Technical):

Original Text
-------------
   !INCOMPLETE     NA, Solicited=0,        -
   unchanged Override=0

Corrected Text
--------------
   REACHABLE       NA, Solicited=0,        -
   STALE Override=0 Different link-layer address than cached.
   !INCOMPLETE     NA, Solicited=0,        -
   unchanged Override=0 Same link-layer address as cached, or not
   REACHABLE.

Notes
-----
   Rule I.a of Section 7.2.5 applies regardless of the Solicited
   flag; the table states "unchanged" for all Solicited=0,
   Override=0 cases.

Proposed erratum RA-1189 (RFC 4861, Section 4.2, 6.2.7, 6.3.2; type: Editorial):

Original Text
-------------
   The default value that should be placed in the Hop Count field of

Corrected Text
--------------
   The default value that should be placed in the Hop Limit field of
   the IP header for outgoing IP packets.

Notes
-----
   Editorial.

RFC 5082: The Generalized TTL Security Mechanism (GTSM)

Depth: deep. Errata: none (the RFC has no errata). Status: Proposed Standard. Obsoletes: RFC 3682.

IDSectionQuoteIssueSeverityErratum
RA-04193, 6.1"This specification mandates setting and verifying TTL=255 of those as well as the main protocol packets. / The exact policies applied to packets of different classifications are not postulated in this document and are expected to be configurable."Section 6.1 (and Appendix B) say the document requires related ICMP errors to be checked for TTL 255, but the receive procedure of Section 3 defines classification only for packets "belonging to one of the GTSM-enabled sessions" and leaves policy for related messages configurable; it never says how an ICMP error is associated with a session (by the quoted inner header) or that one with TTL below 255 is Dangerous. On the sending side, related ICMP errors are usually generated by the IP stack, which has no knowledge of GTSM sessions, so "MUST be set to 255" for them is hard to meet.
