RFC 5116: An Interface and Algorithms for Authenticated Encryption

Depth: deep. Errata: 6 errata: 2 verified, 4 reported. Status: Proposed Standard.

IDSectionQuoteIssueSeverityErratum
RA-08725.1"P_MAX is 2^36 - 31 octets, / C_MAX is 2^36 - 15 octets."GCM (NIST SP 800-38D 5.2.1.1) limits the plaintext to 2^39 - 256 bits, which is 2^36 - 32 octets. The stated P_MAX of 2^36 - 31 octets exceeds that limit by one octet, and C_MAX (P_MAX + 16) is correspondingly 2^36 - 16, not 2^36 - 15. An implementation that accepts exactly P_MAX octets violates the GCM bound.errorerratum 5219 (Reported), technical
RA-08732.2"The authenticated decrypt operation will, with high probability, return FAIL whenever the inputs N, P, and A were crafted by a nonce-respecting adversary"The inputs of authenticated decryption are K, N, A and C ("has four inputs: K, N, A, and C"); P is its output. The sentence should refer to N, C, and A. The preceding definition ("C is generated by the encrypt operation with inputs K, N, P, and A, for some values of N, P, and A") quantifies over N and A, which are given; only P is free.errorerratum 4008 (Verified), editorial

RFC 5227: IPv4 Address Conflict Detection

Depth: deep. Errata: 1 errata: 1 rejected. Status: Proposed Standard. Updates: RFC 826.

IDSectionQuoteIssueSeverityErratum
RA-08742.1.1"the host receives any ARP packet (Request or Reply) ... where the packet's 'sender IP address' is the address being probed for / If, by ANNOUNCE_WAIT seconds after the transmission of the last ARP Probe no conflicting ARP Reply or ARP Probe has been received"The conflict condition during probing is any ARP packet (Request or Reply) whose sender IP address is the probed address, plus ARP Probes for the same target from another hardware address. The concluding sentence narrows the success test to "no conflicting ARP Reply or ARP Probe", leaving out conflicting ARP Requests (for example an ARP Announcement or ordinary Request from a host already using the address). An implementation following the last sentence would accept an address whose current owner only sends Requests during the probe window.contradictionnone: RFC has 1 errata, none on this point; proposed erratum below
RA-08751.3, 2.1, 2.4"Where this document uses the term "host", it applies equally to interfaces on routers ... In those cases, option (c) in Section 2.4 ("Ongoing Address Conflict Detection and Address Defense") applies."For routers the document points to option (c) of 2.4, which is a MAY ("MAY elect to defend its address indefinitely"), while 2.4 also says a host "MUST respond to a conflicting ARP packet as described in either (a), (b), or (c)" and 2.1 makes probing before use a MUST for every address, including a fixed router address that cannot be changed when a conflict is found. What a router is required to do (probe and refuse the address, probe and only log, or skip probing) is not stated; option (c) itself requires a defensive Announcement at most once per DEFEND_INTERVAL and logging.ambiguitynone: RFC has 1 errata, none on this point

Proposed erratum RA-0874 (RFC 5227, Section 2.1.1; type: Technical):

Original Text
-------------
   If, by ANNOUNCE_WAIT seconds after the transmission of the last
   ARP Probe no conflicting ARP Reply or ARP Probe has been
   received, then the host has successfully determined that the
   desired address may be used safely.

Corrected Text
--------------
   If, by ANNOUNCE_WAIT seconds after the transmission of the last
   ARP Probe no conflicting ARP packet (Request or Reply) and no
   conflicting ARP Probe has been received, then the host has
   successfully determined that the desired address may be used
   safely.

Notes
-----
   The third paragraph of 2.1.1 treats "any ARP packet (Request *or*
   Reply)" with the probed sender IP address as a conflict.

RA-08867"Since each character may be up to 6 octets, it is RECOMMENDED that each syslog application be prepared to receive up to 6 octets per character."The document requires UTF-8 "as specified in RFC 3629" (6, 6.4), and RFC 3629 restricts UTF-8 to code points up to U+10FFFF, encoded in at most 4 octets; 5- and 6-octet sequences are invalid, and 6.4 says invalid UTF-8 sequences MUST NOT be interpreted. Sizing buffers for 6 octets per character is harmless, but the statement that a character may take 6 octets conflicts with the normative reference.contradictionnone: RFC has 5 errata, none on this point; proposed erratum below
RA-0887A.8"This document specifies that SD-PARAMS must always be encoded in UTF-8. Other encodings of the message in the MSG portion, including ASCIIPRINT, are not permitted by a device conforming to this specification."Section 6.4 says the MSG character set "SHOULD be UNICODE" and "If the syslog application cannot encode the MSG in Unicode, it MAY use any other encoding", and the ABNF defines MSG-ANY for MSG without a BOM; Example 2 in 6.5 is a valid message without a BOM. Appendix A.8 (non-normative) states the opposite. It also says SD-PARAMs are UTF-8, while 6.3 restricts UTF-8 to PARAM-VALUE and requires US-ASCII for SD-ID and PARAM-NAME. "ASCIIPRINT" is not defined (the ABNF rule is PRINTUSASCII).contradictionnone: RFC has 5 errata, none on this point; proposed erratum below
RA-08886"PARAM-VALUE = UTF-8-STRING ; characters '"', '\' and ; ']' MUST be escaped."UTF-8-STRING is defined as *OCTET, so the grammar itself accepts an unescaped '"' or ']' inside PARAM-VALUE and cannot determine where the value ends; the escaping rule exists only as a comment and in prose (6.3.3), and the invalid-escape rule in 6.3.3 (a backslash followed by another character is kept) is not expressible in the ABNF either. A parser written from the ABNF can split SD-ELEMENTs differently from one written from the prose.ambiguitynone: RFC has 5 errata, none on this point; proposed erratum below
RA-08896.4"If a syslog application encodes MSG in UTF-8, the string MUST start with the Unicode byte order mask (BOM),"The Unicode term is "byte order mark". Other editorial points: 6.3.3 "the invalid sequence MUST not be altered" (mixed case for MUST NOT); 7.1.4 "no later then 9:01:00" (than); Diagram 1 opens a second parenthesis "(transport sender, (transport receiver)".editorialnone: RFC has 5 errata, none on this point; proposed erratum below

Proposed erratum RA-0886 (RFC 5424, Section 7; type: Technical):

Original Text
-------------
   Since each character may be up to 6 octets, it is RECOMMENDED
   that each syslog application be prepared to receive up to 6
   octets per character.

Corrected Text
--------------
   Since each character may be up to 4 octets [RFC3629], it is
   RECOMMENDED that each syslog application be prepared to receive
   up to 4 octets per character.

Notes
-----
   RFC 3629 Section 3 limits UTF-8 sequences to four octets.

Proposed erratum RA-0887 (RFC 5424, Section A.8; type: Technical):

Original Text
-------------
   Other encodings of the message in the MSG portion, including
   ASCIIPRINT, are not permitted by a device conforming to this
   specification.

Corrected Text
--------------
   Other encodings of the MSG portion are permitted (MSG-ANY,
   Section 6.4), but then the MSG MUST NOT start with a BOM.

Notes
-----
   Also O: "SD-PARAMS must always be encoded in UTF-8" C:
   "PARAM-VALUE must always be encoded in UTF-8".

Proposed erratum RA-0888 (RFC 5424, Section 6; type: Technical):

Original Text
-------------
   PARAM-VALUE     = UTF-8-STRING ; characters '"', '\' and ']' MUST
   be escaped.

Corrected Text
--------------
   PARAM-VALUE     = *( %x5C ( %x22
   %x5C
   %x5D )
   PARAM-CHAR ) ; PARAM-CHAR = any UTF-8 character except %x22,
   %x5C, %x5D

Notes
-----
   A precise rule would also need to state how a lone backslash is
   handled (6.3.3 keeps it as a literal).

Proposed erratum RA-0889 (RFC 5424, Section 6.4; type: Editorial):

Original Text
-------------
   byte order mask (BOM)

Corrected Text
--------------
   byte order mark (BOM)

Notes
-----
   Also 6.3.3 O: MUST not be altered C: MUST NOT be altered; 7.1.4

RA-01076.2"&& (RCV.PREV_SEQ > 0x7fff) && (SEG.SEQ < 0x7fff)) {"The Sequence Number Extension pseudocode compares 32-bit sequence numbers with a 16-bit midpoint; it must be 0x7fffffff. RA-01105.2"remote ISN), and the destination (remote) ISN is unknown (and so"In the receive-SYN traffic key both ISNs are called "remote"; the destination ISN is the local one. Erratum 7899 has been verified.errorerratum 7899 (Verified), technical

For a non-SYN segment the text therefore never says how the MKT is selected (by socket pair and KeyID against RecvID, as Sections 3.3 and 4 imply), what happens when the KeyID matches no MKT of the connection, or that a segment without TCP-AO on a connection that uses TCP-AO is discarded. RA-11913.3, 5.2, 7.7"If the ISN pair is not known, e.g., when sending a reset (RST) after a reboot, the segment should be sent without authentication (5.2) / TCP-AO is always used when outgoing segments match an MKT, and is not used otherwise. (3.3)"Section 3.3 requires TCP-AO on every outgoing segment whose socket pair matches an MKT. A rebooted host answering a segment of a lost connection has a matching MKT but no ISNs, and Section 5.2 tells it to send the RST without TCP-AO. The text does not say which rule wins, nor whether such a RST may instead be sent with TCP-AO computed from zero ISNs. Either way the peer discards it (Section 7.7), so the choice affects only whether the host emits an unauthenticated segment on a protected socket pair.contradictionnone: RFC has 8 errata, none on this point
RA-11927.8, 10"A TCP-AO implementation MUST default to ignore incoming ICMPv4 messages of Type 3 (destination unreachable), Codes 2-4 (protocol unreachable, port unreachable, and fragmentation needed -- 'hard errors')"Code 4 (fragmentation needed and DF set) is also the Path MTU Discovery signal of RFC 1191; ignoring it by default disables PMTUD on IPv4 TCP-AO connections in synchronized states, while the next requirement asks implementations to "protect ICMP 'packet too big' messages", which presupposes processing them. The IPv6 list is not the counterpart of the IPv4 list: it includes Code 1 (administratively prohibited), whose IPv4 counterparts (Codes 9, 10, 13) are not listed, and does not include Packet Too Big, so IPv4 and IPv6 connections behave differently by default.ambiguitynone: RFC has 8 errata, none on this point
RA-11933.1, 3.3">> The IDs of MKTs MUST NOT overlap where their TCP connection identifiers overlap."Each MKT has a SendID and a RecvID. RA-11941.1, 3.1, 5.1, 7.5, 7.6"c. Proposed erratum RA-1190 (RFC 5925, Section 7.5; type: Technical):

Original Text
-------------
   b. (missing)

Corrected Text
--------------
   b. If the segment is not a SYN, then determine whether TCP-AO is
   being used for the connection. If it is and the segment has no
   TCP-AO, or its KeyID matches the RecvID of no MKT of the
   connection, silently discard the segment (Section 7.3). Otherwise
   use the MKT whose RecvID matches the KeyID and proceed with step
   2.

Notes
-----
   Section 7.4 has both a SYN and a non-SYN step 1; Section 7.5 has
   only the SYN case, although Section 10 cites Section 7.5 for
   "Incoming all checked".

Depth: deep. Errata: 12 errata: 1 verified, 4 held, 7 rejected. Status: Proposed Standard. Updates: RFC 4291.

IDSectionQuoteIssueSeverityErratum
RA-08954"The recommendation in this section SHOULD be followed by systems when generating an address to be represented as text, but all implementations MUST accept and be able to handle any legitimate [RFC4291] format."Section 4 makes the canonical form a SHOULD, but each rule in 4.1 to 4.3 is stated with MUST ("Leading zeros MUST be suppressed", "MUST be used to its maximum capability", "MUST be represented in lowercase"). It is unclear whether an implementation that generates, for example, uppercase hexadecimal is non-conforming (MUST) or merely not following a recommendation (SHOULD); the subsection MUSTs read as conditions of the SHOULD but are not written that way. Section 4.2.3 also says "the first sequence of zero bits" where it means zero fields.ambiguitynone: RFC has 12 errata, none on this point; proposed erratum below
RA-08965"For these addresses, mixed notation is RECOMMENDED if the following condition is met: the address can be distinguished as having IPv4 addresses embedded in the lower 32 bits solely from the address field through the use of a well-known prefix."ISATAP addresses are listed as an example of addresses with an embedded IPv4 address, but they are identified by the interface identifier (0000:5efe or 0200:5efe) under an arbitrary /64, not by a well-known prefix, so they never meet the stated condition; whether they should be printed in mixed notation is therefore unclear. The well-known prefixes are given only as "defined in [RFC4291] and [RFC2765] at the time of this writing", without listing them (::ffff:0:0/96, ::ffff:0:0:0/96, and the deprecated IPv4-compatible ::/96), so two conforming formatters can disagree on ::192.0.2.1. RA-08984.3"For instance, IPsec tunnel endpoints compatible with RFC 4301 invariably use Internet Key Exchange Protocol version 2 (IKEv2)"RFC 4301 (Sections 4.4 and 4.5) also permits manual keying and does not mandate IKEv2; a manually keyed RFC 4301 ingress can be paired with an RFC 2401 egress that discards the outer header. The conclusion that an IPsec ingress "will never interact with legacy ECN tunnels" and needs no compatibility mode therefore holds only when IKEv2 is used, and a CE mark copied into the outer header could be lost at such an egress (a congestion-control and traffic-security gap). RA-08994.2"Alarms SHOULD be rate-limited so that the anomalous combinations will not amplify into a flood of alarm messages. RFC 6066: Transport Layer Security (TLS) Extensions: Extension Definitions

Depth: deep. Errata: 3 errata: 2 verified, 1 reported. Status: Proposed Standard. Obsoletes: RFC 4366. Updated by: RFC 8446, RFC 8449, RFC 9325, RFC 9846.

IDSectionQuoteIssueSeverityErratum
RA-09004"the record-layer output can be at most 805 bytes: 5 bytes of headers, 512 bytes of application data, 256 bytes of padding, and 32 bytes of MAC. / ... larger than 805 bytes MUST discard the message"The bound omits the explicit per-record IV that TLS 1.1 and TLS 1.2 (RFC 5246 6.2.3.2) carry for CBC cipher suites (16 octets for AES), and the nonce_explicit of AEAD suites. A TLS 1.2 record with 512 octets of data, AES-CBC, maximal padding and HMAC-SHA256 is 5 + 16 + 512 + 256 + 32 = 821 octets, so a receiver applying the MUST discards valid records. The figure is copied from the TLS 1.0 era (RFC 4366) where no explicit IV existed.errornone: RFC has 3 errata, none on this point; proposed erratum below
RA-0901Appendix A, 3"It is provided that the ServerNameList can contain more than only one name of any particular name_type. / The ServerNameList MUST NOT contain more than one name of the same name_type."Appendix A states the opposite of the Section 3 rule and of the Section 3 note ("Multiple names of the same name_type are therefore now prohibited"). The appendix is the change summary from RFC 4366, so the sentence should say the permission was removed.contradictionerratum 3283 (Verified), technical
RA-09025"unint8 padding;"The type "unint8" does not exist in the TLS presentation language; "uint8" is meant. Section 8 also names the field "ocsp_response" and the list "ResponderIDs", which are spelled "response" (type OCSPResponse) and "responder_id_list" in the structures.editorialnone: RFC has 3 errata, none on this point; proposed erratum below
RA-09031, 4, 7"the older session is resumed, then the server MUST ignore the extensions and send a server hello containing none of the extension types. / The negotiated length applies for the duration of the session including session resumptions."On resumption the server ignores the extensions offered, and the values of the original session (max_fragment_length, truncated_hmac) stay in force; but the client SHOULD resend "the same extensions", and nothing says what the client does when the extensions it offers in the resumption differ from those negotiated originally (e.g. a different max_fragment_length). A client that offers a new limit and sees an extension-less server hello cannot tell which limit applies other than by session state, and Section 4 requires the client to abort only when a response "differs from the length it requested", which does not cover an absent response on resumption. Later RFCs: RFC 9846 Appendix E.5 forbids the Truncated HMAC extension, which settles that half; RFC 8449 Section 4 renegotiates the record size limit on resumption, while the max_fragment_length case stays as described.ambiguitynone: RFC has 3 errata, none on this point

Proposed erratum RA-0900 (RFC 6066, Section 4; type: Technical):

-------------
   the record-layer output can be at most 805 bytes: 5 bytes of
   headers, 512 bytes of application data, 256 bytes of padding, and
   32 bytes of MAC.  This means that in this event a TLS
   record-layer peer receiving a TLS record-layer message larger

Corrected Text

   message larger than 821 bytes MUST discard the message

RFC 6234: US Secure Hash Algorithms (SHA and SHA-based HMAC and HKDF)

Depth: deep. Errata: 4 errata: 1 verified, 2 reported, 1 held. Status: Informational. Obsoletes: RFC 4634. Updates: RFC 3174.

IDSectionQuoteIssueSeverityErratum
RA-09078.3, 8.4"int err = USHAReset(&tcontext, whichSha) || USHAInput(&tcontext, key, key_len) || / shaNull(1) when presented with a null pointer parameter"The sample code chains calls with the logical OR operator (hmac(), hmacReset(), hmacResult(), hkdf(), hkdfExpand(), hkdfResult()). In C the value of "a || b" is 0 or 1, so any failure (shaInputTooLong 2, shaStateError 3, shaBadParam 4) is returned to the caller as 1, i.e. shaNull. Section 8 documents distinct return codes, so a caller of hkdf() with okm_len > 255*HashLen receives "null pointer" instead of "bad parameter". The hashes and MACs computed are not affected.editorialnone: RFC has 4 errata, none on this point; proposed erratum below
RA-09081, 6.2, 8, 9"id-sha224 OBJECT IDENTIFIER ::= {{ joint-iso-itu-t(2) / Wt = SSIG1(W(t-2)) + W(t-7) + SSIG0(w(t-15)) + W(t-16)"The id-sha224 OID has a doubled opening brace; Section 6.2 step 1 writes "w(t-15)" in lower case where every other reference is W (6.4 has "W(t-15)"); Section 8 prototype "USHAInput(USHAContext context*," has the pointer star misplaced; Section 9 cites "[FIPS 180-2]", which is not in the reference list (the normative [SHS] is FIPS 180-3); Section 2 c. writes "If Z is an integer, 0 <= z < 2^64" mixing Z and z; the [RFC3874] entry is mis-indented into the [RFC3174] entry.editorialnone: RFC has 4 errata, none on this point; proposed erratum below

Proposed erratum RA-0907 (RFC 6234, Section 8.3, 8.4; type: Editorial):

Original Text
-------------
   int err = USHAReset(&tcontext, whichSha) || USHAInput(&tcontext,
   key, key_len) || USHAResult(&tcontext, tempkey);

Corrected Text
--------------
   int err = USHAReset(&tcontext, whichSha); if (err == shaSuccess)
   err = USHAInput(&tcontext, key, key_len); if (err == shaSuccess)
   err = USHAResult(&tcontext, tempkey);  (and likewise for the
   other "||" chains in hmac.c and hkdf.c)

Notes
-----
   The C logical OR yields 0 or 1; the documented return values 2 to
   4 are lost.

RFC 6398: IP Router Alert Considerations and Usage

Depth: deep. Errata: none (the RFC has no errata). Status: Best Current Practice (BCP 168). Updates: RFC 2113, RFC 2711.

IDSectionQuoteIssueSeverityErratum
RA-09095, 3"a router implementation SHOULD forward within the "fast path" ... a packet carrying the IP Router Alert Option containing a next level protocol that is not a protocol of interest to that router."Section 3 explains that the next level protocol is not a sufficient discriminator (several applications share it, and some RAO users run over UDP or TCP), yet the Section 5 rule is keyed on the next level protocol only. For a router with one RAO protocol of interest over UDP, the rule gives no guidance whether other UDP RAO packets are punted (and so exposed to the DoS of Section 3) or forwarded (and so the protocol of interest may be missed); for IPv6, where the next level protocol may follow further extension headers, "next level protocol" is not defined (the last Next Header, or the one after the Hop-by-Hop header). Section 4.3 also places a "MUST implement strong protection" on service providers without saying what satisfies it.ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata

RFC 6454: The Web Origin Concept

Depth: deep. Errata: 1 errata: 1 rejected. Status: Proposed Standard.

IDSectionQuoteIssueSeverityErratum
RA-09107, 5, 6.2"Two origins are "the same" if, and only if, they are identical. / If the port part of the origin triple is different from the default port ... Append a U+003A COLON code point (":") and the given port"Section 5 compares origins (scheme/host/port triples), but Section 7 gives a server only the serialized form and says nothing about how a server compares a received Origin header with the origin it expects. A server that compares strings will treat "https://example.com" and "https://example.com:443" (or "HTTP://Example.com", which the ABNF of RFC 3986 scheme and host allows) as different, while the triples are the same; a server that parses must apply the default-port and case rules of Section 4, which are written for user agents. The ABNF also allows several serialized origins in one header (origin-list), and Section 7 does not say which of them a server should check.ambiguitynone: RFC has 1 errata, none on this point

RFC 6633: Deprecation of ICMP Source Quench Messages

Depth: deep. Errata: none (the RFC has no errata). Status: Proposed Standard. Updates: RFC 792, RFC 1122, RFC 1812.

IDSectionQuoteIssueSeverityErratum
RA-12801, 3, 4"This document hereby updates Section 4.3.3.3 of [RFC1812] as follows: A router MUST ignore any ICMP Source Quench messages it receives."Sections 3 and 4 say they update RFC 1122 3.2.2.3 / 4.2.3.9 and RFC 1812 4.3.3.3 "as follows" without saying whether the quoted text replaces the whole section or only the reception rule. RFC 1812 4.3.3.3 also says "A router SHOULD NOT originate ICMP Source Quench messages" and that a router that does "MUST be able to limit the rate"; if the section is replaced, router origination is no longer addressed at all, and if it is amended, routers may still originate Source Quench (SHOULD NOT) while hosts now MUST NOT (Section 3), although Section 3's rationale ("no known valid reason ... to generate this message") applies equally to routers. The header also lists RFC 792 as updated, but no section states what changes in RFC 792 (only Section 9 marks type 4 "Deprecated" in the registry). The Introduction says "Processing of ICMP Source Quench messages by routers has been deprecated for nearly 17 years [RFC1812]", while RFC 1812 4.3.3.3 deprecated their generation and only said a router "MAY ignore" received ones.ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below
RA-12813, 8"If a Source Quench message is received, the IP layer MAY silently discard it. (3) / Hosts, security gateways, and firewalls MUST silently discard received ICMP Source Quench packets and SHOULD log such drops (8)"Section 3 makes discarding at the host's IP layer optional (a "performance optimization that is permitted"), leaving discard to the transport layer, while Section 8 requires hosts to discard at once (MUST) and adds a SHOULD to log every drop "as a security fault", which also conflicts with "silently" and with Section 3's description of discard as an optimization. For "security gateways, and firewalls" Section 8 does not say whether "received" means addressed to the device or also forwarded through it; a MUST to discard transit Source Quench is a filtering requirement not stated anywhere else (Section 4 only says a router MUST ignore those it receives).contradictionnone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below
RA-12823"The only known impact of a sender ignoring this requirement is that it may necessarily consume network and endpoint resources.""necessarily" should be "unnecessarily".editorialnone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below

Proposed erratum RA-1280 (RFC 6633, Section 1, 3, 4; type: Technical):

Original Text
-------------
   This document hereby updates Section 4.3.3.3 of [RFC1812] as
   follows: A router MUST ignore any ICMP Source Quench messages it
   receives.

Corrected Text
--------------
   This document hereby updates Section 4.3.3.3 of [RFC1812] by
   replacing the sentence "A router MAY ignore any ICMP Source
   Quench messages it receives." with: A router MUST ignore any ICMP
   Source Quench messages it receives. (And state whether "A router
   SHOULD NOT originate ICMP Source Quench messages" remains or
   becomes MUST NOT, as for hosts in Section 3.)

Notes
-----
   The same question applies to Section 3: RFC 1122 3.2.2.3 also
   contains the rule that the IP layer "MUST report it to the
   transport layer", which conflicts with the new "MAY silently
   discard" only if the paragraph is not replaced.

Proposed erratum RA-1281 (RFC 6633, Section 3, 8; type: Technical):

Original Text
-------------
   Hosts, security gateways, and firewalls MUST silently discard
   received ICMP Source Quench packets and SHOULD log such drops as
   a security fault with at least minimal details

Corrected Text
--------------
   Hosts, security gateways, and firewalls MUST NOT act upon ICMP
   Source Quench messages addressed to them (Sections 3 to 6) and
   MAY log such messages as a possible security event with at least
   minimal details

Notes
-----
   "Silently discard" combined with "SHOULD log" is also internally
   inconsistent; the intent is presumably "discard without sending
   any ICMP message and without affecting the connection".

Proposed erratum RA-1282 (RFC 6633, Section 3; type: Editorial):

Original Text
-------------
   The only known impact of a sender ignoring this requirement is
   that it may necessarily consume network and endpoint resources.

Corrected Text
--------------
   The only known impact of a sender ignoring this requirement is
   that it may unnecessarily consume network and endpoint resources.

Notes
-----
   Meaning-changing typo in the rationale for the MUST NOT.

RFC 6691: TCP Options and Maximum Segment Size (MSS)

Depth: deep. Errata: none (the RFC has no errata). Status: Informational. Obsoleted by: RFC 9293. Updates: RFC 879, RFC 2385.

IDSectionQuoteIssueSeverityErratum
RA-1283Appendix A, 2, 4"implementations ignore the "greater than or" part of "SHOULD be greater than or equal to the MTU of the connected network(s)". Thus, the MSS value to be sent in an MSS option must be less than or equal to: EMTU_R - FixedIPhdrsize - FixedTCPhdrsize"The paragraph first explains that EMTU_R (largest reassemblable datagram) would give 65495 and that implementations instead use the MTU of the connected network, then concludes with a bound expressed in EMTU_R again. Read with the RFC 1122 definition of EMTU_R the conclusion is the 65495 bound just argued against; read with "EMTU_R = MTU of the connected network" it matches Sections 2 and 4 ("effective MTU minus the fixed IP and TCP headers"). The appendix also speaks of "IP options" only; whether IPv6 extension headers that the sender always adds count as options (reduce the data, not the MSS) is not said (RFC 9293 3.7.1 later states it: "IPoptionsize is the size of any IPv4 options or IPv6 extension headers"). Later RFCs: RFC 9293 (obsoletes RFC 6691) drops the appendix, but Section 3.7.1 still bounds the option value by MMS_R - 20 with MMS_R defined from EMTU_R, so the same question remains.ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below

Proposed erratum RA-1283 (RFC 6691, Section Appendix A, 2, 4; type: Technical):

Original Text
-------------

   or equal to: EMTU_R - FixedIPhdrsize - FixedTCPhdrsize

Corrected Text
--------------
   Thus, the MSS value to be sent in an MSS option should be equal
   to the effective MTU (normally the MTU of the connected network)
   minus FixedIPhdrsize and FixedTCPhdrsize, and must be less than
   or equal to EMTU_R - FixedIPhdrsize - FixedTCPhdrsize.

Notes
-----
   RFC 9293 3.7.1, which obsoletes this document, separates the two:
   the value "should be equal to the effective MTU minus the fixed
   IP and TCP headers" and "must be less than or equal to MMS_R -
   20" (MUST-67).
   Status note: RFC 6691 is obsoleted by RFC 9293; an erratum report
   against it may be held or rejected for that reason.

FIPS 186-4 (4.6) and X9.62 also require a new k when s = 0, which Section 2.4 omits; with a deterministic k there is no "new random k", so an implementation must know whether to continue the step h loop (K = HMAC_K(V || 0x00), V = HMAC_K(V)) or fail. RFC 6980: Security Implications of IPv6 Fragmentation with IPv6 Neighbor Discovery

Depth: deep. Errata: none (the RFC has no errata). Status: Proposed Standard. Updates: RFC 3971, RFC 4861.

IDSectionQuoteIssueSeverityErratum
RA-09195"Nodes MUST silently ignore the following Neighbor Discovery and SEcure Neighbor Discovery messages if the packets carrying them include an IPv6 Fragmentation Header"The test is on the presence of a Fragment Header, but the rule does not say at which point it is applied: IPv6 reassembly normally happens below ICMPv6, so an implementation that hands the reassembled datagram to ND no longer sees the header, and the requirement cannot be met without carrying a "was fragmented" flag upward. It also covers atomic fragments (offset 0, M = 0) by its wording, although they are not fragmented; RFC 6946 (later) requires them to be processed in isolation, so whether an NS or RA sent as an atomic fragment is ignored is not settled here. The CPA exception ("SHOULD normally process") has the same layering question in reverse.ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata

RFC 7048: Neighbor Unreachability Detection Is Too Impatient

Depth: deep. Errata: none (the RFC has no errata). Status: Proposed Standard. Updates: RFC 4861.

IDSectionQuoteIssueSeverityErratum
RA-12884, 3"switch to UNREACHABLE after the first three transmissions ... At 4 seconds from the first transmission, the NCE would be marked UNREACHABLE. / After 3 retransmissions, the implementation would mark the NCE UNREACHABLE."The example counts both ways: "after the first three transmissions" (0, 1 and 4 s) and "After 3 retransmissions" (a fourth transmission, at 13 s). Under the Section 3 state table the transition happens on the retransmit timeout after the Nth probe, i.e. at 13 s for three transmissions, not "At 4 seconds"; the comparison with "the 2 seconds using the fixed scheme in [RFC4861]" is also off (RFC 4861 discards the entry at the timeout after the third probe, about 3 s). The example then says the switch to multicast after the fifth transmission (40 s) "corresponds to the action 'Discard entry'", which is the action Section 3 replaces by the UNREACHABLE state (the NCE and its link-layer address are kept). Finally the example points to "the 'SHOULD' in Section 3 to switch to multicast solutions within 60 seconds", but Section 3 says the node "MUST switch to multicast Neighbor Solicitations within 60 seconds of the initial retransmission"; with BACKOFF_MULTIPLE=3 and the fifth unicast probe at 40 s, the next probe (the first multicast one) comes at 100 s (40 + 60 with the clamp), after the 60 s limit.contradictionnone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below
RA-12893"If there is no IPv6 packet sent using the UNREACHABLE NCE, then it is RECOMMENDED to stop the retransmits of the multicast NS until either the NCE is garbage collected or there are IPv6 packets sent using the NCE."The new state has only two rows in the replacement table (entering from PROBE, and the retransmit timeout in UNREACHABLE). There is no row for "sending a packet" in UNREACHABLE, so it is not said whether a packet restarts the stopped retransmissions with the backed-off timer or a fresh one, or moves the entry to DELAY as it would from STALE. The table says UNREACHABLE sends multicast NS, while the text allows "the first few Neighbor Solicitation messages" in UNREACHABLE to be unicast. The first paragraph ties the exponential backoff to sending "more than MAX_UNICAST_SOLICIT/MAX_MULTICAST_SOLICIT packets", but only the NUD (unicast, PROBE) path is changed; address resolution in INCOMPLETE (RFC 4861 7.2.2, MAX_MULTICAST_SOLICIT) is not listed among the places updated, so whether it may also retransmit longer is unclear. Section 6 states no security impact without considering that UNREACHABLE entries now persist (and keep sending multicast NS while packets are sent), which interacts with the Neighbor Cache exhaustion issues of RFC 6583 cited in Section 1.ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata

Proposed erratum RA-1288 (RFC 7048, Section 4, 3; type: Technical):

Original Text
-------------
   After 5 transmissions, i.e., 40 seconds after the initial
   transmission, the example behavior is to switch to multicast NUD
   probes.  In the language of the state machine in [RFC4861], that
   corresponds to the action "Discard entry". [...] In any case, the
   implementation needs to follow the "SHOULD" in Section 3 to
   switch to multicast solutions within 60 seconds after the initial
   transmission.

Corrected Text
--------------
   After 5 transmissions, i.e., 40 seconds after the initial
   transmission, the example behavior is to switch to multicast NUD
   probes while keeping the NCE in the UNREACHABLE state. [...] In
   any case, the implementation needs to follow the "MUST" in
   Section 3 to switch to multicast Neighbor Solicitations within 60
   seconds of the initial retransmission; with the values above, the
   fifth transmission is therefore sent as a multicast NS.

Notes
-----
   Section 3 replaces the RFC 4861 "Discard entry" action by a
   transition to UNREACHABLE and says "it MUST switch to multicast
   Neighbor Solicitations within 60 seconds of the initial
   retransmission". The example's timing (0, 1, 4, 13, 40 s) puts
   the fifth unicast probe at 40 s and the following one at 100 s.
   The example also states "At 4 seconds ... marked UNREACHABLE"
   where the Section 3 table transitions on the retransmit timeout
   after the Nth probe.

RFC 7112: Implications of Oversized IPv6 Header Chains

Depth: deep. Errata: none (the RFC has no errata). Status: Proposed Standard. Updates: RFC 2460.

IDSectionQuoteIssueSeverityErratum
RA-09205, 3"an intermediate system (e.g., router or firewall) that receives an IPv6 First Fragment that does not satisfy the above-stated requirement MAY discard that packet / If an Upper-Layer Header is present, it terminates the header chain"The requirement is that the First Fragment contain "the entire IPv6 Header Chain", which includes the whole Upper-Layer Header, but the length of an Upper-Layer Header is only known for protocols the node understands (TCP data offset, UDP 8 octets, ICMPv6 4 or 8, others unknown). An intermediate system cannot decide whether a First Fragment carrying an unknown upper-layer protocol "satisfies the requirement", so the MAY-discard rule is applied differently (presence of the first octet of the header, a fixed minimum, or protocol-specific lengths). The text also does not say whether the requirement is met when only the Fragment Header and a No Next Header (59) chain are present. The last paragraph ("MUST limit the IPv6 Header Chain length to 1280 bytes") counts the IPv6 and Fragment headers in the 1280 octets but does not account for the rule that the fragmentable part of every non-final fragment is a multiple of 8 octets, so a chain of exactly 1280 octets (or any length leaving a non-multiple of 8 after the unfragmentable part) cannot be sent as a First Fragment; the usable limit is slightly below 1280.ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata

RFC 7527: Enhanced Duplicate Address Detection

Depth: deep. Errata: none (the RFC has no errata). Status: Proposed Standard. Updates: RFC 4429, RFC 4861, RFC 4862.

IDSectionQuoteIssueSeverityErratum
RA-12904, 4.1, 4.2"the sender MUST generate a random nonce associated with the interface address, MUST store the nonce internally (4.1) / so each Enhanced DAD probe uses a different nonce. (4.1)"The first paragraph of 4.1 (and Section 4: "the NS(DAD) for each IPv6 address of an interface uses a different nonce") describes one nonce per address, stored as "the nonce"; the second paragraph says each probe uses a different nonce. With DupAddrDetectTransmits greater than 1, or in the extended round, a node therefore either reuses one nonce for several probes or must keep several. 4.2 compares with "any stored nonce on the receiving interface" but nothing says which nonces are kept, for how long (a probe can be looped back after the next one was sent), or when they are discarded (after the address becomes assigned, a late looped-back NS(DAD) is no longer for a tentative address). The nonce length is not specified either (RFC 3971 5.3.2 allows any length of at least 6 octets), although Section 4 relies on the collision probability being negligible.ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below
RA-12914.1"If any probe is looped back within RetransTimer milliseconds after having sent DupAddrDetectTransmits NS(DAD) messages, the interface continues with another MAX_MULTICAST_SOLICIT number of NS(DAD) messages"The trigger covers only a loop seen in the RetransTimer interval after the last of the DupAddrDetectTransmits probes; a probe looped back while earlier probes are still being sent (the usual case, a loop returns the first probe within milliseconds) is not covered, and the first paragraph then moves the address to the assigned state because a looped-back probe is dropped (4.2) and is no "DAD failure indication". For the extended round, the text only says probing stops when no probe is looped back; if the loop persists it is not said whether rounds repeat without limit (the address staying tentative and unusable) or whether a looped-back probe in the extended round starts a new round, and the use of MAX_MULTICAST_SOLICIT (an address-resolution constant of RFC 4861 10) rather than DupAddrDetectTransmits is not explained.ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below
RA-12923, 3.2"Two mitigation options are described below that do not require any change to existing implementations. (3) / the device MUST temporarily disable DAD on the interface. (3.2)"Section 3 presents the mitigations as needing no implementation change, yet 3.2 makes an L2-loopback-triggered DAD disable a MUST, its default SHOULD be enabled and it MUST be configurable, which existing implementations do not do. 3.2 also says the device "MUST (re-)enable DAD" when the loop disappears but not whether DAD is then run for the addresses that were configured (and became preferred) while DAD was disabled; without that, an address configured during the loop is never checked. The last paragraph speaks of "Detecting looped back DAD messages using a Layer 2 protocol", although the Layer 2 protocol detects a circuit loopback, not DAD messages.contradictionnone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below
RA-12931.2, 6"DAD-failed state - Duplication Address Detection failure as specified in [RFC4862]. (1.2)""Duplication Address Detection" should be "Duplicate Address Detection". Section 6 has a sentence that does not parse: "Disabling DAD has an obvious security issue before a remote node on the link can issue reflected NS(DAD) messages."editorialnone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below

Proposed erratum RA-1290 (RFC 7527, Section 4, 4.1, 4.2; type: Technical):

Original Text
-------------
   If a node has been configured to use the Enhanced DAD algorithm,
   when sending an NS(DAD) for a tentative or optimistic interface
   address, the sender MUST generate a random nonce associated with
   the interface address, MUST store the nonce internally, and MUST
   include the nonce in the Nonce option included in the NS(DAD).

Corrected Text
--------------
   If a node has been configured to use the Enhanced DAD algorithm,
   when sending an NS(DAD) for a tentative or optimistic interface
   address, the sender MUST generate a new random nonce of at least
   6 octets for each NS(DAD), MUST store the nonces of all NS(DAD)
   sent for that address until the address leaves the tentative or
   optimistic state, and MUST include the nonce in the Nonce option
   included in the NS(DAD).

Notes
-----
   Section 4 and the first paragraph of 4.1 suggest one nonce per
   address; the second paragraph of 4.1 says each probe uses a
   different nonce (single-use nonce, RFC 3971 Section 2). Receivers
   (4.2) match against "any stored nonce".

Proposed erratum RA-1291 (RFC 7527, Section 4.1; type: Technical):

Original Text
-------------
   If any probe is looped back within RetransTimer milliseconds
   after having sent DupAddrDetectTransmits NS(DAD) messages, the
   interface continues with another MAX_MULTICAST_SOLICIT number of
   NS(DAD) messages transmitted RetransTimer milliseconds apart.

Corrected Text
--------------
   If any probe is looped back before RetransTimer milliseconds have
   elapsed after the last of the DupAddrDetectTransmits NS(DAD)
   messages was sent, the interface sends another
   MAX_MULTICAST_SOLICIT NS(DAD) messages transmitted RetransTimer
   milliseconds apart, and repeats this for as long as a probe of
   the previous round is looped back, unless probing is stopped by
   manual intervention.

Notes
-----
   The Abstract's "self-heal after a loopback is placed and removed"
   implies indefinite repetition while the loop persists; the text
   states only the stop condition.

Proposed erratum RA-1292 (RFC 7527, Section 3, 3.2; type: Technical):

Original Text
-------------
   When the protocol detects that a loopback is no longer present
   (or the interface state has changed), the device MUST (re-)enable
   DAD on that interface.

Corrected Text
--------------
   When the protocol detects that a loopback is no longer present
   (or the interface state has changed), the device MUST (re-)enable
   DAD on that interface and MUST perform DAD for each unicast
   address on that interface that was assigned while DAD was
   disabled.

Notes
-----
   Section 3 first sentence would read "Two mitigation options are
   described below that do not require the Enhanced DAD algorithm of
   Section 4."

Proposed erratum RA-1293 (RFC 7527, Section 1.2, 6; type: Editorial):

Original Text
-------------
   DAD-failed state - Duplication Address Detection failure as
   specified in [RFC4862].

Corrected Text
--------------
   DAD-failed state - Duplicate Address Detection failure as
   specified in [RFC4862].

Notes
-----
   Section 6 probably means: "Disabling DAD has an obvious security
   issue: any node on the link can use the router's address without
   being detected."

RA-04214, 4.3, 4.2Section 4 (with its NOTE) makes Hop-by-Hop processing at transit nodes optional and configuration-driven, while Section 4.3 still describes the header as information for "every node".ResolvedRFC 9673 (updates RFC 8200), Sections 5.1 and 5.2: a router that does not process the Hop-by-Hop Options header MUST forward the packet normally and MUST NOT drop it solely because it carries the header; options it does not process are skipped as for action bits 00, and the 01, 10 and 11 actions become 'MAY discard, if so configured'. RFC 9673 itself raises new points (RA-1218 to RA-1221).

RFC 8449: Record Size Limit Extension for TLS

Depth: deep. Errata: none (the RFC has no errata). Status: Proposed Standard. Updates: RFC 6066.

RA-13014, 4.1"A TLS endpoint that receives a record larger than its advertised limit MUST generate a fatal "record_overflow" alert"The limit is defined on plaintext (TLSInnerPlaintext in TLS 1.3, the input to compression and encryption in TLS 1.2), but "receives a record larger than" does not say whether the receiver checks the TLSCiphertext length before decryption (which is what a memory-constrained receiver needs, the stated purpose of the extension) or the plaintext length after decryption. A ciphertext bound is given only for CBC block ciphers (Section 4.1); for AEAD ciphers and for TLS 1.3 the permitted ciphertext expansion for a reduced limit is left to the reader, so a receiver that checks the ciphertext against the advertised value would reject compliant records.ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata
RA-13025, 4"A server that supports the "record_size_limit" extension MUST ignore a "max_fragment_length" that appears in a ClientHello if both extensions appear."The rule covers only the ClientHello containing both. It does not say what a server that supports both does with a resumed or renegotiated handshake in which the client now offers only one of them, nor how a TLS 1.3 client treats a server that answers max_fragment_length in EncryptedExtensions after the client offered both (Section 5 makes "receipt of both" fatal but not receipt of max_fragment_length alone). Section 4 also lets a TLS 1.3 limit be 2^14+1 although RFC 6066 limits max_fragment_length to 2^12, so the two cannot be compared when a client "depends on having a small record size" and sends both (Section 5).ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata

A field section that references only absolute index 0 is then encoded with Required Insert Count 0, i.e. as a section with no dynamic references, which the decoder cannot resolve (2.2.3 makes a reference at or above the declared Required Insert Count a connection error); in general the encoded count is one too small, which 2.2.1 also makes a QPACK_DECOMPRESSION_FAILED error. Set the variables: SND.WND <- SEG.WND"In SYN-SENT, the assignment of SND.WND, SND.WL1 and SND.WL2 appears only in the "Otherwise, enter SYN-RECEIVED" branch (simultaneous open, where the received SYN carries no acceptable ACK, so SND.WL2 <- SEG.ACK has no meaning). The branch that enters ESTABLISHED never sets them, and it continues "at the sixth step" (URG), skipping the ACK step that would otherwise set the window. RFC 1122 4.2.2.20 (c), which this document replaces for TCP, says these variables "must be set" when SYN-SENT enters ESTABLISHED. RA-13043.5, 3.5.3, 3.10.7.3"If the receiving TCP peer is in a non-synchronized state (i.e., SYN-SENT, SYN-RECEIVED), it returns to LISTEN on receiving an acceptable reset."Section 3.5 sends every non-synchronized connection that receives an acceptable RST back to LISTEN. Proposed erratum RA-1303 (RFC 9293, Section 3.10.7.3; type: Technical):

Original Text
-------------
   If SND.UNA > ISS (our SYN has been ACKed), change the connection
   state to ESTABLISHED, form an ACK segment
   <SEQ=SND.NXT><ACK=RCV.NXT><CTL=ACK> and send it. [...] Otherwise,
   enter SYN-RECEIVED, form a SYN,ACK segment
   <SEQ=ISS><ACK=RCV.NXT><CTL=SYN,ACK> and send it.  Set the
   variables: SND.WND <- SEG.WND SND.WL1 <- SEG.SEQ SND.WL2 <-
   SEG.ACK If there are other controls or text in the segment, queue
   them for processing after the ESTABLISHED state has been reached,
   return.

Corrected Text
--------------
   If SND.UNA > ISS (our SYN has been ACKed), change the connection
   state to ESTABLISHED, set the variables: SND.WND <- SEG.WND
   SND.WL1 <- SEG.SEQ SND.WL2 <- SEG.ACK form an ACK segment
   <SEQ=SND.NXT><ACK=RCV.NXT><CTL=ACK> and send it. [...] Otherwise,
   enter SYN-RECEIVED, form a SYN,ACK segment
   <SEQ=ISS><ACK=RCV.NXT><CTL=SYN,ACK> and send it. If there are
   other controls or text in the segment, queue them for processing
   after the ESTABLISHED state has been reached, return.

Notes
-----
   RFC 1122 Section 4.2.2.20 (c) corrected RFC 793 here: "When the
   connection enters ESTABLISHED state, the following variables must
   be set: SND.WND <- SEG.WND, SND.WL1 <- SEG.SEQ, SND.WL2 <-
   SEG.ACK". In the simultaneous-open branch the received SYN has no
   ACK, and the variables are set later by the SYN-RECEIVED ACK
   processing in Section 3.10.7.4 (fifth step), as RFC 1122 4.2.2.20
   (f) requires.

Proposed erratum RA-1304 (RFC 9293, Section 3.5, 3.5.3, 3.10.7.3; type: Technical):

Original Text
-------------
   If the receiving TCP peer is in a non-synchronized state (i.e.,
   SYN-SENT, SYN-RECEIVED), it returns to LISTEN on receiving an
   acceptable reset.

Corrected Text
--------------
   If the receiving TCP peer is in a non-synchronized state (i.e.,
   SYN-SENT, SYN-RECEIVED), then on receiving an acceptable reset it
   returns to LISTEN if it reached SYN-RECEIVED from LISTEN (passive
   OPEN), and otherwise aborts the connection and goes to CLOSED
   (see Section 3.5.3).

Notes
-----
   Sentence carried over from RFC 793 Section 3.4. Figure 5 Note 3
   ("receipt of a RST from any state results in a transition to
   LISTEN or CLOSED") and the event processing agree with Section
   3.5.3.

Proposed erratum RA-1305 (RFC 9293, Section 3.3.2 (Figure 5 Note 3), 3.5.2, 3.10.5, 3.10.7.4; type: Technical):

Original Text
-------------
   Note 3:  A RST can be sent from any state with a corresponding
   transition to TIME-WAIT (see [70] for rationale).

Corrected Text
--------------
   Note 3:  A TCP implementation that sends a RST may enter
   TIME-WAIT instead of CLOSED (see [70] for rationale); the event
   processing in Section 3.10 shows the transition to CLOSED.

Notes
-----
   Section 3.5.2 uses "should" in lower case; the reference [70] is
   a measurement paper, not a specification. Either the event
   processing or Note 3 and Section 3.5.2 need to change so that
   both say the same thing.

Proposed erratum RA-1306 (RFC 9293, Section 3.9.2.2, 3.7.2; type: Technical):

Original Text
-------------
   Hard Errors For ICMP these include Destination Unreachable --
   codes 2-4.

Corrected Text
--------------
   Hard Errors For ICMP these include Destination Unreachable --
   codes 2 and 3; for ICMPv6, Destination Unreachable -- codes 1 and
   4.  Destination Unreachable code 4 (IPv4) and Packet Too Big
   (ICMPv6) are processed by Path MTU Discovery [2] [14] and MUST
   NOT cause the connection to be aborted.

Notes
-----
   RFC 1191 and RFC 8201 are normative references [2] [14]. The
   ICMPv6 classification of soft errors is given, but none for hard
   errors. RFC 5927 Section 7 discusses ICMP-based attacks on PMTUD;
   the classification of code 4 as a connection-aborting error
   predates PMTUD (RFC 1122 4.2.3.9).

If the server does not acknowledge the extension, the client MUST generate a fatal handshake_failure alert"RFC 5746 (3.3, 3.4) lets a client signal secure renegotiation in an initial handshake either with an empty renegotiation_info extension or with the TLS_EMPTY_RENEGOTIATION_INFO_SCSV cipher suite value, and most TLS libraries use the SCSV in initial handshakes. It is not stated whether a configured drop of all Hop-by-Hop packets is conformant (the exception) or forbidden (the MUST NOT), nor whether the MUST NOT applies only to routers that otherwise process the header.contradictionnone: RFC has 1 errata, none on this point
RA-12195.2"it SHOULD behave in the same way specified for an unrecognized Option Type when the action bits are set to "00", and it SHOULD skip the remaining options using the "Hdr Ext Len" field"The sentence tells a router that cannot process one option to skip all remaining options using the header length, while the next sentences say "After skipping an option, the router continues processing the remaining options in the header", which needs the option's own Opt Data Len. The text also says Hdr Ext Len "specifies the length of the Options Header in 8-octet units"; per RFC 8200 Section 4.3 it is the length in 8-octet units not including the first 8 octets. It is not stated whether a destination (host or router) processing a Destination Options header, or a Hop-by-Hop header addressed to it, still MUST discard for 01, 10 and 11, or now only MAY. The 01 text also mixes a MAY with a lower-case "should not".ambiguitynone: RFC has 1 errata, none on this point

RFC 9805: Deprecation of the IPv6 Router Alert Option for New Protocols

Depth: deep. Errata: none (the RFC has no errata). Status: Proposed Standard. Updates: RFC 2711.

RA-14764, Appendix A"Appendix A contains an exhaustive list of protocols that MAY continue to use the IPv6 Router Alert option. (4) / Table 1 contains an exhaustive list of protocols that use the IPv6 Router Alert option. (Appendix A)"Section 4 first permits every protocol "that use[s] the IPv6 Router Alert option" to continue, then calls Appendix A the exhaustive list of such protocols. The list omits users that hold IPv6 Router Alert values or require the option: MLDv1 (RFC 2710, value 0, still referenced by MLDv2 for compatibility, RFC 9777), Active Networks (value 2, RFC 2711), and the base RSVP specifications (RFC 2205, and RFC 3209 for RSVP-TE), the RSVP row citing only aggregation, receiver proxy, VPN and admission priority extensions. Read literally, a protocol absent from the "exhaustive" list (e.g. an MLDv1 implementation) is not among those that "MAY continue", which contradicts the first sentence of Section 4.contradictionnone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below
RA-14776, 4, 5"This document mitigates all security considerations associated with the IPv6 Router Alert option."Section 4 lets every existing protocol keep using the option "even in future versions", and Section 5 says the two widely deployed users (MLDv2 and MRD) still rely on it, with replacements left to future work. Routers therefore still have to inspect and divert Router Alert packets, and the control-plane exposure described in RFC 6398 and in Section 3 is unchanged. Deprecation for new protocols limits future growth of the problem; it does not mitigate the existing considerations, and the section gives implementers no guidance (rate limiting, protocol-of-interest filtering per RFC 6398) for the uses that remain.contradictionnone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below
RA-14787, 4, Appendix A"stating that the registry is closed for allocations / The experimental codepoints in this registry have been changed to "Reserved" / Pragmatic Generic Multicast (PGM) is experimental"Closing the "IPv6 Router Alert Option Values" registry conflicts with Section 4, which allows existing protocols to continue using the option "even in future versions": a future version of an existing protocol that needs a new value (as RSVP aggregation did with values 4-35, RFC 3175) cannot obtain one, and the text does not say whether such versions must reuse existing values. The experimental range being withdrawn was defined by RFC 5350, which is neither cited nor listed as updated. Editorial: Appendix A expands PGM as "Pragmatic Generic Multicast"; RFC 3208 and Table 1 use "Pragmatic General Multicast".ambiguitynone: RFC has no errata; proposed erratum below

Proposed erratum RA-1476 (RFC 9805, Section 4, Appendix A; type: Technical):

Original Text
-------------
   Appendix A contains an exhaustive list of protocols that MAY
   continue to use the IPv6 Router Alert option.

Corrected Text
--------------
   Appendix A lists protocols known to use the IPv6 Router Alert
   option; any protocol that used the option before the publication
   of this document MAY continue to use it.

Notes
-----
   Values 0 (MLD, including MLDv1 [RFC2710]) and 2 (Active Networks
   [RFC2711]) of the IPv6 Router Alert Option Values registry, and
   base RSVP [RFC2205] [RFC3209], are not covered by Table 1. MLDv2
   [RFC9777] still requires interoperation with MLDv1, so the
   omission of MLDv1 matters to implementations.

Proposed erratum RA-1477 (RFC 9805, Section 6, 4, 5; type: Technical):

Original Text
-------------
   This document mitigates all security considerations associated
   with the IPv6 Router Alert option.  These security considerations
   can be found in [RFC2711], [RFC6192], and [RFC6398].

Corrected Text
--------------
   This document does not change the security considerations for
   protocols that continue to use the IPv6 Router Alert option;
   these can be found in [RFC2711], [RFC6192], and [RFC6398], and
   routers that process the option remain subject to them.
   Deprecating the option for new protocols limits the growth of
   these risks over time.

Notes
-----
   Sections 4 and 5 keep the existing uses, so routers continue to
   divert Router Alert packets to the control plane.

Proposed erratum RA-1478 (RFC 9805, Section 7, 4, Appendix A; type: Technical):

Original Text
-------------
   Pragmatic Generic Multicast (PGM) is experimental, and there are
   no known IPv6 implementations.

Corrected Text
--------------
   Pragmatic General Multicast (PGM) is experimental, and there are
   no known IPv6 implementations.

Notes
-----
   The registry's experimental range (65502-65534) was created by
   RFC 5350; the IANA note changes it without that document being
   referenced or updated. The PGM expansion differs between the
   Appendix A text and Table 1.

Proposed erratum RA-1312 (RFC 9846, Section 4.2.2, 4.3.1, E.2, E.5; type: Technical):

Original Text
-------------
   If this extension is not present, servers which are compliant
   with this specification and which also support TLS 1.2 MUST
   negotiate TLS 1.2 or prior as specified in [RFC5246], even if
   ClientHello.legacy_version is 0x0304 or later.  Servers MAY abort
   the handshake upon receiving a ClientHello with legacy_version
   0x0304 or later.

Corrected Text
--------------
   If this extension is not present, servers which are compliant
   with this specification and which also support TLS 1.2 MUST
   negotiate TLS 1.2 as specified in [RFC5246] if
   ClientHello.legacy_version is 0x0303, and otherwise MUST abort
   the handshake with a "protocol_version" alert. If this extension
   is present, the server MUST abort the handshake with a
   "protocol_version" alert if ClientHello.legacy_version is not
   0x0303 (Section 4.2.2).

Notes
-----
   Section 4.2.2 is new relative to RFC 8446 4.1.2. Erratum 9040
   aligned Appendix E.2 with 4.2.2 and E.5 but left 4.3.1 ("even if
   ClientHello.legacy_version is 0x0304 or later", "Servers MAY
   abort"). The corrected text is one possible alignment; the
   working group may prefer to keep the 0x0304 tolerance and relax
   4.2.2
   E.5 instead.

   9043 (4.2.3 random) and 9040 (E.2) address two of the places; the

   To provide an extra margin of security, sending implementations

--------------
   To provide an extra margin of security, sending implementations

"Silently dropped ... and logged" also leaves open whether a counter suffices for "logged" (10 then says "All logging SHOULD be rate limited").ambiguitynone: RFC has 2 errata, none on this point; proposed erratum below
RA-148214, 6, 11.4"if (OCS != 0 and OCS fails) or (OCS == 0 and UDP CS != 0) then deliver the UDP user data but ignore other options (14) / Individual UDP fragments MUST NOT be forwarded to the user. (11.4)"The Section 14 procedure delivers the UDP user data whenever the UDP checksum passes, but a UDP fragment has empty user data; if its OCS fails, or it carries a malformed or duplicated FRAG Option or an unsupported UNSAFE Option, the procedure delivers a zero-length datagram, while 11.4 forbids forwarding fragments and says reassembly failures "SHOULD NOT generate zero-length frames to the user", and Section 6 makes UDP fragments the exception to delivery. Section 14 then notes for UNSAFE Options that "this still results in the delivery of a zero-length UDP packet". Whether an option-aware receiver delivers a zero-length datagram for a fragment it cannot use is therefore read both ways.ambiguitynone: RFC has 2 errata, none on this point
RA-1483Appendix A"NB: The JUNK Option is included for debugging purposes and is not intended to be enabled otherwise. / | UDP OPT MDS | Enable UDP MDS Option |"The JUNK Option (Tables 5-7) is not defined anywhere in the document and has no Kind in Table 1, so its format and whether it is an option in the surplus area are unknown. Table 3 writes some socket option names with spaces ("UDP OPT MDS", "UDP OPT MRDS", "UDP OPT REQ", "UDP OPT RES", "UDP OPT AUTH", "UDP OPT EXP", "UDP OPT UEXP") and others with underscores, and Table 2 names the RES sysctl "udp_opt_resp". The appendix is meant "to encourage consistent naming".editorialnone: RFC has 2 errata, none on this point; proposed erratum below

Proposed erratum RA-1479 (RFC 9868, Section 8, 9; type: Technical):

Original Text
-------------
   These alignment bytes, coupled with OCS as computed over the
   remainder of the surplus area, ensure that the one's complement
   sum of the surplus area is zero.

Corrected Text
--------------
   These alignment bytes, coupled with the OCS as computed in
   Section 9, ensure that the one's complement sum of the surplus
   area (with 16-bit words aligned relative to the start of the IP
   datagram) and of its length is zero. If the computed OCS is zero,
   it is transmitted as all ones (0xFFFF).

Notes
-----
   Section 9 includes the surplus length in the sum; Section 8 omits
   it. Without an all-ones rule, a sender whose computed OCS is zero
   cannot satisfy "The OCS MUST be non-zero when the UDP checksum is
   non-zero".

Proposed erratum RA-1481 (RFC 9868, Section 10, 21, 18; type: Technical):

Original Text
-------------
   This document updates [RFC0768] as follows:

Corrected Text
--------------
   This document updates [RFC0768] as follows: [...] *  A UDP
   datagram whose UDP Length is smaller than 8 or larger than the IP
   transport payload is invalid and MUST be silently dropped
   (Section 10); this applies to all UDP receivers, whether or not
   they support UDP Options.

Notes
-----
   RFC 768 itself gives no receiver rule for an inconsistent Length;
   Section 22 says this document "clarifies the interaction between
   UDP Length and IP Length".

Proposed erratum RA-1483 (RFC 9868, Section Appendix A; type: Editorial):

Original Text
-------------
   | UDP OPT MDS  | Enable UDP MDS Option       |

Corrected Text
--------------
   | UDP_OPT_MDS  | Enable UDP MDS Option       | (likewise
   UDP_OPT_MRDS, UDP_OPT_REQ, UDP_OPT_RES, UDP_OPT_AUTH,
   UDP_OPT_EXP, UDP_OPT_UEXP; and either define the JUNK Option or
   remove Tables 5-7)

Notes
-----
   The appendix exists to encourage consistent naming across
   implementations.
